Above the shield, a <term>crest</term> (the symbol appearing above the helmet or shield) depicts a lion's head. The shield is draped with ornamental <term>mantling</term> (decorative cloth tied to the helmet) tied into bows at the top corners. At the base of the design, a ribbon scroll contains the motto.</image-desc>

<header>¶ Prologue.</header>

### ¶ Preamble of the book.

If it is true that things worthy of memory, because of their profit and utility, should remain perpetual without being entirely put to sleep by the long passage and frailty of fleeting and transitory time, then the sting and stimulus of just reason and genuine cause have summoned and exhorted me—as the guardian of all good and honor—to reintegrate and fully restore this book. For a long time before this modern era, it has been so highly esteemed by all people of spirit that everyone deigned to see it and keep it in the highest corner <note>Literally "the highest nook," meaning the most prominent or honored place in a collection.</note> of their library for the fine maxims, discourses, and natural and moral sayings placed and inserted within. This is the pleasant book of the <term>Romance of the Rose|A famous 13th-century French allegorical poem that explores the art of love and the nature of humanity</term>, which was poetically composed by two noble authors worthy of the estimation of all good sense and laudable knowledge: Master Jean de Meun and Master Guillaume de Lorris.

This present book has previously been quite poorly corrected—through the fault, I believe, of the printers, or perhaps of those who provided the copy <note>original: "le double"; the manuscript used as the source for the typesetter.</note> for printing; for either could be the cause of its inaccuracy. To restore it to a better state and a more useful form for the understanding of readers and listeners—notwithstanding the weakness of my own childish understanding and the unworthiness of my rustic wit <note>A common "humility trope" where the editor downplays their own skill to honor the original work.</note>—I wished to reread this present book from the beginning to the end. I applied myself to this very laborious task and corrected it as best I could, adding references <note>original: "quottations"; these refer to marginal citations of classical or biblical authorities.</note> for the most principal noteworthy points and authorities that were relevant. I did this not merely by my own voluntary choice, as you should understand, but as I have said, at the instigation, prayer, and request of the honorable person Galiot du Pré, a sworn merchant bookseller at the University of Paris, who has recently had it printed after seeing its correction—both from the bad and excessive...

### ¶ Preamble of the book.

If it be true that things worthy of memory for their profit and utility should remain perpetually without being entirely lulled to sleep by too long a season and the instability of fleeting and transitory time/ the sting and stimulus of just reason and unfeigned cause has summoned and exhorted me—as the guardian of all good and honor—to reintegrate and restore to its wholeness the book which, for a long time before this modern season, has been so esteemed by all people of spirit that everyone deigns to see and keep it in the highest corner of their library for the good maxims <note>original: "sentences," referring to moral aphorisms or pithy wisdom</note>, purposes, and natural and moral sayings that are placed and inserted within. This is the pleasant book of the *Romance of the Rose* <note>A famous 13th-century allegorical poem concerning the art of love and courtly society</note>/ which was poetically composed by two noble authors worthy of the esteem of all good sense and laudable knowledge: Master Jean de Meun and Master Guillaume de Lorris. This present book has previously been—through the fault, I believe, of the printers—quite poorly corrected/ or perhaps through the fault of those who provided the manuscript copy <note>original: "double," meaning the duplicate or transcript used as a printer's model</note> for printing: for both can be the cause of its inaccuracy. To restore this matter to a better state and more expedient form for the understanding of readers and listeners—notwithstanding the weakness of my own childish understanding and the unworthiness of my rustic wit—I have desired to reread this present book from the beginning to the end/ a very laborious task in which I have employed myself and corrected it as best I could, adding to it the citations of the most principal notable points and authorities <note>This likely refers to marginal references to the Bible or Classical authors</note> which are relevant. This was not done by my own voluntary consent, as you should understand: but as I have said, at the instigation, prayer, and request of an honorable person, Galiot du Pré <note>A prominent Parisian bookseller and publisher active in the early 16th century</note>, bookseller and merchant sworn to the University of Paris/ who has recently had it printed after having seen its correction/ as much of the bad and too...

<meta>This page continues the editor's preface to the "Romance of the Rose." The previous page established the editor's goal of restoring the text. This page specifically addresses criticisms of the poem's potential for immorality by proposing four layers of allegorical interpretation: Wisdom, Grace, the Virgin Mary, and Eternal Glory.</meta>

¶ Prologue.

ancient language showing its aged origins and beginning, as well as the
imperfect quality of the poetic meters which are nearly all corrupted. And for this reason one
could say—as several have already said—that this book, by speaking in vain of the state of
love, might be the cause of turning minds toward evil and applying them to
dissolute things because of the persuasive subject of **foolish love** <note>original: "fol amour," referring to irrational or purely physical passion</note> contained throughout;
because foolish sensual appetite or sensuality—which nourishes all evil and is the
stepmother of virtue—is the driver of this subject / saving and premise of all honor, I
respond that the intention of the author is not simply and in itself ill-
founded or evil/ for it may well be that the said author did not only
cast his thoughts and imagination upon the literal sense / but rather drew his spirit
toward the allegorical and moral sense, like one saying one thing and meaning another.
I do not wish to affirm what I say as absolute / but it seems to me that he may have done so. And if
that author did not so regulate his meaning, or did not enter beneath the moral covering
penetrating to the marrow of the new mystical sense/ nevertheless one can
interpret it morally and in various ways. I say then, first, that by
the **rose** which is so desired by the lover is understood the state of **wisdom**, rightly
and justly conforming to the rose because of the values, sweetness, and scents within her/
which is very difficult to obtain because of the intervening obstacles, upon which
I do not wish to dwell for the present. And in this manner of interpretation, the rose will be
represented by the **Papal Rose** <note>The Golden Rose, a precious ornament blessed by the Pope on the fourth Sunday of Lent as a symbol of spiritual joy</note> / which is composed of three things / that is to say, of gold / of musk /
and of balsam / for true **wisdom** must be of gold, signifying the honor and reverence that
we owe to God the creator / of musk because of the fidelity and justice that we owe
to our neighbor / and of balsam as for ourselves / insofar as we
must hold our souls dear and precious like pure and precious balsam above all
the things of the world. Secondly, one can understand by the **rose** the state of **grace**,
which is similarly difficult to obtain / not on the part of Him who gives it /
for that is God the almighty / but on the part of the sinner who is always
hindered and distanced from the granter of that grace. This kind of spiritual rose,
so fragrant and sweet-smelling, we can represent by the roses through the power of which
the great **Apuleius** returned to his first form, according to what is written in the book of ***The Golden Ass*** <note>A famous Latin novel by Lucius Apuleius where the protagonist is turned into a donkey and eventually restored to human form by eating roses</note>
when he found the garland of rose flowers hanging from the sistrum of **Ceres**,
goddess of grain / for just as the said Apuleius—who had been transformed into
an ass—found again his first figure of a sensible and rational man / similarly the human
sinner, made and converted into a brute beast by irrational likeness, resumes
his first state of innocence by the grace of God which is conferred upon him when he finds
the garland or crown of roses / that is to say, the state of **penitence** hanging from
the sweet sistrum of Ceres / that is, from the sweetness of divine mercy. Thirdly, we
can understand by the **rose** the glorious **Virgin Mary** for her goodness, sweetness,
and perfections of grace / of which I remain silent for the present. And know that this
virginal rose is not easy for heretics to have / even if it were only **Evil Tongue** <note>original: "malle bouche," a character from the poem representing slander or gossip</note> who prevents them from approaching her goodness / for they have spoken ill of her /
wanting to stain and darken her maternal honor / by saying that it is not necessary to greet her
and call her the mother of pity and mercy. She is the **white rose** that we will find
planted in **Jericho**, as the wise man says / *like a rose plantation in Jericho* <note>original Latin: "quasi plantatio rose in Hierico," quoting Sirach 24:14 in the Vulgate</note>. Fourthly,
we can understand by the **rose** the sovereign infinite good and eternal glory

<summary>The editor defends the "Romance of the Rose" against accusations of promoting immorality by offering four allegorical interpretations: Wisdom, Grace, the Virgin Mary, and Eternal Glory. He uses the examples of the Papal Rose and Apuleius's "The Golden Ass" to illustrate these spiritual meanings.</summary>

### ¶ Prologue.

...blessedness which, as true lovers of its sweetness and perpetual pleasantness, we may obtain by avoiding the vices that hinder us / and by having the help of the virtues that will lead us into the orchard of infinite density / even to the rosebush of all good and glory, which is the beatific vision of the essence of God. This rosebush can be symbolized not by the roses of Paestum <note>original: "pestum"; an ancient city in Italy famous for roses that bloomed twice a year</note> in Italy which bloom twice a year / for that is but seldom / but by the rose that the noble Ethiopian Queen of Sheba presented to the wise King Solomon / as we read in the book of his problems and the questions she asked him to test his wisdom / at which she was so marveled that her senses failed her / according to what is written in the Book of Kings. She took two roses, one of which came naturally from the tree and the other was produced by imitation / for she had made it sophistically and by art to closely resemble the natural rose, so subtly was it crafted. "King," she said, "two roses are presented here before your peaceful majesty / of which one is truly natural / but the other is not. Therefore tell me, lord, which is the natural rose; point it out to me with your finger." Solomon, seeing this, had some honeybees <note>original: "mouches a miel," literally "honey flies"</note> brought, thinking and considering through the science he had of all natural things that the said bees, according to their nature, would go immediately to the natural rose and not to the sophisticated one / for such pleasant and honey-making heavenly little birds <note>The author poetically refers to bees as "oyseletz celestes."</note> desire and crave sweet flowers above all things. By this means, he showed the queen the true rose, discerning it from the other which was made of scents imitating nature.

This natural rose can therefore signify the infinite good and true celestial glory, which is in no way sophisticated or deceptive like the glory of the present world which deceives us insofar as we believe it to be true / but it is not. Thus, for whoever would wish to interpret the <term>Romance of the Rose</term> <note>original: "Rommant de la rose"</note> in this way / I say that he would find great benefit, profit, and utility hidden beneath the bark of the text, which is not to be despised / for there is a double gain: recreation of the spirit and delectable pleasure regarding the literal sense / and utility regarding the moral understanding. Fables are made and invented to be explained in a mystical sense / therefore one must not condemn them. If the great eagle of whom Ezekiel spoke when he said: "A great eagle with large wings, full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar" <note>original: "Aquila grandis magnarum alarum plena plumis et varietate / venit ad libanum et tulit medullam cedry." (Ezekiel 17:3)</note>. I say that if that eagle, who had spread his winged plumage so wide, had only stopped upon the bark of the cedar when he flew to Mount Lebanon, he would not have found the marrow of the tree / but would have returned in vain and lost his flight. Similarly, if we do not dig deeper than the bark of the literal sense, we would have nothing but the pleasure of fables and stories without obtaining the singular profit of the <term>spiritual</term> <note>original: "neupmatique," derived from the Greek *pneuma*, meaning spirit or breath</note> marrow / that is to say, that which comes by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit regarding moral understanding.

Even if one thought of nothing but the literal sense / there is still great profit for the doctrines and various sciences contained within / for despite the fact that the principal subject is a course of love / nevertheless it is entirely preserved with good incidents that are included and cited therein, providing many good disciplines. Natural and moral philosophers can learn there / as can theologians / astrologers / geometers / <term>alchemists</term> <note>original: "archimistres"</note> / makers of mirrors / painters, and other people born under the constellation and influence of good stars having their aspect upon the ingenious / and others who desire to know all manners of arts and sciences.

->¶ Here ends the prologue.<-

<summary>The author concludes the prologue by arguing that the "Rose" symbolizes divine glory and that the poem, like a biblical parable, contains a "spiritual marrow" of scientific and moral wisdom beneath its literal story of love.</summary>

# ¶ Prologue.

...ancient language, smelling of its long-standing beginning and origin of speech, as well as the imperfect quantity of the meters, which are almost all corrupted. And for this reason, one could say, as several have already said, that this book, speaking in vain of the state of love, could be the cause of turning understandings to evil and applying them to dissolute things because of the persuasive matter of only love contained throughout it; for the reason that only sensual appetite, or sensuality—the nurse of all evil and stepmother of virtue—is the driver of this subject. Saving all honor and with due respect, I respond that the author's intention is not simply and of itself ill-founded or evil; for it may well be that the said author did not cast his thought and imagination only upon the literal sense, but rather drew his spirit toward the allegorical and moral sense, as one saying and meaning the other. I do not wish to affirm what I say, but it seems to me that he may have done so. And if this author did not have his meaning so regulated and did not enter beneath the moral covering to penetrate to the marrow of the new mystical sense, nonetheless one can explain it morally and in various ways. I say then, first, that by the rose which is so desired by the lover, is understood the state of <term>sapience</term> <note>sapience: a traditional term for divine or higher wisdom</note>, which is well and justly conformed to the rose for the values, sweetness, and scents that are in it; which is very difficult to obtain because of the obstacles placed in the way, upon which I do not wish to dwell for the present. And in this way of explaining, the rose will be figured by the papal rose, which is composed of three things: namely gold, musk, and balm; for true wisdom must be of gold, signifying the honor and reverence that we owe to God the Creator; of musk, because of the fidelity and justice that we must have toward our neighbor; and of balm as for ourselves, insofar as we must hold our souls dear and precious like pure balm, more cherished than all things in the world. Secondly, one can understand by the rose the state of grace, which similarly is difficult to obtain—not on the part of He who gives it, for that is God the Almighty, but on the part of the sinner who is always hindered and distanced from the giver <note>original: "collateur"</note> of this grace. This kind of spiritual rose, breathing and reflecting so well, we can represent by the roses through whose virtue the great Apuleius <note>Apuleius: author of the 2nd-century Roman novel "The Golden Ass"</note> returned to his first form, according to what is written in the book of the *Golden Ass* when he had found the wreath of rosebuds hanging from the <term>sistrum</term> <note>sistrum: a musical rattle or percussion instrument used in ancient religious rites</note> of Ceres, goddess of the grains; for just as the said Apuleius, who had been transformed into a donkey, recovered his first figure of a sensible and rational man, similarly the human sinner, made and converted into a brute beast by irrational likeness, retakes his first state of innocence by the grace of God which is conferred upon him when he finds the wreath or crown of roses—that is to say, the state of penance hanging from the sweet sistrum of Ceres—that is, the sweetness of divine mercy. ¶ Thirdly, we can understand by the rose the glorious Virgin Mary for her goodness, sweetness, and perfections of grace, of which I am silent for the present. And know that this virginal rose is not easy for heretics to obtain; if only there were not the "Evil Mouth" <note>original: "malle bouche"; a personified character in the Romance of the Rose representing Slander or Gossip</note> which prevents them from approaching her goodness; for they have spoken ill of her, wishing to stain and blacken her maternal honor by saying that one must not greet her and call her Mother of Pity and Mercy. This is the white rose that we will find planted in Jericho, as the wise man says: "like a rose plantation in Jericho" <note>original Latin: "quasi plantatio rose in Hierico"; a reference to Ecclesiasticus 24:14</note>. Fourthly, we can by the rose understand the infinite sovereign good and eternal glory.

<summary>The author provides an allegorical defense of the Romance of the Rose, arguing that the "Rose" symbolizes Wisdom (Sapience), Divine Grace, the Virgin Mary, and Eternal Glory rather than mere carnal love.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the prologue's defense of the "Romance of the Rose." The previous page suggested the "Rose" could represent Wisdom; here, the author expands this to include the "Beatific Vision" and argues that the poem contains deep scientific and moral truths hidden beneath its literal narrative of love.</meta>

->¶ Prologue.<-

...blessedness which we, as true lovers of its sweetness and perpetual pleasantness, can obtain by avoiding the vices that hinder us, and by seeking the help of the virtues that will introduce us to the orchard of infinite joy—even to the rosebush of all good and glory, which is the beatific vision <note>The "beatific vision" is a theological term for the direct perception of God in heaven.</note> of the essence of God. This rosebush can be symbolized, not by the roses of Paestum in Italy which bloom twice a year—for that is but a rare occurrence—but by the rose that the noble Ethiopian Queen of Sheba presented to the wise King Solomon, as we read in the book of his problems and the questions she asked him to test his wisdom. She was so marveled by him that her spirit failed within her, as it is written in the Book of Kings. She brought two roses, one of which came from a tree naturally, and the other was produced by imitation; for she had made it <term>sophistically</term> <note>sophistically: here meaning an artificial imitation created with clever human skill rather than nature</note> and with such art that it closely resembled the natural rose, so subtly was it crafted. "King," she said to him, "two roses are presented before your peaceful majesty; one is truly natural, but the other is not. Therefore, tell me, sire, which is the natural rose? Point it out to me with your finger." Solomon, seeing this, had several honeybees brought to him, thinking and considering through the science he possessed of all natural things that the said bees, according to their nature, would fly immediately to the natural rose and not to the artificial one; for such pleasant and honey-making heavenly little birds desire and seek sweet flowers above all things. Thus, he showed the queen the true rose, discerning it from the other which was made of scents counterfeiting nature. 

That natural rose can thus signify the infinite good and true celestial glory, which is in no way artificial or deceptive like the glory of this present world, which deceives us in that we believe it to be true, but it is not. Therefore, if someone wished to interpret the *Romance of the Rose* in this way, I say they would find great benefit, profit, and utility hidden beneath the bark of the text, which is not to be despised. For there is a double gain: recreation of the spirit and delectable pleasure in the literal sense, and utility in the moral understanding. Fables are made and invented to be explained in a <term>mystical sense</term> <note>mystical sense: a deeper, symbolic meaning beyond the surface level of a story</note>; therefore, one must not condemn them. If the great eagle of whom Ezekiel spoke when he said: "A great eagle with great wings, full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar," <note>original: "Aquila grandis magnarum alarum plena plumis et varietate venit ad libanum et tulit medulam cedri." (Ezekiel 17:3)</note> I say that if that eagle, who had spread his flying plumage so wide, had only stopped at the bark of the cedar when he flew to Mount Lebanon, he would never have found the marrow of the tree, but would have returned in vain and wasted his flight. Similarly, if we do not dig deeper than the bark of the literal sense, you would have nothing but the pleasure of fables and stories, without obtaining the singular profit of the <term>pneumatic marrow</term> <note>pneumatic marrow: a spiritual or "breath-inspired" truth (from the Greek *pneuma*), referring here to insights granted by the Holy Spirit</note>—that is to say, that which comes by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit regarding moral understanding. 

Even if one thought of nothing but the literal sense, there is still great profit for the doctrines and various sciences contained within; for although the principal theme is a course of love, it is nonetheless entirely steeped in good incidents that are included and cited, giving rise to many fine disciplines. Natural and moral philosophers can learn there; so too can theologians, astrologers, geometers, alchemists, mirror-makers, painters, and other people born under the constellation and influence of good stars, whose influence looks upon ingenious minds and others who desire to know all manners of arts and sciences.

->¶ Thus ends the prologue.<-

<summary>The author concludes the prologue by comparing the "Rose" to divine glory and the Queen of Sheba's test of Solomon, arguing that readers must look past the "bark" of the literal text to find spiritual "marrow." He asserts that the poem is a treasury of various sciences and arts, useful to both theologians and craftsmen.</summary>

¶ A brief summary of the matters contained in the present book.

¶ First, the dream of the author <note>original: "lacteur" - a common Middle French variant for "l'auteur" (the author)</note>.
¶ The description of the garden of Love.
¶ Description of Hatred, Felony, Villainy, Covetousness, Avarice, Envy, Sorrow, Old Age, Hypocrisy <note>original: "papelardie"</note>, and Poverty. Folios one, two, three, and four.
¶ How Idleness opens the door of the garden of Love to the Lover. Folio 4.
¶ Of Mirth <note>original: "deduit"</note> and his carole <note>A carole was a popular medieval circle dance accompanied by singing.</note>. Folio 5.
¶ How the God of Love spies on the Lover in the garden, in order to wound him with his arrows. Folio 9.
¶ How Narcissus gazes at himself in the fountain where he sighed so much that he died. Folio 10.
¶ How the Lover enters the garden following the [rose]bud, after which he had much difficulty. Folio 11.
¶ How the God of Love took the Lover in the garden, who surrendered to him. Folio 12.
¶ How the Lover did homage to the God of Love. Folio 13.
¶ How Love locked the heart of the Lover. Folio 13.
¶ The rules that the God of Love gave to the Lover. Folio 13.
¶ How Fair Welcome <note>original: "bel accueil"</note> offers the Lover a chance to see the roses he so desires. Folio 18.
¶ How Danger <term>Danger</term> <note>In the "Romance of the Rose," Danger is an allegorical character representing the lady's resistance, pride, or the refusal of her favor.</note> cast the Lover out from the company of Fair Welcome. Folio 18.
¶ How Reason teaches the Lover not to follow Fair Welcome. Folio 19.
¶ The Lover's response to Reason. Folio 19.
¶ How the Lover made his complaint to Friend <note>original: "amys"</note>. Folio 20.
¶ How the Lover begs mercy from Danger. Folio 20.
¶ How Pity and Generosity speak to Danger on behalf of the Lover. Folio 21.
¶ How Fair Welcome led the Lover to the orchard to see the rose. Folio 21.
¶ How the torch of Venus helped the Lover to kiss the rose. Folio 22.
¶ How Foul Mouth <note>original: "malle bouche"</note>, through Jealousy, caused Fair Welcome to be scolded. Folio 22.
¶ How Shame and Fear came to Danger out of concern to remind him to guard the orchard well. Folio 23.
¶ How Jealousy had a tower built to imprison Fair Welcome. Folio 24.
¶ How Reason wishes to give counsel to the idle. Folio 27.
¶ How the needy man asks his friend to help him, who puts his wealth into his hands. Folio 30.
¶ Of the judgment that Appius <note>A reference to the Roman story of Appius Claudius and Virginia, illustrating corruption and injustice.</note> gave regarding the daughter of Virginius, and of the execution. Folio 35.
¶ How Reason shows the Lover the Wheel of Fortune, saying that he should not fear it. Folio 37.
¶ How the cruel and inhuman Emperor Nero had his mother cut open to see the place from which he had come. Folio 38.
¶ How Nero put his master Seneca to death. Folio 39.
¶ Of the cruel death of Nero. Folio 40.
¶ How Phanie predicted to her father that he would be hanged. Folio 40.
¶ The response of Croesus to his daughter. Folio 41.
¶ How Reason left the Lover in great sorrow, who turned toward Friend for help. Folio 45.

# ¶ The Romance of the Rose
## Wherein the whole Art of Love is enclosed

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration framed by a double-line border. It depicts a man, presumably the dreamer, lying in a bed with a high, draped canopy. He is shown from the waist up, resting his head on a pillow, suggesting the commencement of the dream sequence described in the text. The room is simply rendered with vertical wood paneling and a small window in the background.</image-desc>

<margin>
Macrobius on the Dream of Scipio.
</margin>
Many people go about saying that dreams
Are but fables and lies;
But one can dream such a dream
Which nonetheless is not deceitful,
But rather becomes quite apparent afterward.
If I need to find a guarantee for this,
I have Macrobius, a very worthy author <note>original: "acteur," which in the Middle Ages referred to an authoritative source or writer.</note>
Who does not consider dreaming to be a fable;
Instead, he wrote of the Vision
Which happened to Scipio.
Whoever thinks or whoever says
That it is a piece of foolishness <note>original: "musardie," meaning idle distraction or nonsense.</note>
To believe that any dream comes true,
Let them hold me for a fool if they wish;
For as for me, I have confidence
That a dream is a sign
Of the joys and the troubles of people,
The reason being that one dreams by night
Of many things covertly
That one afterward sees openly.

Now, in the twentieth year of my age,
At the point when Love takes his toll <term>takes his toll</term> <note>original: "prent le peage," a metaphor comparing the trials of young lovers to a traveler paying a road tax.</note>
From young people, I went to lie down
One night as I was accustomed,
And indeed, it suited me to sleep.
While sleeping, a dream occurred to me
Which was very beautiful to consider,
As you shall hear described;
For in considering it, it pleased me much,
And never did anything happen in the dream
That did not eventually come to pass
Exactly as the dream recounted.
¶ Which I wish to set down in rhyme

To lead you more toward pleasure.
Love begs and commands me to do so.
And if by chance someone asks
What I wish this romance
To be called, know, lovers,
That it is the Romance of the Rose,
In which the Art of Love is all enclosed.
The matter is beautiful and worthy of praise;
God grant that it be agreeable
To her for whom I have undertaken it:
She is a lady of high value
Who is so worthy of being loved
That she ought to be called the Rose.

It seemed to me at that time—
Truly five years and six months ago—
That I was dreaming in the month of May,
In that amorous time without distress,
In the time when everything laughs and rejoices,
When there is no bush nor hedge
That does not wish to adorn itself in May
And cover itself with new leaves.
The woods recover their greenery,
Which are dry as long as winter lasts;
The earth itself feels proud
Because of the dew that descends,
And forgets the poverty
In which it has been all winter;
In effect, it finds itself so gay
That it wishes to have a new robe <note>original: "robe neufue," a poetic personification of the spring landscape.</note>.
<margin>
Description of summertime.
</margin>
And it knows how to make such an elegant robe,
For it has many pairs of colors;
Of herbs and flowers, red and blue <note>original: "perses," a blue-gray or indigo color.</note>,
And of many diverse colors
Is the robe I describe,
By which the earth prizes itself more.
The little birds who were silent
While they had the great cold,
Because of the harsh, harmful weather,
Are so at ease in the peaceful time
Of May, that they show by singing
That in their hearts there is so much joy
<margin>
Note on the nightingale.
</margin>
That they must sing by force.
The nightingale then exerts itself
To sing, making a sweet sound <note>original: "noyse," which in Old French could mean a pleasant sound or melody, not just "noise."</note>

<header>The Romance of the Rose.</header>

Then the parrot and the lark
Wake and deck themselves out;
So it suits young people to intend
To be gay and amorous
Because of the beautiful, vigorous spring.
Hard is the heart that does not love with true love
When it hears singing upon the branch
The birds' graceful songs
<margin>☞</margin> In that delicious time
When everything rejoices in loving.
One night as I was dreaming,
It seemed to me, sleeping soundly,
That it was truly morning;
I rose quickly from my bed,
Dressed myself and washed my hands.
I pulled a silver needle
From a dainty and pretty needle-case,
And wanting to thread the needle,
I had a desire to go out of town
To hear the sounds of the birds
Who were singing among the bushes.
In that new season,
Sewing my sleeves with a loose stitch <term>loose stitch</term> <note>original: "vuidelle," a decorative or temporary stitch used to fasten sleeves, which were often detachable in medieval fashion.</note>,
I went off all alone, enjoying myself,
And listening to the little birds
Who were striving to sing well
Through the gardens that were flowering,
Pretty and gay, full of joy.
I made my way toward a river
That I heard roaring nearby,
For I never saw a more beautiful place
To enjoy myself than on this river.
From a little hill just behind there,
The water descended, running swiftly,
Fresh, noisy, and as cold
As a well or a fountain;
It was not as deep as the Seine,
But it was more spread out.
Never had I seen or heard of
Such water as flowed there,
Wherefore my eye could not get enough
Of looking at the pleasant place.
<margin>☞</margin> In this clear and gleaming water
I then washed my face;
I saw well-covered and paved
The whole bottom of the water with gravel,
And the great and beautiful meadow
Stretched at the foot of this hill.
Clear, serene, and beautiful was
The morning, and temperate.
Then I went through the meadow,
Wandering all down the valley,
Skirting the beautiful bank.
When I had gone a little further,
I saw an orchard, long and wide,
Enclosed by a high wall, richly
Carved on the outside
With many rich engravings;
The images and the paintings
On the wall I gazed at everywhere,
Wherefore I will gladly tell you
Their form and appearance,
Just as I have remembrance of them.

### Hate.

<margin>Description of Hate</margin>
In the middle, Hate was positioned,
Who, through false reports and bitterness <note>original: "ypre," likely a variation of "aspre," meaning harsh or sharp.</note>,
Indeed seemed to be a stirrer
Of quarrels and a brawler as well;
And this image truly resembled
A woman of very evil spirit.
She was not well-adorned in her dress;
Her face was all wrinkled,
Her nose wide, and her eye deep-set.
She was withered and haggard,
And about her head was wrapped
Hideously a towel
Of a very ugly and base shape.

The other image after Felony
Was named Villainy;
She sat near Hatred on the right,
And was nearly of the same being
As the two [others], and of such manufacture,
She truly seemed a false creature,
Slanderous and too bold,
Like an outrageous woman.
In short, he well knew how to paint and portray,
He who knew how to make such an image,
For she truly seemed a vile thing,
Full of spite and base matters,
And a woman who knew very little
How to honor what she should <note>Villainy here represents the opposite of "courtesy"; it is the lack of manners, nobility, and social grace.</note>.

->¶ Covetousness.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting the personification of Covetousness (Couvoitise). A woman inside a room, with a window showing a diamond-pane lattice, reaches into a large wooden chest filled with coins or treasures.</image-desc>

<margin>Description of Covetousness.</margin>

Afterward, Covetousness was painted;
She is the one who entices people
To take and to give nothing,
And to bring in great treasures.
She is the one who makes Usury <term>Usury</term> <note>original: "Usure," the practice of lending money at interest, which was condemned as a sin by the medieval Church.</note>
Lend because of the great burning desire
To have, to conquer, and to assemble.
She is the one who summons to steal
The thieves full of wretched sorrow;
It is a great sin, but it is a great grief
In the end when they must be hanged.
She is the one who makes one take from another—
I mean to take without buying—
Who makes one cheat and pick locks.
She is the one who makes all the deceivers
And the false pleaders <term>pleaders</term> <note>original: "plaidoyeurs," legal advocates or lawyers.</note>
Who many times by their cunning
Take away from servants and maidens
Their rights and their due rents.
<margin>The hands of Covetousness are hooked.</margin>
Curved, short, and very hooked
Were the hands of this image;
It is well painted, for she always rages,
Covetousness, to take from others;
Covetousness knows not how to understand
Anything but hooking everything from others;
To Covetousness, the property of others is too dear.

She appeared so very languid...

# The Romance of the Rose.

<margin>On the flight of time.</margin>
So secretly it seems to us
That "now" is but a single point,
Yet it never stops there at all,
But never ceases passing on,
Swifter than you could ever think
What time it is at this moment;
For before your very thought
Were finished—if you think on it well—
Three moments would have already passed.
☞ Time, which cannot linger,
But goes forever without returning,
Like water that flows all away
And not a drop comes back upstream;
Time, against which nothing lasts,
Neither iron nor anything however hard,
For time wastes and eats everything;
Time, which changes all things,
Which makes all grow and all die,
And all things wear out and rot away.

<margin>Time consumes everything.</margin>
Time, which ages our fathers,
Which ages pears and princes <note>original: "poyres et prosperes," a wordplay likely referring to both the fruit and those in prosperous states/people.</note>,
And by which we shall all grow old,
Or else perish young by death;
Time, by which shall fail
The sea, the land, and those who have aged;
She of whom I speak was of such a sort
That she seemed less alive than dead.

<margin>All things return to their first nature.</margin>
To help herself she had no more power,
But was returning to infancy,
For she had a weak body and brain
Like a newborn child.
Nonetheless, as I perceive,
She was wise and of great sense
When she was in her rightful age;
But she was no longer so wise,
But was doting; and iron-shod <note>original: "enferree," likely meaning she is heavily burdened or restricted by her age.</note>
She was in a furred cloak
With which she had—as I recall—
Muffled and clothed her body
In order to be more warm;
Otherwise she would have died of cold.
☞ For always subject to the cold
Are old people; it is their nature.

->¶ Papelardie <note>Papelardie is a medieval personification of hypocrisy or false piety, specifically someone who makes a public show of devotion while remaining worldly or wicked at heart.</note>.<-

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicts a woman (Papelardie) in an interior setting, kneeling in prayer before a reading desk or altar with an open book. In the background, there is a bed and a storage chest. The scene illustrates her outward show of piety.</image-desc>

<margin>The description of Papelardie.</margin>
Another image was inscribed after,
Who truly seemed to be a hypocrite;
She is called Papelardie.
She is the one who in secret,
When one cannot be on guard,
Delays not in doing any evil;
And she puts on a meek act outside,
Having a pale and pitiful face
Like a simple creature;
But there is no wicked venture
That she does not think of in her heart.
Much did the image resemble her,
Painted and portrayed in her likeness,
Which was of simple countenance;
She was muffled and clothed
Just like a woman who has taken vows <note>original: "femme rendue," referring to a lay sister or a woman who has retired to a religious life.</note>.
In her hand she held a psalter,
And know that she took great pains
To make feigned prayers to God,
And to call upon the saints, male and female.
She was not cheerful, but quite wretched,
And by appearance very intent

<margin>The fiction of Papelardie.</margin>
Wholly upon doing good works.
She also wore a hairshirt
For fear that she might grow fat,
And from fasting she was so weary
That she had a pale and deathly color.
To her and to those like her, the door
Of heaven is closed without mercy;
For such people make themselves
Thin—so says the Gospel—
To have praise throughout the town.

<margin>Notable point</margin>
And for a bit of vain glory,
Which leads them away from God.

# leaf .iiii.

<margin>The description of poverty.</margin>
**P**overty was painted there last of all;
she would not have had a single penny
even if she were about to hang herself,
no matter how well she might sell her robe.
She was as bare as a worm,
and if it had turned just a little toward winter,
I believe she would have died of the cold.
She had an old, narrow sack
all full of patches and filth,
and for all her robes and coats
she had nothing else to wrap herself in.
She had plenty of time to tremble,
for she was set a little apart from the people;
and like a dog in a corner,
she hid and crouched there.
<margin>Note.</margin>
For poverty, wherever it may be,
is always shameful and despised.
May the hour be cursed
when a poor man was ever conceived;
he will never be welcomed among people,
nor well-clothed, nor well-shod,
nor loved, nor cherished, nor supported.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration within a square decorative border. It depicts a scholar or author, dressed in a long robe and a soft cap, seated at a slanted writing desk. <margin>Description of the place of the images mentioned above.</margin>
**T**he images I have observed,
as I have described them to you,
were painted in gold and azure
everywhere upon the wall.
The wall was high and perfectly square;
it enclosed and barred the way
to a beautiful Orchard <note>original: "Verger," referring to the Garden of Deduit or Pleasure, a central setting in the poem.</note> instead of a hedge.
It was so well-situated, to be brief,
that one could not describe it rightly.
To whoever would lead me inside,
either by ladder or by steps,
I would have been most grateful;
for never was a man led
to such joy or such delight <note>original: "deduict," a term implying pleasure, diversion, or the name of the garden's owner.</note>

as to that of this Orchard.
This beautiful place to house birds
was neither disdainful nor stingy;
<margin>Description of the Orchard <note>original: "Berger," likely a printer's error for "Verger" (Orchard).</note>.</margin>
indeed, no place was ever so rich
in trees and singing birdlings,
for among the sweet-smelling bushes
there were three times more than in all of France.
And so beautiful was the harmony
of their music to listen to,
that it could take away all grief.
As for me, I rejoiced so greatly
when I heard them sing so well,
that I would not have taken a hundred pounds
to miss the passage through the books <note>original: "passaiges de liures," perhaps referring to the written accounts of such places or the physical gates.</note>
so as to enter there, and not miss
<margin>The delight of the little birds.</margin>
the assembly—may God bless it—
of the birds who were within,
who sang with gay courage
the dances and notes of love,
pleasing, courtly, and sweet.

**W**hen I heard these birds singing,
<note>A manicule (pointing hand) in the margin points to the following line</note>
I began to wonder greatly
by what art or by what device
I might enter the garden;
but I could not clearly see
where I might find an entrance.
And know that I did not know
if there were any opening or path,
nor any place by which one might enter.
And there was no man there
to show it to me, for I was alone,
and I sighed many a sigh of distress,
until at last I remembered
that it was impossible
that such a beautiful Orchard had no door,
nor ladder, nor some opening.
<note>A manicule (pointing hand) in the margin points to the following line</note>
Then I went at a great pace,
circling the perimeter
and the great circuit of the square wall,
until I found a door, well-closed and barred,
very small and narrow;
and there was no other way in.
So I began to knock there,
without seeking any other entrance.

### ¶ How Idleness opened the door to the Lover.

<margin>Idleness opens the garden to the Lover.</margin>
I knocked and pushed there quite a bit,

The small wicket door, made of aspen,
moved; then a maiden,
who was quite noble and beautiful,

a shining forehead, and arched eyebrows.
There was a wide space between her eyes, and her feet were small.

<margin>Description of beauty regarding the gifts of nature.</margin>
Her breasts were firm and naturally white,
her nose well-shaped and straight;
she had piercing eyes like a falcon,
casting sidelong glances.
Her face was white and rosy,
her breath sweet and fragrant,
her mouth small and full,
with a dimple in her chin.
Her shoulders were beautifully shaped,
and her neck was of good proportion,
without any blemish or spot.
In short, I know of no woman in this world
who possessed such a beautiful neck;
it seemed polished and smooth to the touch,
and her throat was as white
as snow upon a branch
when it has freshly fallen.
Her body was straight, noble, and slender;
one would never need to seek
a more beautiful woman's body on this earth.

<margin>Description of beauty through artifice.</margin>
She wore a crown of goldsmith’s work,
finely made, elegant, and beautiful,
and more rich, to value it truly,
than I would know how to describe.
Upon this crown of goldsmithery,
she wore a wreath of flowering roses,
and in her hand she held a mirror.
She had her hair tightly braided
with a silk cord quite stylishly.
She laced her sleeves in two places,
and to preserve her white hands
from the tanning of the sun, she wore a glove on each.
Her coat was of a green from Ghent <note>Ghent, in Flanders, was world-famous during the Middle Ages for its high-quality wool textiles.</note>,
with embroidery all around;
and it well appeared by her attire
that she set herself little to work.
For when she was well-combed,
well-dressed, and well-adorned,
her day's work was done.
She lived such a good life
that she had no care nor worry
for anything at all, except only
to dress herself nobly.

<margin>The entrance of the Lover into the Garden of Love.</margin>
¶ When the beautiful one, thus dressed,
had opened the entrance of the orchard to me,
I thanked her humbly,
and then I asked her
what her name was, and who she was.
She was not resistant toward me,

<margin>The response of Lady Idleness to the Lover.</margin>
nor disdainful in answering.
"I am called Idleness,"
she said, "by everyone who knows me.
I am a rich and powerful woman,
and I have a very good time of one thing:
for I attend to nothing in the world
except to play and enjoy myself,
and to comb and braid my hair.
I am an intimate companion, joyful and elegant,

<margin>Mirth, lord of the Garden of Love.</margin>
and I am always in the company of Mirth <note>original: "Deduict." Mirth or Pleasure is the personification of courtly entertainment and the owner of the garden.</note>.
It is he who owns this garden,
who had these trees brought here
from the land of Alexandria
and had them planted throughout the garden.
Then, when each tree was grown,
Mirth—who is never weary—
had this high wall built all around,
and had the images painted on the outside."

### ¶ How the Lover speaks to Idleness.

<image-desc>Decorative initial Q containing an illustration of a woman (Idleness) holding a large key and opening a door for a man (The Lover) to enter a walled garden.</image-desc>
When Idleness <note>original: "Oyseuse"</note> finished her account,
And I had listened well to her story,
I said to her then: "Lady Idleness,
Believe, without being doubtful,
Since now Pleasure and his people
Are here, so handsome and noble,
I will do so much that the assembly
Will not be hidden from me,
And I shall see it before it is night;
If my person does not bother you,
I must see it; it is my will,
For I could not value myself more than by doing so."
<margin>The Lover has entered the garden of love.</margin>
Then I entered the garden, all green,
Through the door that Idleness opened for me;
And when I saw the inside,
I was so ravished with joy
That in all truth I thought I had
Come into an earthly paradise.
So beautiful was this wooded place
That it truly seemed like a divine work,
For as it seemed to me in fact,

In no paradise is it
So good to be as it was
In the Orchard <note>original: "Verger"</note> which pleased me so much.
<margin>The description of the birds in the garden of love.</margin>
There were enough singing birds
Gathered throughout the garden:
In one place there were starlings,
In another, mallards and sparrows,
Finches, plovers, blackbirds, and titmice,
Who did not seem like birds, but angels.
In short, no man ever saw so many;
There was the chattering jay,
The greenfinch was rejoicing there,
The turtle-dove was moaning there,
And the linnet was pouring forth
The song that nature taught it.
In another place, well gathered,
Were the larks, who were
Weary of singing in competition;
For the nightingales and thrushes
Began to sing so loudly
That they came to surpass them.
Elsewhere also are parrots,
Unequal in song and plumage,
Who through these green woods where they haunt
Incessantly whistle and sing.
But above all beak-bearing birds,
The cuckoos made themselves heard,
Who are found there in the greatest number,
For they hatch in the garden of love.
Well-furnished was their chapel,
And full of great harmony,
For their song was gracious
Like a voice coming from the heavens.

<margin>Note.</margin>
¶ Now think if I had
Reason to hear such joy;
To my liking, the greatest sweetness
That was ever heard, for certain.
So sweet and beautiful was this song
That it did not seem like the song of a bird,
But one could instead estimate it
To be a song of the sirens of the sea,
<margin>Sirens.</margin>
Who took the name of sirens
From their enchanting and clear voices,
With which they often lull those at sea to sleep.

# Folio .viii.

**Folio .viii.**
L i

<margin>Enumeration of Cupid’s arrows in the hands of Sweet Look.</margin>
Five he held in his right hand,
Of which these five had hooked points;
The fletchings <note>original: "pennons," the feathers on an arrow</note> were well-made and the notches
Were well-painted with fine gold.
The points were exceedingly sharp
And keen for piercing well;
But there was neither iron nor steel
That was not richly made of gold,
Except for the fletchings and the shaft.
The points were called
Barbed arrows of gold.

<margin>The names of the first five arrows.</margin>
¶ The best and the swiftest
Of these arrows, and the most beautiful,
The one which had the best fletching,
Bore the name of **Beauty**.
¶ The second of those which wounds less
Had the name, in my opinion, of **Simplicity**.
¶ The third was called
**Frankness** <note>original: "Franchise," referring to noble-mindedness and sincerity</note>, very well feathered
With Worth and Courtesy.
¶ The fourth had the name **Company**,
Which brought a very heavy burden,
For it was not ready to go far;
But whoever wished to shoot it from nearby
Could certainly do a great deal of harm.
¶ The fifth had the name **Fair Appearance**,
The least painful of all the others;
Nevertheless, it deals a great wound
To him who experiences its blow.
He who is wounded by this arrow
Ought to be less distressed by it;
For he can soon expect a recovery,
And will have the least amount of pain.

¶ The other five arrows were ill-treated,
Roughly planed and poorly made;
And the shafts and the iron heads were

<margin>The names of the last five arrows of Cupid.</margin>
Blacker than the devils of hell.
¶ **Pride** was the name of the first,
Leading the others like a banner-bearer.
¶ The second was **Baseness** <note>original: "Villennye," the opposite of courtly refinement</note>,
Full of great wickedness.
¶ The third was named **Shame**,
Often spoken of among people.
¶ And the fourth was **Covetousness**,
Which incites people to do evil.

¶ The fifth was **Despair**,
Quick to do harm without doubt,
The very last of all the others.
¶ These five arrows were of one kind
And all resembled one another,
And they were very well-suited
To the two ends of the very crooked bow,
Which was lumpy, twisted, and full of knots.
Such arrows must surely be shot
By those who do the opposite of the others.
I will not tell you of their power now,
For I do not strive to do so at present;
But you shall hear their significance
Without any lack of diligence,
And I will tell you what it all amounts to
Before I finish my account.

# The Romance of the Rose.

Wise, pleasant, gay, and clever,
Slender, noble, lively, and charming.

<margin>Description of Wealth.</margin>
Near Beauty stood Wealth,
A lady of great highness and stature,
Of great worth and great influence;
To her and to her own, misbehavior
In status, deeds, or words
Was considered the boldest of acts. <note>The text suggests that Wealth is so powerful that even small slights against her or her circle are seen as daring or dangerous.</note>

<margin>Wealth, a lady who can harm or help.</margin>
She is one who can either harm or help;
It is not a discovery of today or yesterday
That wealthy people have great power
To provide aid or cause grievance.

<margin>Note: Everyone relies on the rich.</margin>
All the greatest and the least among men
Paid honors to Wealth;
Everyone called her their lady
And feared her as a powerful woman.
All put themselves in her debt <note>original: "dangier," meaning legal jurisdiction or power over someone</note>,
And everyone paid her respect throughout the year.
Many traitors and many envious people
Oftentimes feel very joyful
To despise or to blame
All those who are most worthy of love;
In person, they act as a mockery,
Praising people with flattery
And "anointing" them with sweet words,

<margin>The nature of flatterers.</margin>
But afterward, they sting with their arrows
From behind, even to the bone;
They diminish the praise of the good
And speak ill of those who are praised.

<margin>The evils of flattery.</margin>
Many an honorable man <term>preudhomme: a man of integrity and noble character</term> have they disparaged,
These flatterers <term>losengeurs: deceitful flatterers or sycophants in a courtly setting</term> with their deceits,
And they have caused those who should have been
Intimate friends to be treated as strangers at court.
May evil befall
Such flatterers or those full of envy,
For no man of honor loves their way of life.

The garment of Wealth
Was of purple, so noble
That nothing in the world is more beautiful,
Better made, or more modern.
Portrayed there in fresh gold
Were stories of emperors and kings;
And furthermore, there was
A noble and subtle piece of craftsmanship:
Golden clasps closing at the neck,
Held by bands of azure blue.
Nobly was her head adorned,
Decorated with rich stones
That cast a very great light;
Everything there was well-matched.
She had a very rich belt
Girded over her clothing,
Of which the buckle was made
Of a stone that suited her well.
He who carries it upon himself
Is so well guarded against poisons
That he is in no danger;
That belt or noble girdle
Was worth a great sum of wealth,
For no man had ever seen one so beautiful.
Of another stone were the strap-ends <note>original: "mordens," the metal tip of the belt</note>,
Which cured the aching of teeth;
And the stone brought good luck—
He who had it could be sure
Of his health and of his sight,
Provided he had seen it on an empty stomach.
The studs were of purified gold,
Set upon the gilded fabric,
Which were very large and heavy;
In each one were two bezants <note>original: "besans," gold coins of the Byzantine Empire used here to describe the size or value of the studs</note>.
And with this, Wealth had
A golden scepter placed upon her hair,
So rich, so pleasant, and so beautiful
That never was its equal seen.
It was heavily adorned with stones,
Precious and polished;
Whoever would wish to describe them
Could not even estimate their value.
There are rubies, sapphires, jacinths <term>iagonces: a yellow, orange, or reddish gemstone</term>,
And more than a hundred ounces of emeralds;
But in front, by great mastery,
A carbuncle <term>escarboucle: a mythical gemstone believed to emit its own light</term> was well set.
That stone was so bright
That he who placed it before him
Could very well see in case of need
To lead himself for a league's distance <note>about 3 miles</note>.
Such a great light issued from it
That Wealth shone brilliantly from its glow.

<summary>This page introduces the personification of Wealth (Richesse), describing her immense social power and the dangers of the flatterers who surround her. It concludes with a detailed description of her lavish clothing and magical jewelry, particularly a belt that heals and a carbuncle that glows in the dark.</summary>

Leaf viii.
C ii

<margin>Description of Jollity</margin>
Wealth held by the hand
A youth full of beauty;
This was her lover, **Jollity** <note>original: "jolpuete," a term for mirth, happiness, or youthful elegance</note>.
He was a man who, in the summer time,
Took delight in joyful things.
He dressed himself well and elegantly,
And had hair of great value.
He would have much preferred to be caught
In some murder or theft
Than to lack a riding horse in his stable;
For this reason, he kept the company
And the goodwill of Wealth,
And always had it in his mind
To maintain a grand lifestyle.
He could well afford to maintain it,
Since he was well-supplied;
Wealth delivered money to him
In measures and by the bushel.

<margin>The description of Generosity.</margin>
After them sat **Generosity**,
Who was well-bred and well-taught
In doing honor and spending everything.
She was of the lineage of Alexander <note>Refers to Alexander the Great, the medieval archetype of extreme generosity and "largesse."</note>,
Who took no pleasure in anything
Except when he was giving of his own.
But Avarice, the wretched,
Is not as careful and attentive
To giving as Generosity is;
Therefore God made all her goods
Multiply so greatly that she did not know
How to give enough to keep from having more.

<margin>Generosity draws all hearts to joy.</margin>
Generosity received much praise and many prizes;
She had the wise and the foolish
Completely at her command.
She had done so much through her beautiful gifts
That if there were anyone who hated her,
It was her right that she should win them over
By the fine service of her friends.
And for this reason, she was favored by
The love of the poor and the rich.
Foolish are the stingy and the rich <note>The text plays on the idea that the wealthy are often "poor" in spirit if they are greedy.</note>,
But the rich <insert>who give</insert> have no vice.

<margin>Denunciation of Avarice.</margin>
The avaricious live in pain
And do not sleep a single day of the week;
Nevertheless, they cannot acquire
Neither lordship nor great lands
To do with as they please,
For they do not have a wealth of friends.
But whoever wishes to have friends
Must not hold their wealth too dear.

<margin>Generosity, the nurse and mother of friends.</margin>
Rather, one must seek friends through beautiful gifts,
For that is the virtue of one's being.
Just as the lodestone <term>pierre d’ayment: a naturally magnetized mineral</term>
Attracts iron subtly,
So does the heart of people attract those
Who are diligent in giving.

**Generosity** had a good and beautiful robe
Of a completely new color,
And a very well-formed face;
No limb of hers was deformed.
Generosity, the valiant and wise,
Held a knight of the lineage
Of the good **King Arthur of Britain**;
He is the one who bore the standard
Of valor and the gonfalon <term>goufanon: a heraldic banner or ensign</term>,
He who has a very great reputation,
Of whom great account is still held
Before kings and before many counts.
This knight had recently
Come from a tournament
Where he had performed for his lady
Many a joust and feat of chivalry,
And had by force captured and struck down
Many a knight and fought well.

<margin>Description of Sincerity</margin>
After those came **Sincerity** <term>franchise: a quality of being noble, free-born, and honest</term>,
Who was neither brown nor dark,
But was as white as snow.
She was courteous, joyful, and frank;
Her nose was long and well-shaped,
With bright, laughing eyes and shapely eyebrows.
Her hair was very blonde and very long;
She was as simple as a dove,
Having a sweet and noble heart.
She dared not say or do
Anything that she ought not to do.

And if she knew a man
Who suffered for her friendship
She would immediately have felt pity for him
For she had a pitiful heart,
Very noble, gentle, and amiable.
Her dress was a **tunic** <term>surquenie: a loose, outer garment or smock, usually made of fine linen</term>
Most honest and without baseness;
It was not made of coarse cloth—
No lady as far as Arras <note>Arras was a French city famous in the Middle Ages for high-quality textiles and tapestries.</note> had one so beautiful.
It was so well gathered and joined
That there was not a single stitch
That was not set in its proper place.
**Sincerity** <note>original: "Franchise," representing the qualities of a well-born, noble, and open-hearted person</note> was well dressed,
For no robe is so beautiful
On a lady or a young girl;
A woman is more elegant and delicate
In a tunic than in her kirtle.
The tunic, which was white,
Showed that she was sweet and noble.
A youth who was there,
Standing right beside her, was dressed like her;
He was of great renown,
Though I know not what he was named.
He was noble enough to be held in high account
And seemed to be the son of a count.

<margin>Description of Courtesy.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' with scrolling leaf patterns.</image-desc>
Afterwards stood **Courtesy**,
Highly prized as she was lovely.
She was neither haughty nor foolish;
She is the one who, to the **carol** <term>carolle: a popular medieval circle dance where participants held hands and sang</term>,
Called me by her grace.
She showed no ill-will when I went there;
She was not simple or flighty,
But wise and without any excess.
Beautiful responses and beautiful sayings
Were often spoken by her,
And she bore no grudge against anyone.
She was as clear as the moon;
She had a shining face—
I know not a face so pleasing.
She is worthy in every court,
Whether of a king or a worthy count.
By her side stood a youth,
Approachable, very noble and handsome,
Doing honor to all people.

He was diligent in doing this;
In arms he was well instructed,
Very well learned and very well taught.
By his sweetheart he was well loved,
As he was very graceful and well formed.
She followed him closely
And gladly pursued him.
Of her I have told you without fail
Her whole appearance and stature;
No more of her is recounted to you,
For she is the one who did me the kindness
Of opening the orchard <note>In the poem, Idleness (Oiseuse) usually opens the garden gate; the text here links this act to the figure currently being described in the dance.</note>
Even though I was a stranger.

<margin>Description of Youth.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' with floral motifs.</image-desc>
Next, as was most fitting,
Was **Youth** with the laughing face,
Who had not yet, I believe,
Passed twelve years of age.
She was innocent and thought
Of no evil trick, whatever it might be;
Rather, she was very joyful and gay,
For she fears nothing
Except God, as you know.
Her lover was close to her,
In such a way that he kissed her
And performed every service for her
In front of all those in the dance;
And even if someone had spoken of it,
He would never have been ashamed.
You would have seen them both
Kissing like two doves.
The characters were beautiful;
He was of the same age
As his sweetheart, and of the same spirit.
In this way they danced there,
All these people and others with them,
Who were of their company,
Like people very well-taught
And of very good behavior,
Who were commonly there.

¶ How the **God of Love**, following,
Goes into the garden, spying
Upon the lover until the time is right
So that he may be pierced by his arrows.

The circle-dances were already ending

There they led a joyous life,
Satisfied with every pleasure.
Whoever could have such a life

There is no lesser paradise

From there I departed then,

And the God of Love called...

<margin>Cupid <note>original: "cupido"</note> calls the Lover as he enjoys himself.</margin>

Then, before him, **Sweet Look** <note>original: "Doulp Regard" (Doux Regard), an allegorical figure serving as the God of Love’s squire or companion.</note>—
At no one else did he look—
His golden bow, without waiting longer,

<margin>Sweet Look gives the bow of Love, strung, to Cupid.</margin>

He then commanded him to string;
Wherefore Sweet Look strung it
And returned the well-strung bow to him;
And then gave him five arrows,
Strong, large, and ready to fly far.
The God of Love, soon from afar,
Began to follow me, bow in hand.
God keep me from a mortal wound,
For I fear he may try his aim against me;
He would grieve me sorely,
Of that you should have no doubt.

<margin>Cupid pursues the Lover.</margin>

Through the orchard I went freely,
And he intended to follow me;
But I stopped in no place
Until I had been through every part.
The beautiful orchard, by design,
Was entirely square in shape,
Every bit as long as it was wide.
The border was full of fruit,
Except perhaps for one or two
Of some hideous, bad trees.

<margin>Description of the Garden of Love regarding the trees.</margin>

There were pomegranate trees in the orchard—
I remember it well, to be brief—
Which bore pomegranates <note>original: "pōmes grenades"</note>
Beneficial for the sick.
Walnut trees were there in abundance,
Which bore well in their season
Such fruit as nutmegs,
Which are neither bitter nor bland.
There were almond trees planted
And established within the orchard,
And many a fig tree, and many a date tree
One would find there, if one had need of them.
There was many a good spice:
Cloves and licorice,
Fresh **grains of paradise** <term>graine de paradis: a spice also known as Melegueta pepper, prized in the Middle Ages for its peppery, citrus-like flavor</term>,
Zedoary <note>original: "citail," a root spice similar to ginger</note>, anise, and also cinnamon,
And many a delectable spice.
Very suitable was that place.
There were the trees, not dry,
Which bore good quinces and peaches,
Chestnuts, apples, and pears,
Medlars, plums—both white and black—
Fresh, new cherries,
Serviceberries, wild plums, and hazelnuts.
The tall laurels and the tall pines
Were there, inside these gardens;
Olive trees also, and cypresses,
Of which few are so near at hand.
The elms there were many-branched,
And also great forked oaks.
Why should I go on telling you more?
There were so many diverse trees
That it would be a great burden to me
To declare them to you by number.

<meta>This page continues the narrator's journey through the Garden of Delight. On the previous page, the God of Love was following the narrator with his bow drawn. Here, the narrator discovers the famous Fountain of Narcissus, which serves as a central symbol for the awakening of desire.</meta>

<header>The Romance of the Rose.</header>

<margin>Description of the fountain.</margin>
And more shining than fine silver
Is the end of this fountain,
The most beautiful in all the world;
For the water was fresh and new,
Springing day and night in great waves
Through two hollow and deep pits,
Around which grows the tiny grass,
Which becomes fresh and thick from the water,
And in winter it cannot dry up,
Nor fail, nor cease, nor die.
At the bottom of the fountain below
Were two crystal stones
Which I gazed upon with marvel;
Never had I seen their equal.
About these stones I wish to tell you
Something without refusal:
When the sun, which watches everything,
Casts its rays into the fountain,
And its brightness descends from the sky,
It receives more than a hundred colors
From the crystal, which through the sun
Becomes indigo, yellow, and vermilion. <note>The narrator is describing the prismatic effect of sunlight hitting the crystals, reflecting the primary colors of the medieval palette.</note>
These crystals are very marvelous,
And each of them has such power
That trees, flowers, and all greenery
Appear to anyone who turns their care there.
And to make the matter understood,
I wish to teach you a reason:
Just as a mirror shows
The things that are opposite it,
And one sees there without covering
The entire fashion and figure;
Just so, I tell you for a truth,
<margin>Comparison of the mirror.</margin>
That the crystal, without deception,
Reveals the whole state of the orchard
To him who muses within the water;
For always, wherever he may be,
He sees one half of the orchard,
And if he turns now,
He can see all the remainder;
And there is no thing so small,
So hidden nor so enclosed,
Of which a demonstration is not made,
Just as it is portrayed in the orchard.

<margin>The perilous mirror of love.</margin>
This is the perilous mirror
Of the very proud Narcissus, <note>In Greek mythology, Narcissus was a youth who fell in love with his own reflection and died of longing. Here, the fountain represents the eyes or the initial spark of infatuation.</note>
Who saw his face and his two eyes,
From which he then fell dead, overturned.
Whoever looks at themselves in such a mirror
Can have no need of a physician; <note>original: "mire," a medieval term for a doctor or healer.</note>
There is no one who sees it with their eyes
Who is not set on the path of loving.
Many a valiant man has been caught
In the mirror; for the wisest,
The most pious and most affected,
Has been taken there, and waylaid
There by a very wicked storm;
For the courage changes all too soon.
There, no one goes to seek counsel,
For Cupid, son of Venus,
Sowed there the seed of love,
<margin>Of the seed of love</margin>
Which encumbers the fountain,
And there he stretched out his snares,
And set his engines there to catch
Maidens and young men.
Love wants no other birds <note>A metaphor for the young people Cupid hopes to "trap" like birds in a net.</note>
Because of the seed that was sown.
This fountain was named
The Fountain of Love by right,
Of which many have in many places
Spoken in romance and in books;
But never will you hear it better described,
The truth of the matter,
When I have told you the manner of it.
<margin>Note.</margin>
Now it pleases me to remain
At the fountain, and to gaze again
At the crystals which showed there
A thousand things that were within.
In an evil hour I looked at myself there;
I have since sighed much because of it.
This mirror has greatly deceived me;
But if I had known beforehand
Of its force and of its power,
I would not have made my residence there,
For I found myself greatly dismayed
When I realized I had fallen into the snares.
<margin>Encounter with the rosebush of love.</margin>
In the mirror, among a thousand things,
I chose rosebushes laden with roses,
Which were in a corner...

Nor for all of Paris, until I went

When that rose took me by surprise—
By which many another has been smitten—
I quickly drew back toward the rosebush.
And know that when I was near,
The scent of the most savory
Rose entered into my thoughts,
And I was so strongly perfumed by it
That I lingered too long to smell it.
Never would I have thought
To be blamed for frequenting this place.
Very gladly would I have plucked from them
At least one that I might hold
In my hand to smell its scent;
But then I feared regret,
For it might easily
Displease the master of the orchard. <note>The "master of the orchard" is the allegorical figure Déduit (Delight or Pleasure), who represents the aristocratic lifestyle of leisure.</note>

Description of the
rosebush
of love.

Roses were there in heaps;
I never saw rosebushes so beautiful,
Nor buds so small and tightly closed,
And others that were larger.
There were some of another harvest
Which were tending toward their season
And were preparing to bloom
And come to perfection.
The roses that are open and wide
Are all withered in a single day,
But the buds stay quite fresh
For at least two days or three.
These buds pleased me greatly,
For more beautiful ones were never seen;
Whoever could snag one
Ought to hold it very dear.
If I could have a garland of them,
I would love it more than any wealth.
Among all these buds I saw one
So very beautiful that compared to it
I valued none of the others at all,
When I observed its great beauty;
For a color illuminates it
Which is vermilion <note>original: "vermeille"; a deep, brilliant red pigment highly prized in the Middle Ages.</note> and as fine

As Nature knew how to make it.
There were many pairs of leaves
Which Nature, through her mastery,
Had placed and set there.
The stem was straight as a reed
And upon it sits the bud,
Which neither leans nor hangs;
Its scent spreads everywhere,
And the sweetness that comes from it
Fills the entire place.
Once I had sensed its fragrance,
I wished to return nowhere else.
If I had dared to extend my hand
And approach to take it,
I would have done so; but the stinging
<margin>

to reaching
the bud
of love.

Sharp and piercing thorns,
Nettles and hooked briars

<meta>This page continues the narrative after the Lover has discovered the rosebush in the Garden of Delight. Having been struck by the God of Love’s arrows (an event occurring just before this passage), the Lover now enters into a formal feudal-style contract of service with the deity.</meta>

<header>The Romance of the Rose.</header>

To do your will,
But please receive my service
In good favor, and do not deceive me.
<margin>Note on acceptable service</margin> I do not say this as a shirker,
For I am willing to serve you;
But he labors in vain
Who offers service
When that service is not pleasing
To the one to whom it is presented.

## ¶ Love to the Lover.

¶ Love responds: "Do not be afraid;
Since you consent to my intention,
I will accept your service in good favor
And I will place you in a high degree <note>original: "hault degre" - referring to a higher social or spiritual status within the court of Love.</note>
Unless wickedness draws you back.
But this cannot be done so quickly;
<margin>Note: Great good is not acquired without pain.</margin> Great good does not come in a short hour;
It requires great effort and endurance.
Wait and suffer the distress
Which now harms and wounds you,
For I know for what reason
You will be set on the path to healing.
I will give you such beauty,
If you hold yourself to loyalty,
That it will heal your wounds
When I know and it appears to me
Whether you will serve me with a good heart,
And how you will carry out,
Night and day, my commandments
Which I command to true lovers."

## ¶ The Lover speaks to Love.

¶ "Sir," I said, "by God’s mercy,
Before you depart from here,
Charge me with your true commandments;
And according to your teachings,
I will fulfill them entirely
And never contradict them.
For this reason, I desire to learn them
So that I might not do wrong."

## ¶ Love responds to the Lover.

¶ Love responds: "You speak very well,
<margin>Note.</margin> If you understand and retain them;
For the master loses all his labor
When the disciple who listens
Does not take such care to remember
That he might be able to recall it."

## ¶ The Lover.

¶ The God of Love then charged me—
Just as you will now hear—
Word for word, with his commandments.
And as the romances <note>The word "romman" here refers to the French vernacular language and the poetic tradition of narrative storytelling.</note> say,
Whoever wishes to love should pay attention
Just as Love commands;
For it is good to listen to them
For anyone who wants to focus their mind there,
Because the end of it is beautiful.
And because this is a new subject,
Whoever hears the end of the dream,
I tell you truly that he will be able
To learn enough of the games of love,
<margin>Exhortation of Love.</margin> Provided that he wishes to listen well
And well conceive the substance
And the significance of the dream.
The truth which is hidden
Will then be quite clear to you
When you hear the dream explained;
In no point is it a fable or a lie.

### ¶ How the God of Love teaches the Lover, and tells him to follow and keep the rules he gives to the Lover, written in this beautiful romance.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration depicting the God of Love and the Lover. On the right, the God of Love (Amour) sits upon a throne, wearing a crown and holding a bundle of arrows.
