# The Romance of the Rose.

One continues to love all the more. 
The wise fool knows well 
that he who is near the fire burns the most. 
As long as you remain in this state, 
you will never be able to depart, 
and when you finally must leave, 
you will remember throughout the day 
the one you have seen, 
for which you will consider yourself a fool. <note>original: "grue." Literally a "crane," this was a medieval term for someone who stands around gawking or acting foolishly.</note>

<margin>Note.</margin>
¶ Another thing happens poorly: 
it is that you will have had 
neither the courage nor the boldness 
to speak to her. 
Instead, you stood near her 
speechless, confused and overcome, 
leading you to believe you have failed 
because you did not call to the beautiful lady 
before she had gone away. 
This should cause you great distress; 
for even if you could have gained 
nothing but a simple, fair greeting, 
it would have been worth more to you than a hundred marks of gold. 
Then you will begin to wander, 
seeking an excuse to go 

<margin>Many pains are made in love.</margin>
out again into the street 
where you had seen her 
whom you did not dare to address. 
You would go right into her house 
gladly, if you had a reason. 
It is only right that all your paths, 
your outings and your turns, 
return to that neighborhood.

<margin>A lover must be secret.</margin>
Hide yourself very well from people; 
seek an excuse other than the one 
which makes you go to that place, 
for it is great wisdom to keep oneself hidden. 
And if it happens that you see her 
at the right moment and that you must 
speak to her and greet her, 
then your color will be forced to change, 
for your whole mind will tremble.

<margin>Fear in love.</margin>
Speech and sense will both fail you 
when you intend to begin; 
and if you wish to venture so far 
that you dare to start your speech, 
when you ought to say three things, 
you will not say even two of them, 
so ashamed will you be then. 
Some are not so well-prepared 
that they do not forget quite a lot in such a moment.

<margin>Note.</margin>
When your speech is finished, 
without a single word of rudeness, <note>original: "villenye." In courtly literature, this refers to behavior unbecoming of a knight or noble, specifically lack of manners.</note> 
you will be very displeased in your heart 
if you have forgotten anything 
that was fitting for you to say. 
Then you will be in great martyrdom; 
this is the battle, this is the hardship, 
this is the conflict that always lasts. 
This war will never take an end 
until you wish to seek peace.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a man's face or head profile inside the letterform.</image-desc>
When the nights have come, 
a thousand displeasures will tear at you. 
You will lie down in your bed 
where you will take little delight, 
for when you think to sleep, 
you will begin to tremble, 
to startle, to toss about, 
turning from one side to the other, 
one hour on your back and the other on your stomach, 
like one who has a toothache. 
Then there will come to your memory 
both her face and her appearance, 
to which none other is equal. 
I will tell you a very great marvel.

<margin>Note.</margin>
¶ Sometimes it will seem to you 
that you hold her of the bright face 
between your arms, and completely naked, 
as if she had become 
entirely yours and your companion. 
Then you will build <term>castles in Spain</term> <note>original: "chasteaulx en espaigne." A famous idiom for building "castles in the air" or indulging in impossible daydreams.</note> 
and you will have joy from nothing 
for the time that is open 
in delightful thought,

<margin>Delight in dreams.</margin>
where there is nothing but lies and fables. 
But you will be able to stay there only a little while; 
then you will begin to weep 
and say, "But have I dreamed? 
Am I moved, or did I stir? 
From where could this thought come? 
Would that it happened ten times a day!"

<margin>The description of the rose.</margin>
I had come, it seems to me, from a low hell into paradise; for Fair Welcome <gloss>entirely</gloss> <note>original: "pour tout," meaning completely or for every purpose.</note> leads me, and strives to do my pleasure. When I had approached the rose, I found it a little enlarged, and I recognized that it had grown more than when I had first seen it. And with this, it was expanding at the top, which made it more beautiful to me because it was not so open that the seed <note>original: "graine." This refers to the golden center or heart of the flower.</note> was uncovered; rather, it was still closed between the petals of the rose, which rose up straight and filled the space within. One could not see the seed because the space was full. It was then—God bless it—much more beautiful than when fully bloomed, more gracious and more crimson. I was greatly amazed by the wonder of how it was beautified, because Love binds me more strongly, and tightens his snares all the more as I take more solace there. A long time I remained there, enamored with Fair Welcome, where I found great company. And when I saw that he did not deny me his solace nor his conversation, I requested one thing of him that is well worth remembering. 
"Sir," said I, "know truly that I am very strongly desirous of having a savory kiss

from the rose which smells so strong; and if it should not displease you, I would request this gift from you. For God's sake, sir, grant it then, and I shall have the grant of the kiss. Very sweet friend, now tell me quickly if it please you that I may kiss it; the thing should not displease you."

<meta>Following Fair Welcome’s friendly reception of the Lover into the garden, the narrative focuses on the Lover’s desire for a kiss from the Rose. However, Fair Welcome is hesitant, fearing the disapproval of the allegorical figure Chastity.</meta>

¶ "Friend," he said, "as God may keep me, if it weren't for the watch of Chastity <note>original: "chastete." Here personified as the guardian of the lady's virtue.</note>, I would never deny you. But I dare not for fear of Chastity, against whom I wish not to offend. She has always forbidden me to grant permission for a kiss to any lover who pleads with me. For whoever can attain a kiss can hardly stop there. And know that when a kiss is granted, one has the best and most pleasing part of the prize—and with it, all the rest."

### ¶ The Lover.

¶ When I heard him respond this way, I did not want to urge him further, so much did I fear making him angry. One must not press anyone against their will nor plead too much. You know well that at the first stroke, <margin>Note.</margin> an oak tree is not felled, nor does one get the wine from the press <note>original: "lesne," likely referring to the *ais* or boards of the wine-press.</note> until the grapes are squeezed and crushed. The granting of the kiss I desired was long delayed; but Venus, who is always at war with Chastity, came to my aid. She is the mother of the great God of Love, who has rescued many a lover. <margin>The description and adornment of Venus.</margin> She held a flaming torch <note>original: "brandon." A torch or firebrand, the traditional attribute used by Venus to ignite the fires of passion.</note> in her right hand, whose flame has warmed many a lady. She was elegant and well-coiffed; she looked like a goddess or a fairy because of the great finery she wore. Anyone who saw her could easily see she was not a woman of religion <note>A subtle way of saying she did not lead a monastic or ascetic life.</note>. I shall not mention here her highly decorated gown, nor her beautiful golden cloth, nor her brooch or her belt, for I would dwell too long on that. But know for certain she was elegantly dressed, and there was no pride in her. Venus drew near to Fair Welcome and began to speak to him.

### ¶ Venus to Fair Welcome.

¶ "Why, fair sir, are you so distant and resistant <note>original: "dangereux." In medieval courtly literature, this implies being difficult, haughty, or refusing a request.</note> toward this lover? You should not refuse him a loving kiss, for you can see and know well that he serves and loves with loyalty, and there is enough beauty in him that he is worthy of being loved. See how well-formed he is, <margin>Venus praises the lover to Fair Welcome.</margin> how handsome and noble, gracious and courteous to all; moreover, he is not old, but young, which makes him all the better. There is no lady or noblewoman whom I would not consider rude if she were difficult with him in granting this reward. Therefore, grant him the kiss; you could not employ yourself better. I believe his breath is sweet, and his mouth is not foul nor made to harm anyone, but rather to comfort and delight; for his lips are bright red, and his teeth are white and clean, and there is no stain or filth upon them. In my opinion, it is only right that a kiss be granted to him; it will be well-bestowed upon him, for the longer you wait, know that you lose just as much time."

¶ Just as the burning torch of Venus aided the lover more than anyone else, so at last he went to kiss the Rose to better appease his love.

### The Lover.

Despair? Alas, that I shall not do.
I will not despair.
If hope were failing me,
I would not be brave;
In it I must take comfort.
Love, to better bear my ills,
Told me he would protect me

along with Jealousy and Evil Tongue,
<margin>The obstacles to love.</margin>
who loves nothing but wicked reproach;
for through an evil tongue, blame

He <note>Referring to the personification of Jealousy.</note> holds Fair Welcome in prison,

But now my grief increased

<margin>The three gifts that Cupid gives to the Lover.</margin>
I had them, but I lose them here:

Without fail he gave me beautiful gifts, but

By my hand this graft <note>original: "impe." A botanical metaphor for a young shoot or a graft, continuing the garden theme of the poem.</note> will not be made;

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Reason and the Lover. Following Jean de Meun’s takeover of the poem, the tone shifts toward the philosophical. # Leaf xliiii.

# The Romance of the Rose.

<margin>Reason teaches the lover the way to love.</margin>

¶ By my head, I wish to teach you
¶ Your lesson, if you wish to listen;
For I shall show you, without any fable,
A thing that is not at all demonstrable.
From it, you shall know all good without science,
And you shall recognize without knowledge
That which can never be known,
Nor demonstrated, nor recognized.
As for what more might be known of it,
By anyone who attaches his heart to it,
He will not wish for it any less on that account,
Unless he is one who wishes to follow it.
The knot shall be untied for you,
Which you will always find knotted;
Now, pay close attention,
And you shall see the description.

<margin>The true description of love.</margin>

Love is a hateful peace;
Love is an amorous hate.
It is a disloyal loyalty,
And a loyal disloyalty.
It is a fear that is entirely assured,
A desperate hope.
It is a reason gone entirely mad,
A reasonable madness.
It is a sweet peril in which to drown,
A heavy burden light to carry. <note>original: "Soif fais legier a manyer" – likely a transcription error for "faix" (burden), as it contrasts with "heavy" in typical rhetorical style.</note>

<margin>Note.</margin>

It is Charybdis <note>original: "caribdis" – a dangerous whirlpool in Greek mythology, used here to represent the treacherous nature of love.</note> the perilous,
Disagreeable and yet gracious.
It is a languishing sickness with its own medicine,
It is a health that is entirely sickly.
It is a hunger sated in abundance,
It is covetousness and sufficiency.
It is the thirst that is always pure,
A purity that is fouled by thirst.

<margin>The good epithets of love.</margin>

It is a foolish delight, a bound sadness,
And a joy that is heavy. <note>original: "matrye" – likely meaning dejected or heavy-hearted.</note>
A sweet ill, a malicious sweetness,
A sweet flavor that tastes foul.
Stained by a gift of sin,
By sin through a gift unstained.
It is a pain that is much too joyous,
It is a piteous villainy.
It is the game that is never stable,
A state unstable and far too changeable;
A force too enclosed and yet strong,
Which moves everything by its efforts.
It is foolish sense, it is wise folly,
A prosperity both sad and jolly.
It is a laugh full of weeping and tears,
A rest that labors at every turn.
It is a hell that is most sweet,
It is a paradise full of sorrow.
A charity that relieves the prison,
A springtime full of a great winter.
It is a moth <note>original: "taigne" – refers to the clothes-moth, which destroys fabric regardless of its quality.</note> that refuses nothing,
For it wears out both purple cloth and coarse wool, <note>original: "bureau" – a cheap, rough woolen cloth worn by the poor.</note>
And little love-affairs happen just as well
Under coarse wool as under fine dark silks; <note>original: "brunettes" – a high-quality, expensive dark-dyed fabric.</note>
For no one is found so very wise,
Nor of such high or powerful lineage,
Nor of such proven strength,
Nor is anyone found now so bold,
Nor possesses so much of any other virtue,
That they may not be tamed by love.
All the world goes this way;
It is the god who leads them all astray,
Except for people of a wicked life
Whom Genius <note>In this poem, Genius is a character serving as the priest of Nature, who excommunicates those who do not follow the natural order of procreation.</note> excommunicates
Because they do wrong to Nature.
But for all that, if I do not care for them,
I do not wish for people to love
With that love for which they call themselves
Wretched and grieving in the end,
So much does love go about maddening them.
But if you wish to avoid it well
So that love cannot harm you,
And you wish to be cured of this rage,
You can drink no better potion
Than to think of fleeing it;
You cannot enjoy it in any other way.
If you flee it, it will flee you,
And if you flee, it will fly away.

<margin>Good teaching for fleeing love.</margin>

### ¶ The Lover to Reason.

¶ When I had heard Reason out,
Who had argued all for naught,
"Lady," I said, "my heart boasts
That it knows no more than it did before
As to how I might withdraw from it.
My lesson has so many contradictions..."

The Lover responds by expressing his confusion at these contradictory descriptions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous leaf, where Reason has just finished a long list of paradoxical definitions of love. The Lover now admits that while the definitions are poetic, they are difficult to grasp, and he asks for a formal, logical definition of the passion that grips him.</meta>

Though I cannot understand it well,
I still know how to repeat it by heart
So well that my heart will not forget it;
And I understand well what is written there.
To read it to everyone in common,
Let them come to me alone.
But since you have described love to me,
And both praised it and despised it so much,
I wish to pray you to define it,
So that I might better benefit from it;
For I have never heard a proper definition of it.

## Reason to the Lover.

<margin>Exposition and definition of love</margin>
Gladly; now pay attention.
Love, as I have well considered,
Is a sickness of the thought
Between two connected persons,
Free between themselves, of different sexes,
Coming to people through a passion born
Of disordered vision,
For the sake of embracing and kissing,
To ease themselves carnally.
Love intends nothing else,
But rather serves and delights in such a way
That it cares nothing for having fruit <note>Meaning the "fruit" of procreation or children.</note>;
For it strives for pleasure and nothing more.
There are some of such a manner
Who do not hold this love dear;
<margin>The lover must be subtle.</margin>
But nonetheless, they feign to be "fine lovers,"
Pretending to love when they do not deign to love at all.
And they also mock the ladies,
Promising them their bodies and souls;
They swear lies and fables
To those they find easy to deceive,
<margin>Note.</margin>
Until they have had their pleasures.
But those [the ladies] are the ones less deceived,
For it is always better to be a master
At deceiving than to be deceived oneself,
Especially in this war [of love],
When they know how to seek the means.
But I know well—and I am no diviner—
That one ought to continue the divine work.
With all his will and power,
Whoever lies with a woman should
Take good care of his own kind,
Because everything is corruptible <note>Meaning mortal or subject to decay.</note>;

<margin><image-desc>A hand pointing to the following lines</image-desc></margin>
So that through succession,
Procreation shall never fail.
For since fathers and mothers pass away,
Nature wills that sons spring forth
To continue this work,
So that by the one, the other is recovered.
For this reason, Nature put pleasure into it
For her own purpose; thus she chose it
So that the workers would not cease
And would not abandon this work;
For many would never take part in it
If they were not attracted by pleasure;
Thus Nature acted subtly there.
Know that no one goes the right way,
Nor has a right intention,
Who covets it for pleasure alone.
For he who goes seeking only pleasure,
<margin>Note.</margin>
Certainly makes himself, quite strictly,
Like a very wretched and foolish slave
To the prince of all vices.
For this is the root of all evil,
As Tully <note>original: "tulles" — Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> determines
<margin>Cicero in the book on Old Age.</margin>
In the book he wrote on Old Age <note>original: "Vieillesse" — refers to Cicero's treatise *De Senectute*.</note>,
Which he praises much more than youth;
For youth pushes man and woman
Into every peril of body and soul.
It is too difficult a thing to pass through
Without death or breaking a limb,
<margin>Note on foolish youth.</margin>
Or without causing shame and damage
Either to oneself or to one's lineage.
Through youth we act foolishly
In all sorts of debauchery,
And we follow bad company
And disordered lives,
And we change our intentions often;
Or we give ourselves by covenant
To someone, as if in their service,
Which is a matter of crime and vice.
One cannot keep the freedom
That Nature has placed in man;
And he thinks he can catch a crane in the sky <note>A proverbial expression for attempting something impossible or delusional.</note>
When he puts himself there in a cage <note>Likely referring to the "mue" or coop of a monastery.</note>
And stays there until he is professed <note>Having taken final religious vows.</note>.
<margin><image-desc>A hand pointing to the following lines</image-desc></margin>
And then if he feels the burden too heavy,
He repents of it, and then he leaves.

<summary>Reason provides a formal definition of love as a mental sickness driven by physical desire, contrasting pure lust with Nature's intent for procreation. # The Romance of the Rose.

I put nothing into practice,
even though I well understood
the whole matter, word for word;
but Love pulls me back so much
that he passes through all my thoughts,
like one who hunts everywhere,
and he always holds my heart under his seal,
having shoveled it right out of my body.
<margin><image-desc>manicule pointing right</image-desc></margin> I throw this whole sermon into the street;
it goes in through one ear
and kills what Reason puts in the other,
so that all her effort is wasted,
filling me with anger and wrath.
Then, quite piteously, I began to say:
"Lady, you certainly wish to betray me!
<margin>Note.</margin> Must I then hate people?
I would then hate all persons,
since love is not good for me.
I shall never love with 'fine love,' <note>Original: "amour fine" — the refined, courtly love celebrated by poets, which Reason has just criticized.</note>
but instead live always in ruin;
and then I shall be a mortal sinner,
worse than a glutton or a lecher.
In this, I cannot fail to miss the mark;
one way or another, I must err:
I will either hate or love.
But I hope that I would pay
too much for hate in the end;
love would not even be worth a penny <note>Original: "denier" — a coin of very little value.</note>."

"You have given me such good advice,
and you have always preached to me
that I should give up on love!
He is truly a fool who will not believe you.
You have also reminded me
of another love that I have not known,
one which I did not hear you blame,
through which people can love one another.
If you would like to define it,
I would consider myself a fool
if I did not listen most willingly,
to see if I could learn
the natures of love,
if it pleased you to explain it."

->Reason to the Lover.<-

"Certainly, fair friend, you are a fool,
for you do not value even a straw <note>Original: "festu" — a blade of straw; a common medieval idiom for something worthless.</note>
<margin>¶ Reason instructs the lover on how to love.</margin> that which I preach for your own good.
I wish to give another sermon on it,
for I am ready with all my power
to fulfill your good request—
though I do not know if it will be of any use to you."

"Love comes in many forms,
aside from the one that has so changed you
and moved you from your right senses.
<margin><image-desc>manicule pointing left</image-desc></margin> Misfortune gave you his acquaintance;
take care that you do not know him any longer.
One is called Friendship;
it is a common goodwill
between people without discord,
according to the benevolence of God.
For those people make a community
of all their goods in charity,
so that by no intention
does anyone have an exemption
from helping the other as needed,
but acts as one strong and very valiant
and loyal—for nothing would be worth
anything where sense or loyalty were lacking.
For everything he dares to think
he can recount to his friend,
just as to himself, in all security,
<margin>Different ways of loving</margin> without suspicion of accusation.
Such manners must and should have
those who wish to love loyally.
A man cannot be friendly
unless he is so firm and stable
that he does not move for the sake of Fortune,
<margin>Note on constancy.</margin> and that he is always found to be the same,
whether for his rich or poor friends
who have placed their whole hearts in him.
In poverty, they must give back to him
without waiting at all
for him to request their help;
for a kindness done by prayer <note>Meaning a favor done only after being asked or begged for.</note>
<margin>Note. Singularly remarkable.</margin> is sold far too dearly
to hearts that are of great value."

"Here is the needy man before
his true friend, asking
that he might wish to help him in his need,
placing his wealth into his hand."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Reason begins to define a "good" and "virtuous" love to the Lover, contrasting it with the blind passion he currently feels. Here, Reason describes the nature of true friendship and the dangers of feigned love driven by greed.</meta>

<page-num>Leaf ppp.</page-num>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration at the top left depicts two men in a landscape. One stands on the left, gesturing towards another who stands or sits near a large tree on the right. The scene is set outdoors with hills and additional vegetation in the background.</image-desc>

Shame brings a man much distress
when he must ask for help with a task; <note>Original: "sembesongne" — a need or a piece of business.</note>
he thinks of it much and worries greatly,
and suffers much before he prays for it.
He feels great shame in speaking his word,
and so he fears a refusal.

<margin>A friend is known in time of need.</margin>
But when such a man has found one
whom he has well tested,
so that he is certain of his love,
he may make his complaint and outcry to him
of every case he dares to think of,
without having shame for anything;
for how could he be ashamed
if the other is such as I describe?
When he has told him his secret,
a third person shall never know it,
<margin><image-desc>manicule pointing right</image-desc> / <image-desc>manicule pointing right</image-desc></margin>
and he need not fear any reproach;
for the wise man guards his tongue;
a fool would not know how to do this—
no fool knows how to keep his tongue still.
Such a good friend will help him
in everything just as much as he can,
happier to do this deed, in truth,
than the other is to receive it.
And if he does not make his request,
the friend will feel no less distress
<margin>The conditions of true friendship.</margin>
than he who required the help,
so great is the mastery of love;
he bears half of the other’s grief,
comforting him as much as he can,
and takes his share of the joy,
if the love is shared rightly.

<margin>Note the saying of Cicero on friendship.</margin>
By the law of this friendship,
Cicero <note>Original: "Tulles" — referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, whose treatise *De Amicitia* (On Friendship) was the standard medieval authority on the subject.</note> says in a treatise of his,
that we ought to make requests
of our friends that are honest,
and return their requests
if they contain right and reason;
otherwise, it should not be done,
except in two cases which he excludes:
if one wished to deliver him to death,
we must deliver him entirely;
if one assaults his reputation,
let us guard so that he is not defamed.
<margin>Note.</margin>
In these two cases, one must defend them
without ever waiting for a reason;
as much as love can excuse,
a man must not refuse this.
This love that I propose to you
is not contrary to my purpose.
This one I truly wish for you to follow,
and that you do not pursue the other love.
One devotes itself to all virtue,
but the other puts people to death.
I want to describe another love to you
which is the opposite of the good one,
and truly much to be blamed.
<margin>Feigned love is to be blamed.</margin>
This is the feigned will to love
in a heart sick with the venom
of great covetousness and gain.
This love hangs in such a balance
that as soon as it loses hope
of the profit it wishes to attain,
it must fail and be extinguished;
for a heart cannot be a lover
if it does not love people for themselves,
<margin><image-desc>manicule pointing right</image-desc></margin>
but instead fakes it and goes about flattering
for the profit that it expects.
That love comes from fortune,
which eclipses like the moon
that covers and shadows the earth
when the brightness falls into its shadow—
it has lost as much brightness
as it loses sight of the sun;
and when it has passed the shadow,
it returns all illuminated
by the rays that the sun shows it,
which shines against it from the other side.
<margin>Note on feigned love.</margin>
This love is of such a nature,
for it is quickly bright and then obscure.

# The Romance of the Rose.

As soon as poverty clothes him
In her hideous, dark-clouded mantle,
And when riches no longer shine on him
To lead him back in bright light,
Love flees when riches fail,
And disappears as soon as they depart.

<margin>In avarice there is little love.</margin>
**A**nd the love that I name to you here
Is well-loved by every rich man,
Especially the avaricious one
Who does not wish to wash
His vicious heart of the heat of vice,
Of covetousness and avarice.
He is more "horned" than a branching stag <note>The "horned stag" is a metaphor for a fool or someone being mocked; the rich man is deluded if he thinks people love him for his character rather than his money.</note>,
That rich man who believes he is loved,
Which for him is a great cowardice.
It is certain that he does not love at all;
How then does he think he is loved?
He is a fool for this, and so he is called;
In this matter he is not wise at all.
He is like a great, handsome savage

<margin>Note.</margin>
Who understands neither rhyme nor reason,
At any time, hour, or season.
Certainly that man is lovable
Who desires a true friend.
If he does not love, I can prove it:
If he loves for the sake of wealth,
Since he is so covetous—
More so than the poor, needy man.
The good man watches over all his friends
And keeps them in his care before him,
And always proposes to keep them
Until his mouth is closed <note>A euphemism for death.</note>
And death comes bursting forth;
For he would sooner allow
His limbs to be severed from his body
Than to suffer his friends to depart from him.

<margin>The man who does not love ought not to be loved.</margin>
But would friendship ever begin
In a heart that has no pity?
It is certain when he acts this way,
For everyone knows his own heart’s business.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Certainly he ought to be greatly blamed:
The man who loves not, yet wishes to be loved.

<margin>Note on Fortune</margin>
**A**nd since we come to Fortune,
And hold a sermon on love,
I want to tell you a proud marvel,

---

Such that you never heard the like.
I do not know if you can believe it,
But nonetheless it is a true thing,
And so one finds it written,
Which is of great value and profit to people.

<margin>Adverse Fortune is sometimes more profitable than Prosperous Fortune.</margin>
Adverse and contrary Fortune
Is better than the sweet and gracious one;
And if this seems doubtful,
It is a very weak argument [to say otherwise].
For the gracious and soft Fortune
Lies to them, wounds them, and drives them mad;
She nurses them like a mother
Who does not seem to be bitter.
She makes a show of having a loyal heart
By dealing out her jewels to them,
Such as coins and riches,
Dignities and nobilities;
And she promises them stability
In a state of ruin,
And soon feeds them on vain glory

<margin>The variety of Fortune.</margin>
In worldly happiness.
When she places them upon her wheel <note>The "Wheel of Fortune" (Rota Fortunae) was a ubiquitous medieval concept: as the wheel turns, those at the top are brought low, and those at the bottom are raised up.</note>,
Each one thinks he is such a great master
And sees himself in such a high state
That he could never fall from it.
When she has put them in such a position,
She makes them believe they have so many friends

<margin>Note.</margin>
That they do not know how to number them,
And they cannot rid themselves
Of those who come and go around them,
And who hold them as their lords.
They promise to seek riches for them,
Even to the point of spending their shirts—
Indeed, even to the shedding of blood
To warrant and defend them,
Ready to obey and follow them
Through all the days they have to live.
And those who hear such words
Glory in them and believe them
As if it were the Gospel;
Yet it is all useless flattery,
As they will well know afterward

<margin>In adversity, few friends are found.</margin>
If they had lost all their goods
And had no way to recover them.
Then you would see "open" friends <note>A play on words: when a man is poor, his "friends" are openly revealed as false, or they "openly" depart.</note>.

<summary>Reason explains that a rich man who is greedy cannot truly love or be loved, as his "friends" are only attracted to his wealth. She introduces the paradox that Adverse Fortune is better than Prosperity because it reveals who one's true friends are.</summary>

Having previously discussed how the rich are often surrounded by "friends" who only love their wealth, Reason now explains how adversity serves as a sieve to reveal who a person’s true friends really are.</meta>

<page-num>xxxvi.</page-num>
<sig>G i</sig>

For out of a hundred apparent friends,
Whether they be companions or kin,
If a single one were to remain with them,
They should truly adore God for it.
<margin>Note on adverse fortune</margin> This Fortune of which I spoke,
When she dwells among men,
She clouds their understanding
And nourishes them in ignorance;
But the contrary and perverse Fortune,
When she topples them from their high estate,
Tumbling them around her wheel
Until she casts them down into the mud,
And seats herself like a cruel stepmother <note>In medieval literature, the "stepmother" was a common archetype for someone harsh and unloving, often contrasted with a nurturing natural mother.</note>
To apply a painful plaster to the heart,
Moistened—not with sour wine—
But with weary and meager poverty,
She shows quite clearly that wealth is fleeting,
And that no one ought to trust
In the good favor of Fortune;
For there is no security to be found there.
She makes it known and understood,
As soon as they have lost their possessions,
<margin>☞</margin> With what sort of love they were loved
By those who were previously their friends;
For those to whom prosperity gives
A sense of security are greatly shocked [by the loss],
And they become like enemies;
Not one remains, not even half a one;
Instead, they flee and renounce them
As soon as they see them become poor.
And yet they do not stop there,
But in every place they go,
They go about blaming and defaming them,
Calling them miserable fools.
<margin>Note.</margin> Even those for whom they did the most good
When they saw them in their high estates,
Now testify with a cheerful voice
That they want no part of their "folly";
Such people find no one to help them.
But the true friend remains,
Who does not love for the sake of riches,
So full of nobility is his heart,
Nor for any gain he expects from it.
Such a friend succors and defends them,
For Fortune has no power over him;

---

<margin>He who loves well is slow to forget.</margin>
Loyal friends love always.
If one were to draw a sword against a friend,
Even then, such love would not be severed,
Except in these cases which I will name:
One can lose a friend through pride, or worse,
Through reproach, and by revealing
The secrets which ought to be hidden,
And by the painful wound
Of venomous detraction <note>Slander or backbiting.</note>.
In these instances, friends would part;
No other thing would harm their bond.
<margin>Note.</margin> But such [loyal] people prove themselves well
If one can find even a single one among them,
So vain is the love of this world,
And so full of ingratitude.
And because no amount of wealth
Can match the value of a friend—
<margin>Note the good comparison of friendship</margin> For wealth never climbs so high
That the worth of a friend does not surpass it—
It is always better to have a friend on the road
Than to have coins in one’s belt.
But most wicked Fortune,
When she falls upon the living,
She makes them, through their misfortune,
See all things so very clearly
That she makes them find such friends,
And find through experience
That they are worth more than any possession
One could have in this world.
<margin>Adversity is often worth more than prosperity</margin> Therefore, adversity profits them
More than prosperity ever does;
For through the latter they have ignorance,
And through adversity, knowledge <note>original: "science" – used here in the medieval sense of true knowledge or wisdom.</note>.
And the poor man, who through such testing
Distinguishes the true friend from the false,
Knows him and describes him well;
When he was as rich as he desired,
What would he have wished to buy then
If he had known then what he knows now?
Certainly, he would have been much less deceived,
And would have perceived the truth then;
Thus he has a greater advantage,
Since poverty, which deceives him [out of his goods],
Has made a wise man out of a fool,
More so than the wealth that received him.

<summary>Reason explains that while Prosperity blinds men with false friends, Adversity is a gift that reveals true loyalty and grants wisdom. A single loyal friend is proven to be more valuable than any material wealth.</summary>

All other goods belong to Fortune,

A wise man will not prize;
He will be neither joyful nor sorrowful
If he sees her wheel spinning now;

Because they are never stable.

When she falls and eclipses for so little.

Though you are not yet stained by it,
Yet it would be a great sin for you
If from now on you became entangled,
And that you troubled yourself with people
So that you might call yourself their friend,
And merely loved their wealth,

No worthy man would consider that a good thing.

But in one thing I see you are foolish,
When you placed me in her <note>Referring to the "Hate" mentioned in the next line.</note> malice,

#### ¶ Reason to the Lover.

¶ Who responded now, Reason:
"But understand, it is not fields nor houses,
Nor robes nor your ornaments,
Nor any earthly holdings,
Nor limbs, in any manner;
You hold a much better thing dear:
These are the goods of all your intellect <note>Reason refers to 'biens de tout ton sens,' meaning the faculties of the mind and soul which cannot be taken away by external circumstances.</note>
Of which you have certain knowledge,
Which will remain with you without ceasing,
So that they can never leave you
To do such service for another.
These goods are yours by right of office.
But as for those others that are external,
You do not possess two dozen [pennies'] worth of them;
Neither you nor any man who lives
Has the value of a single chive;
For know that all your things
Are enclosed within yourselves.
All other goods belong to Fortune,
<margin>The goods of the soul are immortal and those of Fortune are transitory.</margin>
¶ Who disperses them and gathers them,
Takes away and gives at her will,
Making fools laugh and grieve;
But that which Fortune shall do,
A wise man will not prize;
He will be neither joyful nor sorrowful

Because they are not stable.
Therefore, love of her is not good;
Never did she seem beautiful to a worthy man,
Nor is it right that she should be seen as beautiful
When for so little she falls and eclipses.
And therefore I want you to know
That you must not attach your heart to her,
Though you are not yet tainted by it;
But it would be a great sin for you
If from now on you tainted yourself,
And if you troubled yourself for people
So that you might call yourself their friend
And merely amass their wealth;
Neither the wealth nor the benefit that would come to you from them
Would any worthy man consider a good thing.

Flee from it as something vile and despised,
And stop loving with such [fickle] love,
And be discreet, and believe me;
But in one thing I see you are foolish,
When you have placed me in your malice
Because Hate commands you;
Tell me when, and by what scandal?"

<meta>The previous page established Reason's argument that Justice is a flawed human construct compared to divine Love. She now uses the Roman story of Virginia—a classic example of judicial corruption from Livy—to illustrate how even the law can be used for evil ends.</meta>

# The Romance of the Rose.

Appius <note>Appius Claudius Crassus, a corrupt Roman judge who lusted after Virginia.</note>, without making any distinction between right and wrong, had the maiden surrendered to the servant <note>Appius conspired to have Virginia claimed as a "runaway slave" by his henchman, Marcus Claudius, so he could legally take possession of her.</note>. And when the good man named before, the well-renowned knight Virginius, heard of this matter and saw that he could not defend his daughter against Appius, but instead was forced by power to hand her over to a life of shame—he chose death over dishonor <margin>Note.</margin> through a wondrous thought, if Titus Livius <note>Livy, the Roman historian who recorded this story in *Ab Urbe Condita*.</note> does not lie.

### ¶ How, after the judgment, Virginius hastily cut off his daughter's head, from which death she did not escape; and he preferred to do this rather than have her live in vile circumstances. Then he presented her head to the judge, which resulted in a great disaster for him.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' containing a scene of a man standing before a seated judge, likely representing the trial of Virginius.</image-desc> That man, out of sweet and pure love, immediately cut off the head of his beautiful daughter, Virginia, and then presented it to the judge before everyone in the open court <term>consistory</term> <note>A formal assembly or council; in this context, the judge's tribunal.</note>. According to history, the judge immediately ordered him to be seized, to be taken away to be drowned or hanged. However, he was not hanged because the people defended him, for they were moved by great pity as soon as the deed was known. Then, for this crime, Appius was cast into prison, where he killed himself hastily before the day of his judgment. <margin>The punishment of Appius and of Claudius.</margin> And Claudius, the false traitor, suffered death for his faults—unless he was saved by Virginia <note>The text likely means "for Virginia's sake" or "by the mercy Virginius showed in her name." In most versions, Virginius successfully pleaded for Claudius to be exiled rather than executed.</note> who, through her great pity, prayed so much to the people that she had him sent into exile.

And all those who were condemned died, those who had been false witnesses in the case. Some judges are far too excessive. <margin>Note. The saying of Lucan.</margin> Lucan <note>original: "Lucam"; a Roman poet. This is a reference to a sentiment found in his work *Pharsalia*: virtue and absolute power do not go well together.</note>, who was among the wise, says that virtue and great fear are never safely found together. And know that if they do not amend themselves and return what they have wrongfully taken, the powerful, eternal Judge will make them cry "Alas!" in Hell alongside the Devil. I exclude no one from this—neither kings nor prelates, nor any kind of judge, whether secular or of the Church. For they do not hold their honors for such purposes. Without seeking a bribe <term>loier</term> <note>From the Old French "loier," meaning reward or payment, often implying a bribe in a legal context.</note>, they must bring to a conclusion the disputes brought before them; they must open the door to plaintiffs and hear, in their own persons, both false and true grievances. They do not hold their honors for nothing, nor should they boast of them, for all their subjects are the common people <margin>The office of judges is to do right to everyone.</margin> who increase and populate the country. And the judges make oaths and swear to them to do right as long as they last. They must live in peace by their own hand and pursue all wrongdoers, and with their own hands hang the thieves, unless they wish to take such an office upon themselves <note>The duty of the judge is to uphold the law directly as a servant of the people.</note>. Since they must provide justice, they should focus their intentions there; for this reason, the people provide them with their rents <note>Taxes or public income.</note>. Thus it was proven to the people by those who first took up these honors. "I have now, then, rendered to you what you requested of me, and you have the proper reasons for it, which seem quite suitable to me."

Which approaches ribaldry <note>The Lover is reacting to Reason’s previous use of plain, anatomical language (specifically the word "testicles" in the story of Saturn), which he considers vulgar.</note>.

### ¶ Reason to the Lover.

Since you oppose me out of hatred,

Do you not know that it does not follow,
If I wish to abandon a folly,

<margin>The maxim of Horace.</margin>
Do you not remember Horace, <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus, the Roman lyric poet. Reason refers here to his *Satires* (1.2.24).</note>
Who had such great virtue and boldness?
Horace says—and he was no fool—
That when fools flee from vice,
They turn to its opposite,
Which makes the matter no better.
I do not wish to forbid love,
So that one cannot be occupied with it,
Except for that love which wounds people.
Likewise, if I forbid drunkenness,
I do not wish to forbid drinking.
For that would not be worth a pear.
If foolish extravagance were forbidden,
One would surely take me for a madwoman
If I then commanded avarice;
For both the one and the other are vices.
I do not make such arguments.

### ¶ The Lover to Reason.
Yes, you certainly do.

### ¶ Reason to the Lover.
Truly, you lie.
I do not seek to flatter you in this;
You are not well-equipped to defeat me.
Search the ancient books,
Even those of the good logicians,
And you will not read such things of love.
Never did you hear from my mouth
That we should hate anything;
One can certainly choose a middle path.
It is that love which I hold dear and ready,
Which I have prepared for you to love.

---

<margin>The love of beasts by natural inclination as well as that of men.</margin>
There is another, natural love
Which Nature created in the beasts,
By which they care for their young,
And suckle and nourish them.
Of the love which I am accounting for here,
If you want me to tell you
What the definition is:
It is a natural inclination
To wish to preserve one's own kind
Through a proper intention,
Whether by the way of procreation
Or through the care of nurturing.
To this love both men and beasts
Are equally ready and inclined.
This love, however much it profits,
Has no praise, blame, nor merit.
They are not to be blamed or praised;
Nature makes them swear to it.
But if they did not do so,
They would deserve to receive blame,
Just as a man does when he eats.

They were never in sadness.

He is not a good or strong wrestler

<margin>Note.</margin>

Let her turn her wheel,
Which turns without ever resting.
Seated in the middle like a blind woman,
She blinds some with great wealth,

To others she gives poverty;

He is a great fool who is comforted by her,

Since a defense against her is apparent

On the other hand, it is a very clear thing

It is neither right nor reasonable

A rock is situated in the sea,

Fools strike against it and struggle,

It makes little flowers appear
Like brightly flaming stars,

The little flowers and the greenery
With the sword of cold.

--- Page 72 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded Reason's exhortation to the Lover to remain steadfast against the fickleness of Fortune. She now begins a vivid, allegorical description of Fortune’s strange and contradictory domain, where nature itself is inverted.</meta>

-># The Romance of the Rose<-

So that the flower loses its being
As soon as it begins to grow.
The rock bears a fearsome forest
Where every tree is strange.
One is barren and bears nothing,
And another is so burdened with fruit;
One never stops turning green,
Another is orphaned of its leaves.
And when one remains in its greenness,
Many others there are without greenery;
And when one begins to bloom,
The flowers of many others go to their death.
One rises up, and its neighbors
Remain bowed toward the earth;
And when buds come to one,
The other withers, or holds its place.
There, the broom plants <note>original: "geneſtz"; a low-growing shrub, here grown unnaturally large</note> are like great giants,
And pines and cedars sit like dwarves.
Every tree is thus deformed
And takes its shape from another.
The laurel, which should be green,
Holds its leaves all withered there;
And the olive tree becomes dry,
Which ought to be fruitful and alive;
And the willows, which should be barren,
They bloom and receive fruit.
The elm tree strives against the vine,
Taking away the shape of the grape. <note>In nature, vines were often grown up elm trees; here, the elm unnaturally competes with or chokes the vine.</note>
The nightingale sings late there;
But much braying and madness occur.
<margin>The owl, prophet of ill fortune.</margin>The owl with its great head,
Prophet of ill fortune,
Hideous messenger of sorrow
In its voice, form, and color.
Throughout that place, be it summer or winter,
Two different rivers run,
Springing from different fountains
Which come from different veins.
One makes its waters so lovely,
Honeyed and savory,
That there is no one who does not drink of it,
Drinking much more than one ought.
He who can well quench his thirst,
So sweet and dear is this drink;
For those who drink the most of it
Burn with more thirst than before;
And no one drinks of it who does not become drunk,
But they are not delivered from their thirst,
For its sweetness so strongly entices them
That there is no one who swallows so much
That they do not wish to swallow more,
So well does sorrow know how to entice them;
For lechery <note>In this context, "lecherie" refers to a general craving for worldly pleasures or over-indulgence.</note> so pricks them
That everyone becomes hydropic. <term>hydropic: a medical condition (dropsy) where a person suffers from swelling and an unquenchable thirst.</term>

---

<margin>Description of the domain of Fortune.</margin>The river runs prettily
And makes such a murmuring
That it resounds like a drum and a timbrel,
Sweeter than a drum or a timbrel;
And there is no one who drinks of it
Whose whole heart does not rejoice.
Many are those who hasten to enter there,
Who are all ruined at the entrance;
For they have no power to go forward,
Hardly moving even with feet lifted.
Reluctantly they touch the sweet waters,
Although they approach the river;
A very little, and no more, do they drink.
And when they perceive the sweetness,
They would gladly go so far forward
<margin>Note on the inconstancy of Fortune.</margin>That they would plunge themselves entirely within.
Others pass so far forward
That they are washing in broad daylight,
And they praise themselves for the ease they have,
And thus they bathe and swim.
Then comes a light wave
Which casts them back to the bank
And puts them back on dry land,
Wherefore their whole heart burns and withers.

---

<margin>Note.</margin>So I will tell you of the other river,
In what manner one finds it:
Its waters are sulfurous,
Dark, and ill-tasting,
Like smoking chimneys,
All foaming with filth.
This one does not flow gently,
But descends so hideously
That it storms the air in its being
More than any horrible thunder.

Upon this river, I tell no lie,
Zephyrus <note>The gentle west wind of springtime.</note> never blows,
Nor do his breaths touch its waves,
Which are most hideous and deep;
<margin>Description of the second river of Fortune.</margin>
But the sorrowful North Wind <note>original: "vent de bise"; a cold, dry wind from the north or northeast.</note>
Has taken up battle against it,
So that it is necessary—and this is the truth—
For all its waves to be stirred up.
It makes its depths and its plains
Leap up in the manner of mountains,
Making them battle amongst themselves,
So much does the river strive to labor.
Many remain upon the bank,
Who sigh so much and weep so much,
Without putting an end or limit to their tears,
That they all plunge themselves into their own weeping,
And never cease to be dismayed
By the fear they have of drowning.
<margin>☜</margin>
But a man enters into this lower river
Not only up to his belly,
But is entirely buried there,
So deep is he plunged into its floods.
There they are squeezed and cast down
By the hideous, dreaded rivers;
The water absorbs and sinks many,
Many are battered by the waves;
And these floods swallow many up,
And they strike them down so deep
That they do not know how to keep the track
By which they might return;
Rather, they must remain there
Without ever returning to the heights.

This river goes twisting so much,
Straying through so many straits
With all its sorrowful venom,
That it enters the sweet river
And transforms its nature
By its stench and great coldness,
And imparts its pestilence to it,
Full of too much evil misfortune.
It makes it become bitter and troubled,
So much does it poison and disturb it,
And it takes away its tempered value
By its own intemperate heat;
Its good scent is entirely taken away,
So much stench does it give to its host.

High there, at the crest of the mountain,
On the slope, not on the plain,
<margin>The house and dwelling of Fortune.</margin>
Are precarious heights, ready to fall,
Poised to receive ill winds;
And there is the house of Fortune.
There is no storm nor lunar wind,
Nor any torment that one could offer,
That she must not suffer there.
There she receives all tempests,
Both the assaults and the vexations.
Zephyrus, the sweet wind without peer,
Blows there but rarely to temper
The horrible assaults of the harsh winds
With his soft and peaceful breaths.
One part of the hall
<margin>☜</margin>
Goes upward and the other sinks down,
And it seems as if it must fall,
So much can one see it hanging on the slope.
Such a disguised house,
I believe no man has ever described.
<margin>Note.</margin>
It shines greatly on one side, for noble
Is every wall of gold and silver;
And the entire roof is
Of a similar manufacture,
Blazing with precious stones,
Most dear and most virtuous <note>In the Middle Ages, "virtuous" stones were believed to possess literal healing or magical powers (virtues).</note>;
Everyone praises it as a marvel.
On the other side, the walls are of mud,
Which are not a full palm's width thick.
The other part is covered in thatch.
On one side it stands proud
For its great and marvelous beauty;
On the other side, it is all trembling and terrified,
Feeling itself so weak and decayed,
And split apart by cracks
In more than five hundred thousand places.
Furthermore, it is a thing that is not stable,
Being fickle and changeable;
Without a certain habitation,
Fortune moves within her house,
And when she wishes to be honored,
<margin>Note on prosperous Fortune.</margin>
She retreats to the gilded part.

Because of the length of the matter,
Which would be too long to tell in full.
That miserable and wicked man
Wished to set fire to Rome,
<margin>Nero, cruel and murderous.</margin>

When he had his brother killed,
And dismembered his poor mother
So that he might soon see
The place in which he was conceived.
And when he saw her dismembered,
According to the history remembered,

## How Seneca the wise man, teacher of the Emperor of Rome, was put into a bath to die; Nero caused him to perish thus.

After these words, without delay,
Nero had a bath prepared
And placed the wise man inside,
And then bled him, as the text says.
He made him shed so much of his blood
That he had to give up his soul;
And for this he had no cause,
Except for the habit he had:
Nero, who from his early childhood,
Used to show him reverence
As a disciple does to his master;
"But this must not be," he said,
"Nor is it right in any place,
That any man should show reverence
Once he is Emperor,

No matter if it be his master or his lord."
And because it annoyed Nero
When [Seneca] rose to meet him
<margin>The cause of Seneca's death.</margin>
And he saw his master coming,
He could not stop himself
From showing him reverence
By the force of habit.
Thus he put the wise man to death;
So did he hold the Empire of Rome,
The disloyal man of whom I tell you,
And over the East and the South,
The West and the North,
He held jurisdiction.

<margin>Riches and the goods of Fortune often harm men.</margin>
And if you can understand me well,
Through these words you can learn
That riches and reverences,
Dignities, honors, and powers,
And every grace of Fortune—
For I except not a single one—
Do not have such great strength
That they make those who have them good,
Nor worthy of possessing riches,
Great honors, and high status;
But if they have within them cruelty,
Pride, anger, or disloyalty,
The great estate in which they are enclosed
Rather shows and reveals it
More than if they had a very small estate,
Whereby they could not do such harm;
For when they use their power,
Their deeds accuse their wills,
Which give signs and demonstrations
That they are neither good nor worthy
<margin>Note.</margin>
Of riches, of dignities,
Of honors, and royalties.
Therefore people say a word
Commonly, which is very foolish,
And some hold it as true
By their foolish sense which leads them astray;
<margin>Honors often change character.</margin>
It is that "honors change manners," <note>original: "honneurs les meurs muent"; based on the Latin proverb *honores mutant mores*</note>
But such people argue poorly;
For honors do not create changes,
But rather provide signs and demonstrations
Of what manners they already had within them.

### The Romance of the Rose.

When they were in humble states,
Some held to such fine paths
That they attained great honors;
For those who are foolish and proud,
Disdainful and ill-tempered,
Once they have received honor,
They act as though they had always been
As you see them now,
If they had the power to be so.
Yet I do not call power
The knowledge of evil or disorder,
For the text <note>The author frequently refers to "Scripture" or "the writing," often meaning the *Consolation of Philosophy* by Boethius, which heavily influenced this section.</note> tells us well
<margin>Note.</margin>
That all power comes from good,
Where no one fails in doing well,
Except through weakness or defect.
And whoever was clear-sighted
Would see that evil is nothingness,
For thus says the text.
And if you care nothing for authority—
For you perhaps do not wish to believe
That every authority is true—
<margin>All power belongs to God.</margin>
I am ready for Reason to step forth,
For there is nothing that God cannot do;
But whoever wishes to tell the truth of it,
God has no power to do evil.
And if you are truly knowledgeable
And see that God is all-powerful,
Yet has no power to do evil,
Then you can clearly see
That whoever counts the essence of things,
Evil counts for nothing at all;
But just as a shadow settles
In the dark air, there is nothing there
Except a failure of light.
It is exactly the same way
With him in whom goodness is lacking;
For evil is not there except by the default
Of the goodness that should be present.
And the text says even more,
Which sums up the state of the wicked,
<margin>Note on the power of men.</margin>
That the wicked are not truly men <note>A Boethian concept: by abandoning their human end (goodness), the wicked lose their human nature and descend to the level of beasts.</note>;
And it brings forward living reasons for this,
But I do not wish to take the trouble now
To include all that I can find there,
Since you can prove it in writing.

But nonetheless, if it does not grieve you,
I can, through brief speech,
Bring forward some of the reasons;
It is that they abandon the common end
Toward which they strive and ought to strive,
Just as their morals conceive it;
<margin>Note well the sentences of Reason throughout.</margin>
It is the sovereign of all goods,
Which they call the primary good.
There is another reason, fair master,
Why the wicked have no true being,
If one understands the logic;
It is because they do nothing in an orderly way
In which they have placed their whole existence,
And all the things they do;
From which it follows for the clear-sighted
That the wicked are as nothing.

<margin>Fortune is always changeable.</margin>
Thus you see how Fortune serves
Down there and serves the world,
And how she acts to be despised
When from the wicked she chooses the worst,
And made him stand above all men
As lord and master of this world,
And thus caused Seneca <note>The Roman philosopher Seneca the Younger, who was forced to commit suicide by his former pupil, the Emperor Nero.</note> to be destroyed.
Therefore it is good to flee her grace,
Since no one, no matter how fortunate,
Can ever hold her with certainty.
Therefore I want you to despise her
And to place no value on her path.
Claudius <note>Claudian, a late Roman poet; the reference is specifically to his poem *In Rufinum*, which struggles with the prosperity of the wicked.</note> himself was
Astonished by this, and wished to blame
The gods because they consented
That the wicked should thus rise

But he himself responds to this
And explains the cause to us
As one who makes use of Reason,

So that they may torment them even more,
To be all the more heavily burdened;
For they are raised up high for this:
So that afterward one might see them
Tumble and fall from a greater height.

And if you grant me the liberty

The great Emperor himself,

For the more he called out,
The more they locked their doors and hid,
And no one wished to answer him,

### Reason to the Lover.

"Fair friend," said wise Reason,

For it is true—may it not displease you—

I would avenge myself quite differently

I can only take it upon myself
To discipline and teach you

Without blame and without defamation,

Upon my good and true word,

I do not wish to quarrel with people,

I have no desire to act with folly

Nor is any ugliness spoken by me;

<margin>Note the proverb.</margin>
But to speak of things that should be kept silent

The tongue must be bridled;

And through false pretense <note>The original French uses "simulation," meaning a calculated performance of an emotion one does not feel.</note>

That sorrowful, savage woman

And is so cruel and gluttonous

But if she allowed everyone to take from it,
She would never find herself with less.
He is a great fool who hoards such a thing;
It is like the candle in the lantern:

One would find no less fire there.
Everyone knows this comparison,
Unless their understanding is too dull.
If such women have need of you,
Serve them with your skills;
You must show them courtesy,
For that is a very fine thing—
But they must not perceive
That you intend to deceive them.

For they keep such a close watch

Afterward, you shall also conduct yourself

Thus they thoroughly deceived the maidens
By such tears and such trifles; <note>The original French "flauelles" refers to deceptive flattery or empty talk.</note>
Tears stain the hearts of such people,
Provided they suspect no further trickery; <note>original: "barat". In medieval literature, "barat" is a key term for deceit, fraud, or clever schemes.</note>

Never would they have mercy on you.

If you cannot go to them in person,

Whether by voice, by letter, or by tablet;
But never put your own name there,
For this speech must be kept hidden.
Let no person be named there,
So the matter will be better concealed,
Whether she be a lady or a woman of high rank. <note>original: "dame ou de lempire". This refers to women of various high social standings.</note>

<margin>The Lover must be secret in his affairs.</margin>
Write to her of your martyrdom,

Lovers are accused because of it,

Do not trust in children at all,

They are not good for carrying messages.
Children always have a flighty heart,

Because they are not at all wise.

Whether refused or well received,

But it would not please me at all

I want no lover to wait

Let him not fear that she will strike him,

Provided that he carries himself wisely.

Shame blush, or Danger shudder,

And show that you are a man
Virtuous enough to carry a great burden.
For nothing could please them so much
As such "force" as one knows how to apply; <note>This reflects a common medieval courtly trope where the lady's guardians (or her own modesty) must be "overcome" so she can grant her favors without losing her reputation for chastity.</note>
For many people are accustomed
To having such diverse manners
<margin>Note.</margin>
That they wish to give by force
What they dare not abandon freely,
And they pretend that what they have
Suffered and desired was taken from them.
But know that they would be sorrowful

If, through such a failure [on your part], they escaped,
Whatever joy they might show you;
Fear that they might seize you,
So angry would they be,
Though they might have grumbled at you.

But if, through open words,
You see them truly become angry
And defend themselves with genuine shame,
You must not stretch out your hand there;
But instead, you shall stay near,
Crying for mercy, and you shall wait
Until these three porters go away,
Leaving behind the grief and labor they cause,
And Fair Welcome remains all alone,
Who will make the rose safe for you.
Thus conduct yourself toward them
As one who is brave, valiant, and wise.
Take heed of Fair Welcome,
By what look he regards you,
What his state is and what his face;
Conform yourself to his manner.
<margin>The Lover must conform himself to his lady.</margin>
If she is old or mature,
Apply all your care
To carrying yourself wisely.
If she carries herself foolishly,
Then carry yourself foolishly,
And take pains to follow her lead.
If he is joyful, be joyful;
If he has sorrow, have sorrow.
If he laughs, laugh; weep if he weeps;
Thus hold yourself at every hour.
What he loves, you must love,
And what he blames, you must blame,
And praise what he shall praise,
For he will trust in you much more.
Do not think that a worthy lady
Loves a man who is [outwardly] wise but failing [in secrecy],
Who goes about by night
As if he were meant to dine,
And will sing from midnight on
To whomever it pleases or annoys;
She would fear being blamed for it,
<margin>The Lover must be secretive.</margin>
Held as cheap and defamed.
Such loves are very quickly known.

<summary>The Friend advises the Lover to mirror the moods of "Fair Welcome" and to persevere in taking the Rose, suggesting that the guardians' resistance is often a performative mask to preserve their honor.</summary>

# Leaf xviii.

Whether one plays the flute through the streets /
It matters little to those who know them;
foolish is he who attaches his heart to it.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'S' containing a human profile in the upper curve.</image-desc>If the wise man speaks of love
To a frivolous young lady,
And he pretends to be wise,
He will never have her heart /
Do not think it will happen to him
As long as he carries himself with such wisdom.
<margin>Conformity of manners in love</margin>He must make his manners match hers,
Or otherwise he is shamed /
For she will think him a mocker,
A fox <note>In medieval literature, the fox (Renard) is the ultimate symbol of cunning and trickery.</note> or an enchanter.
Soon the poor girl leaves him
And takes another with whom she can debase herself,
And she pushes the giver aside
Taking the worst of the crowd.
There she nourishes and hatches her love,
<margin>Comparison of love to the she-wolf.</margin>Just as the she-wolf does
Who makes her folly so much worse
That she takes the worst of all the wolves. <note>A common medieval folk belief held that female wolves would choose the ugliest or most wretched male in the pack to mate with; here it serves as a warning against ladies who reject "noble" suitors for base ones.</note>
If you can find a fair welcome,
And he <term>Fair Welcome: The personification of the lady's receptivity.</term> can play with you
At chess, at dice, or at the tables <note>The "tables" refers to backgammon or similar board games.</note>
Or other delightful games,
In these games, always take the worst,
And always be the loser
Whenever you take part in the game.
Lose whatever you stake there /
Let her take the lordship of the games.
Let your lady friend joyfully
Mock and laugh at your loss;
This will serve you greatly.
Praise all her ways,
<margin>The enemies of love.</margin>And her finery and her appearances.
Serve her with all your power;
Even when she is about to sit down,
Bring her a cushion or a stool;
Your suit will be the better for it.
If you can see any speck
<insert><image-desc>A manicule (pointing hand icon) directed towards the following line.</image-desc></insert>Falling upon her from anywhere,
Quickly remove that bit of dust,
Even if there was none there at all.
Or if her dress is too dusty,
Blow the dust away for her.
Do her will and give her ease,
And do everything that pleases her.
If you do this, have no doubt
That you will not be rejected,
But you will achieve your purpose
Just as I have proposed it.

### ¶ How the Lover shows to his lady friend
### His three enemies before him,
### And says that the time will soon come
### When he will complain of them to the judge.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'D' with stylized floral or leaf patterns.</image-desc>Sweet friend, what is this you say?
No sons <note>Referring to "sons of God" or young men.</note> are such hypocrites;
They would not do such devilry,
I never heard of such great trickery.
You want me to honor and serve
These people who are false and slavish /
They are surely slaves and false,
Except for Fair Welcome alone.
Is your advice truly such?
By this I would be a traitor and a murderer,
And I would serve only to deceive;
For I can truly say this:
When I want to make war on people,
I must first defy them.
At least allow me to defy
Slander <note>original: "Malle bouche." One of the primary antagonists in the poem, representing the malicious gossip that ruins reputations.</note> who spies on me so much,
Before I go about deceiving him /
And I pray that this wind
He has raised, that he might lower it,
Or else I must strike him /
<margin>One must challenge before striking.</margin>Either let it please him to make amends,
Or I shall take satisfaction myself /
Or else I shall complain
To the judge, who shall take vengeance for it.

### ¶ The lady friend to the Lover.

¶ Companions, companions—that is what they should be,
Those who engage in open warfare;
But Slander is too hidden,
He is not an open enemy.
For when he hates a man or woman,
Behind their backs he blames and defames them.
He is a very great traitor; may God shame him.

# The Romance of the Rose.

¶ Therefore it is only right that one should betray him.
<margin>One must not trust a traitor.</margin>
¶ Of the treacherous man I say this:
Since he has no faith, I do not trust him.
He hates people in his heart within,
And laughs at them with his mouth and teeth.
Never was I made better by such a man;
Let him watch out for me, and I for him.
It is right that he who has plotted a death
Should meet his own death through treason,
If one cannot otherwise
Avenge oneself more honorably.
<margin>Note.</margin>
¶ And if you wish to complain of him,
Do you think you can silence his tongue?
You could never prove such a thing,
Nor find sufficient witnesses.
And even if you had proved it well just now,
He still would not keep silent about it;
The more you speak of it, the more he will babble;
You will lose more by it than he will.
The more the matter is known,
The more your own shame is increased.
<margin>He who thinks to lower his shame only increases it.</margin>
¶ For such a man thinks to lower his shame,
Who increases and raises it much more.
To pray that he be struck down
And to demand that he be beaten—
That would not strike him down at all,
No, by God, even if one beat him.
To wait for him to make amends to you,
To that goal one must not aspire;
I would never accept amends from him,
Even if he offered, but rather I would forgive him.
And if there is a challenge,
I swear to you truly that
Fair Welcome <note>Fair Welcome (Bel Accueil) is the personification of the lady's receptivity and kind spirit, currently imprisoned by her guardians.</note> will be shackled,
So that you will never see him;
Or he will be bound in rings,
Burned in the fire or drowned in the waters.
Then you will have a heart more sorrowful
Than ever Charlemagne or Roland had
When he met his death at Roncevaux
Through Ganelon, who deceived him. <note>A reference to the *Song of Roland*, where the traitor Ganelon's betrayal leads to the death of the hero Roland and his peers at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass.</note>

->The Lover to the Friend.<-

¶ This is not what I am seeking;
Let him go to the devil, I command it.
I would wish to see him hanged
Since he has ruined my plans. <note>original: "ma mon poiure espendu" – literally "spilled my pepper," a Middle French idiom meaning to ruin one's business or cause frustration.</note>

->The Friend to the Lover.<-

¶ Companion, do not trouble yourself with hanging;
Another vengeance must be taken.
Such an office does not suit you;
It is better suited to justice.
But you must use treason
If you wish to follow my counsel.

->The Lover to the Friend.<-

¶ Companion, I agree to this counsel;
I shall never depart from your agreement.
Nevertheless, if you knew
Any art by which you could
Teach me in another manner
To take the castle more easily,
If you are willing to teach it to me,
I would very much like to hear it.

->The Friend to the Lover.<-

¶ Yes, a path that is fair and noble,
But it is not good for poor people.
Companion, to defeat the castle
One may choose several ways
Without my art and without my doctrine,
And break even to the root
The fortress that has been built.
The gate would be held there for a year,
For then everyone would let it be taken;
Nothing exists that could defend them from it,
No one would dare utter a word.
The path has the name "Too Much Giving." <note>original: "trop donner"</note>
<margin>Note on foolish generosity.</margin>
"Foolish Giving" <term>Folle Largesse: The vice of excessive or reckless spending/generosity to win favor.</term> founded it,
Where many lovers have sunk.
I know the path well,
For I came out of it the day before yesterday,
And I have been a pilgrim there
For more than a winter and a summer.
If you take "Giving" to the right,
Without turning to the left hand,
You will already have, in more than one bowshot,
The path beaten and trodden
Without wearing out your shoe at all.
There you will see the wall crumble
And the towers and turrets shake,
However strong or beautiful they may be,
And by themselves they will open the gates.

<summary>The Friend advises the Lover on how to deal with traitors and introduces the concept of "Folle Largesse" (Foolish Giving) as the most effective, albeit expensive, way to bypass the castle's defenses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of the "Friend" to the Lover. After advising on how to deal with social obstacles and the guardians of the lady’s heart, the Friend now explains the vital role that wealth plays in the "Castle of Love." He warns that without money, the path to love is barred, introducing the personified figures of Wealth and Poverty.</meta>

<page-num>xlix</page-num>
<header>Leaf xlix.</header>

<margin>
A way to obtain the Castle of Love.
</margin>

For the guards act as if they were dead.
On that side, the castle is
So weak that a small cake
Is harder to break in four
Than the walls are to knock down.
The castle would be taken there quickly;
It would not require so great an army
As King Charlemagne <note>The King of the Franks and later Holy Roman Emperor, famous in medieval literature for his massive military campaigns.</note> needed
When he wished to conquer Germany.

<margin>
Note.
</margin>

On this path that I name for you,
A poor man never enters;
No one can lead a poor man there,
And no one can succeed on his own.
But he who had Wealth to lead him in
Would immediately know the path
Just as well as I would know it,
Even if I had never learned it so well.
And if it pleases you, you shall know it,
For you will have learned it soon enough

<margin>
Poverty cannot enter the Garden of Love.
</margin>

If you can simply have great possessions
To afford outrageous expenses.
But I will not put you there;
Poverty has denied me the passage.
At the exit, I was forbidden;
I spent all my wealth there,
And all that I received from others.
I deceived all my creditors,
So that I could pay none of them,
Even if I were to be hanged or drowned.
"Never come back," she said,
"Since there is nothing left to spend."
You will enter there with great difficulty

<margin>
Wealth: the means to enjoy one's loves.
</margin>

Unless Wealth leads you there.
But for all those whom she conducts inside,
They refuse a guide upon their return.
Upon entering, she will stay with you,
But she will never cling to you <note>Original: "se prendra"—meaning she will not necessarily remain your permanent possession once spent.</note>;
And of this much be certain:
If you enter there by any luck,
You shall never leave, evening or morning,

<margin>
Poverty chases away lovers.
</margin>

Unless Poverty puts her hand to it,
By whom there is distress and delay.
Foolish Generosity <note>original: "Folle largesse"—the personification of reckless and unmeasured spending.</note> dwells within,
Who thinks of nothing but games
And making outrageous expenditures;
Who spends his coins in such a way
As if he harvested them from granaries,
Without counting and without measuring,
No matter how long it must endure.

<insert>
¶ How Poverty makes very shameful requests to Wealth, who does not value or prize any of her words, but gives her refusals for everything.
</insert>

<image-desc>
A woodcut illustration depicting two allegorical figures in a landscape with trees. On the left stands a woman in elegant, layered robes and a headdress (representing Richesse). On the right, a figure in simple, coarse garments with a hood (representing Pourete) stands in a humble or supplicating posture, gesturing toward the first figure.
</image-desc>

Harshness stands at the other end,
Full of shame and misfortune,
Suffering great torments in the heart.
She makes so many shameful requests,
And receives so many harsh refusals,
That she has neither good deeds nor good words,
Nor anything delectable or pleasing.
Never will she be so well-doing

<margin>
Note on Poverty.
</margin>

That everyone does not blame her works;
Everyone reviles and defames her.
But do not let Poverty concern you,
Except to think, however things go,
How you might avoid her.
Nothing can so grieve a man
As falling into poverty.

<margin>
Note well the misfortunes that happen through poverty.
</margin>

The indebted man knows this well,
Who has spent all his own;
Many a man is hanged because of poverty.
Well do those know it and say it
Who must beg against their will.
Much pain must they suffer
Before people give them of their own.
Also, those may know it
Who wish to have joy in love;
For because of this, Love has nothing to feed on,
As Ovid <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, the Roman poet whose works, like the *Ars Amatoria*, were the primary authority on love for medieval writers.</note> confesses.

<sig>k i</sig>

<summary>The Friend explains that the Castle of Love is easily breached by those with money, while personified Poverty is a source of shame and a barrier to romantic success. The text emphasizes that love cannot flourish without the financial means to support "Foolish Generosity" and "Wealth."</summary>
