<meta>This page continues the "Friend's" discourse to the Lover. Following the previous advice on how to adapt one's manners to suit a lady's whims, the Friend now shifts to a personal anecdote. He uses his own life story to illustrate the dangers of "foolish generosity" and the fickle nature of social circles, specifically focusing on how poverty reveals the difference between fair-weather companions and true friends.</meta>

<header>The Romance of the Rose.</header>

Poverty makes a man much worse,
causes him to be hated and delivers him to martyrdom /
and even takes away the senses of those same men.
You have no understanding of poverty /
but strive well to believe
my words, which are proven and true /
for know that I have proven this
by tested experience,
all that I preach to you here
in my own person.
I know well how much poverty weighs
by my own hardship and my shame,
sweet friend, more than you could know /
for you have never suffered such want.
<margin>Note on good correction.</margin>
You ought to trust in me;
I say this to correct and guide you /
for he who corrects himself through the example of others
leads a very happy life.
I used to be called a valiant man
and was loved by all my companions,
and I spent freely
<image-desc>manicule</image-desc>
in all places and very generously,
as long as I was considered rich.
Now I have become poor
through spending and foolish generosity <note>The medieval concept of "largesse" (generosity) was a knightly virtue, but "folle largesse" referred to the vice of wasting one's inheritance on those who do not deserve it.</note>
which have put me in such distress
<margin>In adversity, there are no friends.</margin>
that I have nothing except with great difficulty—
nothing to drink and nothing to eat,
nothing for my feet and nothing to wear—
so much does poverty make me feel anguish,
stripping me of every good thing.
Now know, companions, that as soon
as Fortune had placed me thus,
I lost every one of my friends,
except for one single man, I truly believe,
who alone remained with me /
Fortune thus took them from me
through the poverty that was in me.
She took them by her own hand—no, I lie—
rather, she simply took back what was hers /
for I know well that if they had been mine,
they would never have left me for her sake;
she did me no wrong in anything
when she took back her own things.
They were hers, truly / but I knew nothing of it,

for I had bought them so dearly
with heart and body and wealth
that I believed I possessed them all.
And then when it came to the end,
when I did not have a single penny's worth,
<margin><image-desc>manicule</image-desc> All friends flee in adversity.</margin>
all those friends fled away
from me / and they all abandoned me,
each one making a mocking face at me <note>original: "la moe" — a grimace or pout used to show contempt.</note>
when they saw me beneath the wheel
of Fortune, struck down and overturned;
thus has my poverty beaten me.
Yet I must not complain at all /
for she was courteous to me without pretense,
and yet I did not deserve it /
for I saw so clearly all around me,
she anointed my eyes with such an eye-salve <term>Eye-salve (collyre): A medicinal ointment for the eyes; here, a metaphor for the harsh clarity that suffering brings to one's perception.</term>
which she made me build and concoct
as soon as poverty arrived,
which took more than twenty friends from me—
truly, by God, I do not lie,
more than four hundred and fifty.
Not even Lynceus, who set his eyes upon it, <note>In Greek mythology, Lynceus the Argonaut was famous for his supernatural sight, capable of seeing through walls or underground.</note>
saw then what I am telling you /
for Fortune immediately made room
and showed me the good love, full-faced,
of my one good friend,
through the poverty that met me,
whom I would never have known
if my need had not arrived /
but when he knew of it, he came running,
and he succored me as best he could,
and offered me all that he had
because he knew of my need.

### ¶ How the Friend recalls here
### to the Lover that one single true friend
### he had in his poverty,
### who offered him all his possessions.

At this point my friend said to me
when he had approached me:
"My dear friend, I want you to know
that here is my body and my wealth;
you have as much of it as I do.
Take from it without asking leave /"

<summary>The Friend recounts how he lost his wealth through "foolish generosity" and was abandoned by hundreds of false friends, only to discover one true friend who offered everything. The passage serves as a philosophical meditation on the Wheel of Fortune and the clarifying power of poverty.</summary>

--- Page 97 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse of the Friend (Ami) to the Lover. Having previously discussed trust and betrayal, the Friend now speaks of the unparalleled value of a true friend in times of poverty and need, contrasting this with the hypocrisy of "sturdy beggars" and the legendary loyalty of Theseus and Pirithous.</meta>

# Folio 50
## Signature k ii

<margin>
A good, true, and faithful friend is worth more than all worldly wealth.
</margin>

But how can you know
Everything of which you have great need?
For a friend does not value a prune <note>original: "ne prise une prune" — a common medieval idiom meaning "to value something at nothing," similar to "not worth a straw."</note>
Worldly goods compared to a friend,
Nor even natural gifts,
Since we have come together thus;
And as we are well-armed,
Known to each other, and firm in love;
For we found one another out
So well that we found ourselves friends;
For no one can know without testing
If he can find a loyal friend.
All my goods are pledged to you,
So powerful are the bonds of love
That for your healing, he said,
You may put me in prison,
Hold me for security and as a hostage,
And sell my goods or put them in hock.
He did not even stop there,
So that he might not go about flattering me,
Instead, he made me take by force;
For I did not dare reach out my hand,
So terribly ashamed was I
By the hideous law of poverty.

<margin>
Shame in speaking of one's necessities.
</margin>

He who has shame keeps his mouth closed,
So that he does not dare speak of his need;
But he suffers, stays enclosed, and hides,
So that no one may know his poverty,
And shows the most beautiful face outside;
Exactly so did I do then.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' containing a profile of a human face.</image-desc>

Those are not at all the same
As the sturdy beggars <note>original: "mēdiēs puissās" — This refers to "sturdy beggars" or powerful mendicants, often a critique directed at friars or those who could work but chose to beg through deception.</note>
Who go about thrusting themselves everywhere,
Flattering with sweet words,
And show the ugliest face outside
To all those whom they encounter,
And hide away the most beautiful face within
To deceive those who give to them,
And go about saying they are poor
While they have fat portions
With great piles of money in their treasury;
But for now, I will keep silent about them,
For I could certainly say so much
That I would go from bad to worse;
For hypocrites always hate
The truths that are spoken against them.

<margin>
A note on feigned friends and hypocrites.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' containing a figure of a person (likely a clerk or scholar) seated at a desk or lectern.</image-desc>

Thus this aforementioned friend
Has put his effort into my single heart, <note>original: "mon sol cueur"</note>
And I am by my own sense transformed,
Destroyed, defamed, and seized,
Without occasion for any other desert
Than the aforementioned loss
From all people generally,
Except from you alone
Who do not lose your love;
But you adhere to my heart,
For which, as long as I live,
I shall never cease to love you.
If it please God, may you take heart in it;
But nevertheless, you would lose me
As far as bodily company goes
In this earthly life
When the final day comes to us,
When death takes its right from our bodies;
For that day, I recall well,
Will take nothing from us but the body
And all the things that belong
To the physical substances.

<margin>
A good friend is not lost even unto death.
</margin>

For I know well that we two shall die,
All too much sooner than we would wish;
For death disassembles all companions;
But there is no hope of remaining together.
Yet I know well and certainly
That if loyal love does not lie,
If you live and I should die,
I would always live in your heart,
And if you died before me,
You would always live in my heart
After your death through memory;
Just as, according to history,
Pirithous lived after his death, <note>original: "Pyttheus" — a medieval spelling of Pirithous, the companion of Theseus.</note>
Whom Theseus loved so strongly.

<margin>
The love of Theseus for Pirithous.
</margin>

He sought him so much, he followed him so much;
For he held him within his heart.
He had loved him so much upon the earth
That he went to seek him in hell; <note>Refers to the Greek myth where Theseus descended into the underworld to help Pirithous rescue Persephone.</note>
And poverty does worse than death;
For it torments and kills both soul and body.

<summary>The Friend explains that a true companion is the only remedy for the shame of poverty, contrasting this genuine bond with the deceit of "sturdy beggars" who feign need while hiding wealth. He cites the mythological friendship of Theseus and Pirithous as the ultimate example of love that transcends even death and the underworld.</summary>
<keywords>loyalty, poverty, hypocrisy, sturdy beggars, Theseus, Pirithous, death, friendship, worldly goods</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Friend’s" counsel to the Lover. The previous page established that the "Castle of Love" is easily breached by those with money, but barred to the poor. The Friend now elaborates on the moral and social degradations of poverty, contrasting it with the social power of gift-giving.</meta>

<header>The Romance of the Rose.</header>

<margin>In poverty there is no great loyalty.</margin> So long as one or the other remains
Not just for a single hour,
It adds to their damnation
Theft and perjury,
Along with every other hardship
By which each one is heavily struck;
Which death does not wish to do,
But rather makes them withdraw from it all;
And so it makes them remember
That all temporal torment must end;
For however grievous it may be to them,
In a single hour it causes them grief.
Therefore, listen well to my sermon,
<margin>The saying of Solomon.</margin> Remembering Solomon,
Who was King of Jerusalem;
For many good things are said of him.
He says, if you take good heed:
"Fair son, keep yourself from poverty
All the days that you have to live."
<margin>☞</margin> And he gives the reason in his book:
For in this earthly life
It is better to die than to be too poor.
For those who appear poor,
Their own brothers will hate them
Because of their very doubtful poverty.
He speaks of that wretched state
That we call indigence,
Which brings all things to ruin.
There were never people so despised
<margin>Some poor people are too contemptible.</margin> As those whom one calls indigent;
As witness, even the law rejects them,
Those who practice the written law,
Because in the law they are proclaimed
Equivalent to the infamous. <note>In medieval law, the extremely poor (indigents) were often legally classified alongside "infamous" persons (criminals or those of ill repute), meaning their testimony in court was considered unreliable or invalid.</note>

<image-desc>Large ornamental initial 'T' with floral patterns.</image-desc>
**T**oo much is poverty an ugly thing.
But nevertheless, I dare to say truly
That if you had enough goods,
Jewels or hoarded coins,
And you wished to give as much
As you were able to promise,
Then you would gather buds and roses,
However much they were shut or enclosed.
But you are not so rich,
And yet you are neither miserly nor stingy.

Give then, in a friendly way,
Small gifts, reasonably,
<margin>From small means, a small alms.</margin> So that you do not fall into poverty,
Indigence, or beggary.
Many would mock you
Who would help you with nothing.
So it is very fitting that, as a present,
You give a gift of new fruit
In cloths or in baskets.
<margin>Note on the manner of giving.</margin> Do not be slow in this;
Give them walnuts or cherries,
Cornels, plums, or fresh wild cherries,
Chestnuts, quinces, also hazelnuts,
Peaches, grapes, or service-berries, <note>Original: "aliettes," likely the fruit of the service tree or sorb-apple.</note>
Grafted medlars and raspberries,
Sloes, or joyous wild plums,
Or have some noble blackberries;
Send them such new fruits.
And even if you have bought them,
<margin>Note.</margin> Say that they were presented to you
By your friends come from afar,
Even if you had obtained them by purchase.
Or give crimson roses,
Primroses or violets
In bouquets according to the season;
Such gifts are made with good reason.
Know that gifts drive people mad;
They take away the words of slanderers,
For if they knew ill of the givers,
They would say only all the good in the world.
Fine gifts of wine and meat

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the corruption of modern love compared to the idealized "Golden Age" of antiquity, a common theme in Jean de Meun's continuation of the Romance of the Rose.</meta>

# The Romance of the Rose.

Whoever has such a reputation for wisdom.
Nevertheless, if he were to ask me
For advice to know if it would be good
For him to compose pretty rhymes,
Motets, virelays, or little songs
To send to a lady
To hold her interest and support his suit—
Alas, that would matter very little;
A beautiful poem has little value there.
The poem might perhaps be praised,
But that would accomplish very little;
Rather, a large, heavy purse,
<margin>Note.</margin>
Well-stocked with many a bezant <note>A gold coin originally from Byzantium, used here to signify great wealth.</note>,
If she saw it appear in that place,
She would quickly run to it with open arms.
Women are so very greedy
That they seek nothing but pursefuls of money.
<margin><image-desc>pointing hand</image-desc></margin>
In the old days, it used to be otherwise;
Everything has gone from bad to worse.
In the days of old, our first fathers,
And also our first mothers,
As the written word testifies—
Through which we know of these matters—
Were loyal and refined lovers,
Without the roots of greed.
And that age, most precious,
Was not so luxurious
In either clothing or fine foods;
Instead, they gathered acorns in the woods
For their bread, their meat, and their fish.
And they searched through the bushes,
Through vales, plains, and mountains,
For apples, pears, walnuts, and chestnuts,
<margin>
The abstinence of the ancients, living on simple things alone.
</margin>
Blackberries, rosehips, and sloes,
Raspberries, strawberries, and hawthorn berries;
Beans and peas and such small things,
Like fruits, roots, and herbs.
And they took the ears of the corn,
And they ate the roots
Without putting them in a press or a kiln.
Good honey flowed from the oaks,
Which they commonly ate,
And they drank simple water
Without seeking spiced wine or claret <note>term: pigment/clare (sweetened, spiced wines highly prized in the Middle Ages)</note>,
For no prepared wine was drunk then.

<column-break/>

<margin>
At the beginning of the world, the earth was not labored, for the people were content.
</margin>
At that time, the earth was not plowed,
But just as God had adorned her,
She brought forth from herself everything
With which each person comforted themselves.
They did not seek out salmon or pike,
But rather wore shaggy skins
And made garments of wool
Without dyeing them with herbs or seeds,
Just as they came from the beasts.
They were covered with broom-plants,
With little leaves and branches—
Their small houses and hamlets.
They made pits in the earth,
And used caves and thick trunks.
<margin><image-desc>pointing hand</image-desc></margin>
Into hollow oaks they would retreat
When they feared the tempests,
The people, when bad weather appeared,
And there they went for safety
To avoid that storm
And to cast themselves out of peril.

And when they wished to sleep at night,
Instead of quilts, they brought
To their places heaps of sheaves,
Of leaves, of moss, or of herbs.
<margin>Note.</margin>
And when the air was calmed
And the weather clear and very pleasant,
The wind soft also and agreeable,
As if in a permanent springtime,
When the birds in their Latin <note>original: "latin" — a common medieval metaphor for the song of birds, implying a language of their own.</note>
Study each morning
To salute the dawn of the day,
Which made their hearts change.
<margin>
<image-desc>pointing hand</image-desc>
Zephyrus and Flora, masters of flowers.
</margin>
Zephyrus <note>The West Wind.</note> and Flora, his wife,
Who is the mistress and lady of flowers,
For these two make every flower be born;
Flowers know no other master,
For throughout the world, truly,
He and she go about sowing them.

<meta>This page continues the monologue of the Jealous Husband (Le Jaloux) from the Roman de la Rose, a seminal 13th-century allegorical poem. The husband is in the midst of a misogynistic tirade against his wife, accusing her of infidelity and vanity.</meta>

# The Romance of the Rose.

Since I cannot chastise you otherwise.
You have built a spiteful trap for me
By feeling no shame for such misdeeds.
Everyone knows well that you are lying.
For me—alas, sorrowful for me—
I locked great evils within my own misfortunes
And was villainously deceived
When I first accepted your faith <note>original: "vostre foy"; referring to the marriage vow</note>
On the day of your wedding,
Only to give me such mockery
By putting on such a show of vanity.
Whom do you think you are tricking?
Certainly, I do not have the power
To look upon such finery
That these gluttonous scoundrels,
Who go spying on whores,
Admire and gaze upon in you
When they escort you through these streets.
For whom are you roasting such chestnuts <note>A metaphor for preparing charms or attractions for others</note>
Which cause me so much resentment?
You use me as both cloak and rain-shield <note>Meaning she uses him for protection/status while seeking pleasure elsewhere</note>
When I lean near you at present.
<margin>Note.</margin> I see that you appear more simple
In this surcoat and in that wimple <note>A head covering worn by medieval women</note>
Than turtledoves or pigeons;
It matters not to you if they are short or long <note>Referring to the cut of the garments or perhaps the duration of her flirtations</note>
When I am alone. By the good saints,
Even if someone gave me a hundred gold coins <note>term: besans (bezants); gold coins originally from Byzantium, used here to denote great wealth</note>
Though I am usually of a noble nature,
If I did not refrain for the sake of shame,
I would not hold back from beating you
To utterly strike down your pride.
And know that it does not please me at all
That there should be such finery in you,
Whether for the carol <note>term: lakarolle (carole); a popular medieval circle dance accompanied by singing</note> or for the dance,
Except only in my presence.

<margin>👉</margin> Elsewhere I can no longer hide
What goes on between you and that bachelor,
Robichonnet with the green hat,

Who comes so quickly at your call;

That I will make you quiet and still.
And you shall never go out without me,
But shall serve me here at home,
Riveted in good rings of iron.
The devils make you so intimate
With these scoundrels full of flattery
<margin>Woman subject to man.</margin> From whom you should rightly be a stranger.
Did I not take you to serve me?
Do you think to deserve my love
By getting to know these filthy rascals,
Just because they have such bold hearts
And they find you so brazen?
You are a wicked jade <note>original: "ribaude"; a term for a woman of loose morals</note>
In whom I will put no trust;
Satan surely made me marry.

<margin>¶ Theophrastus says that one should not marry.</margin> But if I had believed Theophrastus <note>note: Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher; the text refers to the "Golden Book on Marriage," a lost work cited by St. Jerome that was a staple of medieval anti-marriage literature.</note>
I would never have had a wedded wife.
For he does not consider a man wise
Who takes a wife in marriage,
Be she beautiful or ugly, poor or rich;
For he says, and posts it as truth
In his noble "Golden Book" <note>original: "liure aureole"; referring to the Liber Aureolus de Nuptiis</note>
Which ought to be read in the schools,
That there is a life too grievous,
Full of labor and of pain,
So much contention and brawling
Caused by the pride of foolish women,
And of dangers and reproaches.

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the tribulations of marriage and the nature of women, transitioning from the complaints of husbands to the classical examples of virtuous women like Penelope and Lucretia.</meta>

# Leaf liii.

<margin>A man’s purgatory is to have a brawling wife.</margin>
What women say with their mouths,
Both in requests and in complaints,
Which they find many an occasion for.
It is a very great pain to guard them
In order to delay their foolish sorrows;
And he who wishes to take a poor wife
Must apply himself to feeding her,
And to clothing and warming her;
And if he thinks to advance himself so much
That he takes one who is very rich,
He will have great torment to suffer,
Finding her so proud and fierce,
And so conceited and boastful,
That she will prize her husband
Not at all; and everywhere she will despise
His parents and all his lineage
With her overbearing language.

<margin>Women are troublesome in all things.</margin>
¶ If she is beautiful, everyone runs to her,
Everyone pursues and honors her,
Everyone knocks there, everyone labors there,
Everyone wrestles there, everyone battles there;
Everyone studies how to serve her,
Everyone is around her and deceives <note>original: "pypent" - to pipe or chirp like a bird, used here to mean trickery or cajoling</note> her,
Everyone reaches for her and covets her,
And in the end they exploit her so much,
For a tower besieged on all sides
Never escapes being taken.
If she is ugly, she wishes to please everyone;
<margin>A woman's beauty deceives man.</margin>
And how could anyone manage
To guard that which everyone wars against,
Or to hate all those who see her?
If he goes to war with the whole world,
He has no power to live on earth;
No one can keep them from being taken
When they willingly allow themselves to be sought.
<margin>Note.</margin>

<margin>Penelope, chaste woman of Greece.</margin>
¶ One could even take Penelope,
If one set their mind to taking her;
Though there is no better woman in Greece;
So too would be Lady Lucretia,
Even though she killed herself
After she had been taken by force
By the son of King Tarquinius,
As Titus Livius <note>The Roman historian Livy</note> says.
Neither her husband nor all her kin
Could be her protectors,

<margin>Lucretia put herself to death.</margin>

<column-break/>

Despite the effort any of them made,
She killed herself before them.
They begged her to leave off her grief
And told her many fine reasons;
Even her loyal husband
Comforted her piteously
And with a good heart forgave her
The whole deed, and preached to her,
And studied to find
Divine reason to prove to her
That her body had not sinned
When the heart does not commit the sin;
<margin>No sin exists if it is not voluntary, as Saint Augustine says.</margin>
For the body is never a sinner
If the heart is not a consenting party.
But she, who carried her grief,
Held a knife in her bosom,
So hidden that no one saw it,
Until she took it to strike her heart,
And she answered him without shame:
"Fair lord, whoever may forgive me
The sin which weighs on me so heavily,
It is not fitting that I drink of the pardon;
It does not excuse me from the pain."

### ¶ How Lucretia, through great ire,
### Pierced, broke, and tore her heart,
### And fell dead upon the earth face-down
### Before her husband and kin.

Then, full of great anguish, she strikes
Her heart so that it splits, and she falls
Dead to the ground before them;
But first she prayed that they would labor
So much for her that they would avenge her death.
This example seeks to provide
Better assurance for women
That no force should move them <note>To sin or lose their honor</note>.

# The Romance of the Rose.

She dares not oppose her,
So that she can conquer nothing there.
Ugliness has spoiled the entire affair
When she attacked Chastity,
Who ought to have defended and guarded her,
Even hiding her, if she could,
Between her flesh and her chemise;
For there she ought to have placed her.
<margin>Ugliness with Beauty.</margin>
Beauty is certainly much to be blamed,
Who truly ought to have loved her [Chastity]
And procured for her, if she could,
A very good peace between them.
At least she did all in her power,
Since she put herself at her great mercy,
If she were courtly and very wise;
<margin>Note the saying of Virgil.</margin>
For a well-made person should owe her homage,
Not bring her shame and disgrace;
For the text bears witness to us
In the sixth book of Virgil <note>original: "livre sixte de Vergille"; referring to the Aeneid</note>
By the authority of the Sibyl,
That no one who lives chastely
Can come to damnation.
<margin>Note on Beauty</margin>
Wherefore I swear by the Celestial King
That a woman who wishes to be beautiful,
Or who strives to resemble beauty,
And admires herself and exerts herself
To adorn and deck herself out,
Does not wish to wage war on Chastity,
<margin>Chastity has many enemies.</margin>
Who certainly has many enemies.
Throughout cloisters and abbeys,
All are armed against her;
They will never be so secluded
That they do not hate Chastity so strongly
That they all gape to do her harm.
All do homage to Venus,
Without heed for tribute or damage,
And they deck themselves and paint their faces
To mock those who look at them,
And go trailing through the streets
To see, or to be seen at that time,
And to make the companions desire
<margin>The gestures of dissolute women.</margin>
To want to lie with them;
And they make a great display of finery <term>cointises: elaborate ornaments or fashionable clothing</term>
In the streets and in these churches,
None of them would do so

<column-break/>

If she did not think she was being seen,
And that for this reason she might sooner please
Those whom she might deceive.
But certainly, whoever takes this into account,
Women do great shame to God,
Like foolish and straying women,
When they do not remain satisfied
With the beauty that God gives them.
<margin>Dissolute women are much to be blamed</margin>
Each has upon her head a crown
Of little flowers of gold or of silk,
And grows proud and decks herself out
When she goes showing herself through the Town;
Whereby she greatly debases herself,
The most unhappy one, the weary one,
When she wishes to draw a viler and lower thing
Of silk upon her head
To increase or perfect her beauty;
And thus she goes despising God,
And holds Him to be insufficient,
And so thinks in her foolish heart
<margin>Note.</margin>
That God did her too great an outrage
When He fashioned her beauty,
That He went about it too negligently.
So she seeks beauty from creatures
That God makes in many forms,
Either of metals or of little flowers,
Or of other strange little things.
Without fail, it is the same with men,
<margin>Note on the presumption of many men.</margin>
Who put into various forms
Their chaplets and their finery
Upon the beauties that God has placed
In us; then we misbehave too much
When we do not hold ourselves satisfied
With the beauties He has given us
Above all born creatures.
But I have no care for these trifles;
I want sufficient clothing
Which keeps me from the cold and the heat;
For likewise, he who pays attention,
It protects both my body and head
From wind, from rain, and from tempest—
Lamb's fur on coarse cloth
As well as <unclear>pers foutre d'escupreaux</unclear>. <note>Likely referring to expensive imported dyed fabrics or furs</note>
My money, it seems to me, is lost

<meta>This page continues the monologue of the Jealous Husband (Le Jaloux) from the Roman de la Rose, a seminal medieval French poem. The speaker is berating his wife, accusing her of infidelity and general deceitfulness.</meta>

# leaf. lvi.

When I buy for you a father’s robe
Of camelot <note>a costly fabric made of silk and camel hair</note> or of brunette <note>a fine dark wool</note>
Of green or of scarlet dye
And line it with fur of green and gray,
It only makes you run into the ditch
And dance in circles and wheels
Through the dust and through the mud;
You prize neither God nor me.
Even at night when you lie
Near me in bed, completely naked,
You cannot be held;
<margin>Note.</margin>
For when I wish to embrace you
To kiss you and to play,
And I am very strongly heated,
You grumble like a demon <note>original: "mauffe," a medieval term for a devil or bogeyman</note>
And toward me, whatever I do,
You will not turn your face;
Instead, you feign being very ill,
And you sigh and you complain,
And you act so disdainful <note>original: "faictes le dangereux," a courtly term for playing hard to get or being haughty</note>
That I become so very afraid
That I do not dare to assail you,
So great is my fear of failing.
When I wake up after sleeping,
I wonder to myself with great marvel
How those rascals succeed,
Who keep you clothed by day,
If you twist yourself away like this.
<margin><image-desc>manicule pointing right</image-desc></margin>
When you sport with them,
And do as much for them by night
As you do to me by day and night—
But you have no lack of desire for that!
Rather, you go singing and dancing
Through those gardens and through those meadows
With such disloyal rascals
Who lead my bride away
<margin>Jealousy is a great evil</margin>
Upon the green grass in the dew,
And go there despising me,
And saying among themselves in spite:
"This is to spite the villainous jealous one!
May his flesh now be delivered to the wolves
And his bones to the rabid dogs,
By whom my deeds are shamed."
<margin>Note.</margin>
It is because of you, false beggar-woman,
And because of your foolish ways.

<column-break/>

Filthy slut, smooth whore!
May your body never leave this year <note>A curse wishing for her death or confinement</note>
Since it is delivered to such people.
By you I am delivered to shame;
By you and your lechery
I am placed in the confraternity
Of Saint Arnoul, lord of the cuckolds,
From which no one can be rescued.
<margin>Note on the lord of the cuckolds.</margin>
He who has a wife, to my knowledge,
No matter how much he guards and spies,
Even if he had more than a thousand eyes,
They all get themselves "knocked" <note>original: "hurtebillier," a vulgar slang term for sexual intercourse</note>
And there is nothing that can stop it.
And if it happens that the deed fails,
The will shall never fail;
Therefore, if she can, she will come to the deed,
For the will always carries her away.
But you are strongly comforted in this
<margin>Note the saying of Juvenal.</margin>
By Juvenal <note>Roman satirist known for his misogynistic Sixth Satire</note> who speaks of the trade
That one calls "patching up,"
Saying it is the least of the sins
With which your desires are stained;
For their nature commands them
That each one intends to do worse.
Does one not see how stepmothers
Give poisons to their stepsons,
And make charms and sorceries
And other great devilries
That no one could recount,
No matter how fully he could think.

---

<margin>Note.</margin>
All of you are, will be, or were
Whores in deed or in desire,
And whoever searched you very well
Would find you all to be whores;
For he who cannot extinguish the deed,
No one can constrain the will.
<margin>An obstinate woman does not change for a beating.</margin>
Such an advantage have all women
Who make themselves mistresses of their wills;
One cannot change their hearts
For beating or for scolding;
But he who could well change them
Would have the lordship of hearts;
But let us leave that which cannot be,
Fair sweet God and fair celestial King.

## L iiii

And when the lady feels and notices
This torment and this riotous behavior
From this seductive Old Woman <note>original: "Vielle" - likely referring to the character of the Old Woman or a personification of vice</note>

She would wish him away at Lisieux,
Or truly as far as Romania.
I will say more: I do not believe

She will make a show of hope, but
Even if he could fly to the clouds
Or raise his sight so very high

See all the deeds of all men,
And weigh them all at his leisure,
He would still find it hard to choose

Unless he has seen every trick

He ought to fear very greatly
That she might, to avenge herself,
Cause his body to die or go mad,
Or lead a life of wasting away
Through desperate cunning,
From which he cannot think to flee

A woman fears neither honor nor shame

Valerius speaking of wicked women.</margin>

->The Friend to the Lover.<-

¶ Companions, this false, villainous jealous man,
Whose flesh should be delivered to the wolves,
Who sows so much jealousy
As I have shown you here in example,

Who ought not to be a lady <note>In this context, "lady" implies a distant ruler rather than a partner</note>,

<column-break/>

But his equal and his companion,
As the law joins them together;
And he ought to be her companion
Without making himself lord and master.
When he prepares such torment for her
And does not hold her as his equal,
But makes her live in such unease,
Do you think it does not displease her
And that the love between them does not fail?
Whatever she may say, yes, it fails without doubt.
<margin>Note.</margin>
He is never loved by his wife
Who wishes to be called "Sire" <note>Lord/Master</note> over her;
For love must necessarily die
If he will not come to her aid.
Love cannot endure or live
Unless it is in a free heart at liberty.
Therefore, it commonly happens
To all those who at first
Vow to love one another through "Fine Love" <note>Courtly love or romantic affection</note>
When they later wish to marry,
That such trouble can come to them
That love can no longer hold;
For he who loved through "Fine Love"
Called himself a servant to her
Whom he wished to be his mistress.
Now he calls himself lord and master
Over her whom he would have called "Lady"
When he was loved through "Fine Love."

And in marriage they are wedded,
Then the wheel of fortune turns,
So that if he used to serve her,
He now commands that she serve him,
As if she were his slave;
And he keeps her on a short leash and commands
That she give him an account of her deeds,
Though he called her "Lady" before.
He dies unwillingly who has not learned this.
<margin>Note.</margin>
Then she finds herself in my custody <note>The speaker here is likely "Friend" or "Reason" discussing the constraints of marriage</note>,
Seeing herself thus assailed
By the best and most proven man
She has found in this world,
Who now wishes to thwart her so much.
She knows not in whom to trust
When she looks upon her master at her neck,
Of whom she never before took heed.
The verse is badly changed <note>A metaphor meaning the situation has turned sour</note>.
Then the game becomes so diverse to her,
So cruel and so strange,
When he has changed the dice on her
So that she cannot and knows not how to play.
<margin>Love is changeable.</margin>
How can she praise herself for this?
If she does not obey, he becomes angry;
If he insults her, she grumbles;
Thus they will be set in wrath,
And by wrath soon become enemies.

<margin>Note on liberty and servitude.</margin>
For this reason, companions, the ancients,
Without servitude and without bonds,
Peacefully and without villainy,
Supported one another in company.
And they would not have given up their freedom
For the gold of Arabia or of Nisa <note>original: "nise"; likely referring to Nysa, a legendary mountain/land associated with riches</note>,
For he who could take all their gold
Could not truly sell that freedom.
In those days there was no pilgrimage;
No one left their own shore
To seek a strange country,
Nor had anyone crossed the sea.

### ¶ How Jason went in great haste
To seek the Golden Fleece across the sea,
And it was a very marvelous thing
To the onlookers, and very frightening.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration within a decorative rectangular border. It depicts a sailing ship with three figures on board navigating a turbulent sea. Jason, who first crossed the water
When he designed the ships
To go seek the Golden Fleece,
Truly thought he would be taken by war.
Neptune, seeing him swim <note>original: "nager"; in Middle French this often refers to sailing or rowing</note>,
Thought Triton would go mad,
And Doris <note>original: "thorus"; likely a corruption of Doris, mother of the Nereids</note> and all her daughters,
Because of the marvelous seeds <note>The Argonauts</note>,
Thought they were being betrayed,
So greatly were they astonished
<margin>Jason first sailed upon the sea.</margin>
By the ships they led through the sea
Just as the mariners wished.
But the first people of whom I tell you
Did not know what it was to sail,
For they found everything in their own land
And whatever seemed good to them to seek.
They were equally rich
And loved each other loyally;
Thus they lived peacefully,
For by nature they loved one another,
The simple people of good life.
<margin>Note on natural love.</margin>
Love was then without envy,
Without villainy and without clamor,
And they lived in loyal love.
One asked nothing of the other,
Until Deceit <term>Barat: a personification of fraud or trickery</term> came from all sides,
And sin and ill adventure,
Which care nothing for sufficiency.
Pride, disdaining his equal,
Came to them in great finery,
And Covetousness and Avarice.
Pride and every other vice
Then caused Poverty to break out
From Hell where she had been so long
That no one knew anything of her;
She had never before been upon the earth.

# Page 59

Ill-fated was she to have arrived so soon,
For her coming brought too much evil.

<margin>Theft: the son of Poverty.</margin>
Poverty, who knows no ease,
Brought along her son, Theft,
Who runs headlong toward the gallows
To bring some aid to his mother;
And sometimes he finds himself hanged,
For his mother cannot protect him,
Nor can his father, Faint-Heart,
Who is the overseer of all sorrow.
This is not the case for Lady Tavern,
<margin>Note.</margin>
Who guides and governs the thieves;
For she is the goddess of larcenies,
Who covers up sins in the thick of night
And hides deceits with clouds,
So they do not appear outwardly through their works
Until the moment they are discovered
And then, in the end, all are proven guilty.
He can expect no mercy
When the rope is placed around his neck,
Nor can anyone protect him from it,
No matter how well he knows how to repent.
Then the sorrowful demons,
Inflamed with madness,
With wrath, with grief, and with envy,
Seeing people lead such a life,
Ran through all the lands
Sowing contempt, discord, and wars,
Slander, grudges, and great hatreds,
Through wrath and also through provocation.
And because they held gold dear,
<margin>Gold is hidden in the earth.</margin>
They caused the earth to be flayed <note>original: "escorchier"; a vivid metaphor for mining or stripping the land</note>
And tore from her entrails
Her ancient hidden treasures:
Metals and precious stones,
Which people became envious of.
<margin>Avarice and Cupidity.</margin>
For Avarice and Covetousness
Have seated within the hearts of mortals
The great burning desires to acquire money.
One acquires it, the other locks it away,
And never will that cowardly, wretched woman <note>referring to the personification of Avarice</note>
Spend a penny as long as she lives,
But her heirs and her executors
Will be its masters and guardians—

<column-break/>

Unless some other misfortune befalls her.
And if she goes to her damnation,
<margin>Avarice is a damnable thing.</margin>
Do not think that anyone will pity her;
For if she has done well for herself, let her take the consequences.

And when, through this covetousness,
The people were thus set on an evil path,
They abandoned their former way of life.
They never ceased from doing evil,
For they all became like cheaters
And took hold of private properties,
And even divided the land among themselves,
<margin>The division of lands made through Cupidity and Avarice.</margin>
And in dividing it, they placed boundaries there.
And when they were placing the boundaries,
They frequently fought one another
And seized what they could from each other;
The strongest had the largest shares.
And when they ran off on their acquisitions,
The shepherds who remained behind
Would enter into their dwellings
And destroy their savings.
Then it became necessary to ordain
Someone who would guard the homes,
And who would quickly capture the wrongdoers
And do justice for the plaintiffs;
No one dared to contradict this.
Then they assembled to elect him.

¶ Here you may read without confusion
How the first king was made,
Who then swore to them without delay
To loyally guard their possessions for them.

A great peasant <note>original: "vilain"; in this context, a commoner or man of the fields</note> among them they elected,
The most sturdy of all those who were there,
The most big-boned and the largest,

Take care that she does not come
To that place or that spot
Where the first one <note>The primary mistress or wife</note> is blessed,

There is no one who can give good counsel;
For no old, bristling wild boar

<margin>Way to appease jealous women.</margin>

If he wishes that she grumble no more.
<margin><image-desc>A small hand with a pointing finger</image-desc></margin>

So many have boasted of many women

Whose bodies they could not have.
They defamed their names with great wrong;
<margin>Note.</margin>
But those have failing hearts
Who are neither courtly nor valiant;
Boasting is too base a vice.

For even if he had done well,
Nevertheless he ought to conceal it.
<margin>Note on well concealing one's affairs in love.</margin>
Love wishes to hide its jewels,
Except to loyal companions
Who wish to keep them silent and hidden;
There one can well reveal them.

It is right, if he can, that he studies
To be very serviceable to her,
To be more agreeable to her afterward;
Take good care that boredom does not take him.
If her sickness lingers,
Be near her, remaining
In kissing her and in weeping.
Such a man must play his part if he is wise.

-># The Romance of the Rose.<-

I no longer wish to concern myself with them,
No matter how wise or full of learning they may be;
Then they may well go to their ruin,
They are at their final thousand <note>original: "dernier millier" - a metaphor for being at the end of one's rope or resources</note>.

As to later make their peace with me,

Every time it pleased them.
I would never be so weary

So much do they fret and suffer anguish.

That you will come late to repentance
If you once set your feet therein.
Never were men more stupefied,
Nor so brought low,
As you shall be if you go there.
<margin>☞</margin> If Poverty <note>original: "pourete"</note> can give you a blow,

She who was formerly her chambermaid,
Serving her in such a manner

Was burning and consumed by hunger;

<margin>Theft, Barlet, and Poverty</margin> Theft <note>original: "Larrecin"</note>, the ugly little Barleton <note>A traditional name for a thief's accomplice or a personification of petty crime</note>,

But she finds them very sparsely born,

<margin>The description of Hunger and Famine.</margin> Scattered among the thick rocks.
If I wished to describe her,

Her hair is all standing on end,

The roundness of her knees is lost;
Her heels are high and protruding,
It does not appear that any flesh is within,
So much does thinness hold and compress her;
For the bountiful goddess
<margin>Ceres, goddess of grain, according to the foolish ancients</margin> Ceres, who makes the wheat grow,

The very bountiful goddess

Turns its wealth by another way

That path which I have spoken of here,
Toward weary, despised Poverty,

You might well fail in the taking;

Just as it must happen

<margin>The names of the subjects of Love.</margin>

But Constrained Abstinence,

They brew Deceit <note>original: "Barat," meaning fraud or trickery</note> in their thoughts.

His mother was named Hypocrisy,

Hypocrisy with the rotten heart,

Then, when the God of Love saw him,
His whole heart was moved.
"What is this?" he said, "Have I dreamed?

He does not wish to love people so much,

"If no ill comes of it, I am welcomed,

# The Romance of the Rose.

And it was right, for by him specifically
In this pain, briefly,
We were gathered for our people
In order to steal Fair Welcome <note>original: "bel accueil" — a personification of the Lady's receptivity</note>;
But he says he is not wise enough,
So it would be a very great pity
If I were to lose such a loyal servant
When I can and must help the people,
Since he has served me so very well
That he has well deserved my favor.
I must take up my equipment
To break the walls of the tower
And to besiege the strong castle
With all of my power.
He must serve me even more,
For to deserve my grace
He must begin a Romance
Where all my commands shall be placed,
And he shall finish it up to the point
Where he and Fair Welcome shall say
That he now languishes in prison
In sorrow and without misdeed.
All my senses are now dismayed
Lest you have forgotten me;
I have great grief and discomfort from it.
There is never anything that comforts me
If I lose your goodwill,
For I have no trust elsewhere;
Nevertheless, I have lost hope,
Whereof I am almost in despair.
Here Guillaume shall rest,
Whose tomb may be full of balm,
Of incense, of myrrh, and of aloes,
So much has he served me, so much praised me.

That no one will be able to answer it;

I ought to advise myself promptly.

The case is so very pressing

As soon as he leaves childhood,

He will never be able to succeed.

<margin>False Seeming among the religious orders.</margin>
In no place but these two do I dwell,
But in one more, in the other less.
To be brief, I must lodge myself
Where I can best hide;
For concealment is most secure
When placed under the humblest clothing.
Religious folk are very covered,
And secular folk more exposed;
Yet I do not wish to blame
Religion, nor defame it,
In whatever place I might see it.
Never would I blame a religion
That I find humble and loyal;
But for all that, I shall never love it—
<margin>☞</margin> I mean the false religious,
The treacherous and malicious,
Who wish to wear the habit
But do not wish to subdue their hearts.
Religious folk are very piteous;
You will never see a spiteful one among them,
For they have no care to follow pride.
They all wish to live humbly.
With such people I will not stay;
If I do stay there, I will feign.
I might well take their habit,
But I would sooner let myself be hanged
Than depart from my purpose,
Whatever face I might put on.
<margin>False Seeming with the wicked and worldly.</margin>
I am with the proud,
The usurers, the crafty ones
Who covet worldly honors
And exploit great affairs,

And they make themselves out to be poor, yet live

On good, delicious morsels

And they often preach of poverty,
But they fish for great riches
With large nets and trawls.
By my head, great evils come of it,

They make an argument to the world
Of which the conclusion is shameful.

<margin>A simple habit does not make the monk.</margin>

In robes of feigned color,
False religion may well flourish;
Many saints have been seen to die,
And many glorious female saints,
Devout and religious,
Who always wore common cloths;
But for that, they were no less holy.
I could name many of them for you,
Indeed, almost all the female saints
Who are prayed to in the churches,
Chaste virgins and married women,
Who gave birth to many fair children,
Wore the garments of the world
And died in those adornments,
<margin>Note concerning saints and holy women.</margin>
Who are, will be, and were saints—
Especially the eleven thousand virgins <note>A reference to Saint Ursula and her legendary companions.</note>
Who hold their candles before God,
Whose feasts are celebrated in churches.
They were captured in secular clothes
When they received their martyrdoms;
By their habits they were not judged.
A good heart makes the thought good;
The robe neither takes away nor gives;
<margin>A good heart makes a good thought.</margin>
And the good thought produces the work
Which reveals one's religion.
Therein lies religion,
According to the right intention.

# The Romance of the Rose.

### ¶ How the traitor False Seeming
### Steals away the hearts of people
### Beneath his garments of black and gray
### With his face pale and thin.

<margin>
False Seeming in all estates <note>original: "estatz" - referring to social classes or ranks.</note>.
</margin>
I know well how to change my clothes,
Taking one and then another strange one.
Now I am a knight, now I am a monk,
Now I am a prelate, now I am a canon,
Now I am a cleric, at another hour a priest,
Now I am a disciple, now I am a master,
Now a castellan, now a forester;
In short, I am of every trade.
Now I am a prince, now a page,
And I know every language by heart.
At another time I am old and white-haired,
Now I have become young.
Now I am Robert, now I am Robin,
Now a Franciscan <note>original: "cordelier"</note>, now a Dominican <note>original: "iacobin"</note>.

<margin>
Constrained Abstinence accompanies False Seeming.
</margin>
I take to be my companion,
Who solaces and accompanies me,
Lady Constrained Abstinence,
Who wears many disguises
Just as it comes to her pleasure
To fulfill her desire.

<margin>
False Seeming deceives the world.
</margin>
At another hour I wear a woman's robe;
Now I am a damsel, now I am a lady,
Now I am a nun, now I am an abbess,
Now I am a novice, now I am professed <note>One who has taken formal religious vows.</note>,
And I go through all regions
Seeking out all religious orders;
But of religion, without fail,

If I had nothing to live on,

There is too much pain in laboring.
It is better to pray in front of people

The strongest robs the weakest;

Through my deception I pile up and amass

<margin>The desire of usurers.</margin>

Acquisition is my entire intent;
My "purchasing" <note>illicit gain or "hustle"</note> is worth more than my rent.
Even if I were to be killed or beaten,

Confessing these emperors,

I do not love such confession,

Their estate is neither beautiful nor fine.
<margin>Dissimulators love only the rich.</margin>
These empresses, these duchesses,
These queens and these baronesses,
These other ladies of the palace,
These abbesses and these beguines <note>Members of a lay religious sisterhood</note>,
These wives of bailiffs and knights,
These townswomen, elegant and proud.

# Folio 84

Thus for the Antichrist we shall wait
And all together surrender ourselves to him.

It is thus written in the book

John cannot show his strength.

By Peter, I mean the Pope to be understood,

And hold to the Antichrist,

<column-break/>

Which is understood by us through John.

I would be in a high enough state;
Indeed, I have many great friends
Who have already placed me in great standing.
Of all the world, the empress is
Deceit <margin>Deceit.</margin>, my lord and my father,

Our powerful lineage reigns;
We reign now in every kingdom,
And it is quite right that we reign
And that we hold the whole world;
For we know how to deceive so many
That one cannot perceive it,
Or if one knows how to choose the truth,

But that man thrusts himself into the wrath of God <margin>Note the words well</margin>

Nor have God before his eyes;
So God will punish him without fail.
But I do not care how it goes, <margin>No one wants to be chastised.</margin>

We are held for such good people

Without being reproved by anyone.
What people then ought one to honor
Except us, who never cease to wander
Openly before the people
Through our false governance?

<margin>It is a singular virtue to restrain the tongue.</margin>
Sir, the primary virtue,
The greatest and most sovereign
That a mortal man can have
Through science or through knowledge,
Is to restrain his tongue;
At this everyone should labor.
For it is much better to keep silent
Than to speak an evil word;
And he who willingly listens to them
Is not a man of worth, nor does he fear God.
<margin>The manner of speaking of False Abstinence.</margin>
Sir, above every other sin,
You are tainted by this one;
A trick <note>or "mockery"</note> you told a while ago,
In which you were most wickedly mistaken,
Concerning a youth <note>the Lover</note> who used to frequent this place;

Nothing but to deceive Fair Welcome <note>original: "bel acueil"; the personification of a lady's receptivity</note>.

He no longer comes or goes here,

Fair Welcome is locked away because of it,
<margin>Foul Mouth harms many.</margin>

He no longer dares to take solace there,

<column-break/>

He who used to enjoy himself here.
What moved you to harm him so much,

Which have devised many lies?
Also your foolish eloquence,
Which brays and cries out noise and strife,

Dishonoring and grieving them
By things for which there is no proof,

I wish to tell you quite openly,

<margin>Foul Mouth drove away the messenger.</margin>

And you lie in wait, legs crossed <note>an idiom for sitting idle or waiting expectantly</note>,

The idler idles there all day,
Night and day you keep watch there,
And you labor there in vain.
Jealousy, who waits so long,
Will never gain so much from you.
Yet it is a shame for Fair Welcome,
Who, without believing anything, is in a cage.
Without a crime he remains in prison;
There the captive languishes and weeps
Night and day without ceasing;
It is a pity to look upon him.
<margin>Note.</margin>
If you had never done more wrong
In the world than this misdeed,
One should—doubt it not—
Thrust you out of this jurisdiction,
Put you in a dungeon or bind you in iron;
You will go to the fires of hell
If you do not repent of it.

The other knows not how to answer the proof,
And it must indeed seem apparent
That he nearly fell into repentance,
And says to them:

### ¶ Foul Mouth.

By God, it may well be!
Seeming, I hold you to be a good master,
And Abstinence to be very wise;
You truly seem to be of one heart.
What do you ordain that I should do?

### ¶ False Seeming to Foul Mouth.

<margin>
False Seeming’s persuasion of Foul Mouth.
</margin>
You shall be confessed in this place,
And you shall speak of this sin no more;
You shall repent of this one,
For I am of an Order and I am a priest,
Fit to confess the greatest master
Who lives as long as the world endures.
I have the care of the whole world,
Such as no priest or curate ever had,
No matter how sworn he was to his prelate.
And so, by the High Lady <note>The Virgin Mary</note>,
I have a hundred times more pity for your soul
Than your parish priests,
However special they may be to you.
And I have a great advantage,
For no prelate was ever so wise
Nor so lettered as I am;
For by God, I can do everything,
Because the Creator has chosen me;
I have had this gift for hearing confession.
If you wish to confess yourself
And leave this sin behind at once,
Without mentioning it ever again,
You shall have absolution.

### ¶ How the tongue was cut / With a razor, not a sword / By False Seeming from Foul Mouth / Whereby he fell dead like a log.

<column-break/>

Foul Mouth <note>original: "Malle bouche"; the personification of Slander/Gossip</note> immediately bows down;
He kneels and confesses
As one contrite and repentant;
And the other takes him by the throat,
With two fists he grips and strangles him,
And has pulled out his tongue,
Which he removes from him entirely.
Thus they dealt with their host;
They have no other use for him.
Then they tumble him into a ditch.
Defenseless, they break the gate;
Having broken it, they pass through;
And then they found sleeping within
All the Norman soldiers <note>The guards of the castle</note>.
They had drunk so much in revelry
Of the wine that I did not pour!
Drunk and sleeping, they strangle them
So that they might never prattle again.

### ¶ How False Seeming, who consoles / Many a lover, soon passed the gate / Of the castle with his companion / Also Generosity and Courtesy.

Then Courtesy and Generosity <note>original: "Courtoysie et Largesse"</note>
Pass the gate without delay;
Thus the four of them are assembled,
Having stolen in very secretly.
The Old Woman <note>original: "La Vieille"; the cynical guardian of the Fair Welcome</note>, who was not on her guard,
And who kept Fair Welcome <note>original: "Bel Acceuil"</note> within,
Was seen by all four together.
She had descended from the tower
And was amusing herself in the courtyard,
With a hood in place of a veil.
Upon her wimple she had covered her head.
<margin>
Generosity and Courtesy, friends of False Seeming.
</margin>
They ran toward her joyfully
And all four greeted her;
She feared they were going to beat her
When she saw them thus assembled.

### ¶ The Old Woman.

Truly, she said, you seem
To be a valiant and courtly people.
Tell me, without making a noise—
Should I not consider myself a prisoner?—
What do you seek in this enclosure?

### The Old Woman to Fair Welcome.

¶ "Fair son," she said, "I am troubled
That I find such great distress in you.
Tell me all your thoughts;
If I can help you in any way,
You will never see me hesitate for a single day."

### The Author.

¶ Fair Welcome did not dare complain,
Nor tell her what or how;
He did not know if she spoke truth or lies.
He denied all his thoughts to her,
For there was no service to be had there.
He did not trust her at all;
Even his heart was wary of her,
Which he felt fearful and trembling.

She should not dip her fingers into the broth up to the knuckles,
Nor should she have her lips greased
<note>The manicule points to the start of the instructions on eating.</note> With soup, with garlic, or with fatty meat,
Nor should she pile up too many morsels,
Nor put too large a piece in her mouth.
With the tips of her fingers she should touch the bit
That she must moisten in her sauce,
Whether it be green, or cameline <note>A common medieval sauce made of cinnamon, ginger, breadcrumbs, and vinegar.</note>, or yellow;
And she should take her mouthful so carefully
That not a drop falls upon her breast
From the soup or from the dark sauce;
And she must drink so wisely
<margin>Note.</margin> That she does not spill a drop upon herself;
For anyone who saw such a thing happen
Might well consider her
Too rude or too gluttonous.
And she must take care not to touch the cup
While she has a morsel in her mouth,
Which she must wipe so well
That she leaves no grease clinging there,
At least on the upper lip;
For when grease remains upon it,
It spoils the wine's "bubbles" <note>original: "maillettes" - referring to the clear beads or droplets on the surface of the wine.</note>
Which are then neither beautiful nor clean.
And she should drink little by little,
However great her appetite may be;
She should not drink in one breath,
Neither a full bowl nor a full cup,
<margin>Note always the beautiful conduct of women at the table.</margin> But drink little and often,
So that no one is moved
To say that she swallows too much
Or drinks too greedily with a full throat;
But she should let it flow very delicately,
Not gulping from the cup too greedily
As many nurses do,
<margin>Note.</margin> Who are so gluttonous and foolish
That they pour wine into a hollow throat
Just as if into a boot,
And pour it in with such large gulps
That they lose their way and become dazed.
She must take good care not to get drunk;
For in a woman, or in a man for that matter,
Nothing can be kept secret
Once a woman is intoxicated,
She has no defense left in her,

<column-break/>

But says everything that she thinks
And is abandoned to everyone
When she is given over to such mischief.
She should beware of sleeping at the table;
That would make her much less agreeable.
Many ugly things happen
To those who maintain such a habit of sleeping;
It is not beautiful to slumber
In places established for waking;
Many have been deceived by it,
And many times have fallen from their seats,
Forward, or backward, or to the side,
Breaking an arm, a head, or a rib.
Let no such sleep take hold of her;
Let her remember Palinurus <note>The pilot of Aeneas's ship in Virgil's Aeneid.</note>
Who steered the ship of Aeneas;
While awake he had steered it well,
But when sleep had overcome him,
He fell into the sea and was betrayed,
And nearly drowned his companions,
Who mourned him greatly afterward.

**S**o must the lady take care
That she is not too slow to be praised,
For she might wait so long
That no one would want to reach out a hand to her.
She must seek the delight of love
While youth leads her;
For when old age assaults a woman,
She loses the joy and the onset of love.
The fruit of love, if a woman is wise,
<margin>The time for loving passes quickly.</margin> She must gather in the flower of her age;
For the weary woman loses as much of her time
As she lets pass without enjoying love.
If she does not believe my counsel,
Which I advise for the common profit,
Know that she will repent of it
When old age flatters her;
But I know well that they will believe me,
Those at least who are wise,
And they will hold to our rules
And say many Paternosters <note>The Lord's Prayer (Latin: Our Father).</note>
For my soul when I am dead,

# Leaf 84

It shall be read in many a school.
Fair, very sweet son, if you drink <note>original: "biuez"; likely a metaphor for absorbing knowledge</note>
For I know well that you write
In the book of your heart, most willingly,
All my commandments in their entirety.
When you depart from me,
If it pleases God, you shall read them again
And you shall be a master of them as I am,
Despite all the chancellors.
And through chambers and through cellars,
In meadows, in gardens, in groves,
Under pavilions and under curtains;
But let this lesson be read:
When you have retained it well,
Take care that it is not too enclosed;
For when she rests at home,
She is seen less by all people,
And her beauty is much less known,
Less coveted, and less sought after.
<margin>Note.</margin>
Let her go often to the high church
And make visitations
To weddings and processions,
<margin>A well-dressed woman desires to be looked at by everyone.</margin>
To games, to feasts, to carols <note>A medieval circle dance accompanied by singing.</note>
For in such places the God of Love
And the goddesses hold their schools
And sing masses to their disciples.
But she must first look in the mirror
To see if she is well-adorned.
And when she feels she is ready,
And she goes through the streets,
Let her walk with a fine gait,
Neither too soft nor too stiff,
Neither too upright nor too hunched,
But very pleasing in every crowd.
Let her move her shoulders and sides
So nobly that one finds
No one with a more beautiful movement;
And let her walk prettily
In slippers or small shoes,
Which shall be made so skillfully for her
That they fit the foot so perfectly
That there shall be no wrinkle at all.
If her long robe trails on the ground,

<column-break/>

Near the pavement in a very fine manner,
Let her lift it at the side or in front
As if to take a little air,
To have her step more free.
Let her take care that if the step is free,
Everyone who passes the way
May see the beautiful shape of her foot.
And if she is such that she wears a mantle,
She must wear it in such a way
That it does not encumber the view
Of the noble body which it shades;
And so that the body is better adorned,
And the belt with which she decks herself—
Which is neither too thick nor too slender,
Of gilded silver with tiny pearls—
With two hands she must take the mantle,
Broadening and extending her arms,
Whether by a fine path or through mud.
<margin>Note.</margin>
And let her remember the wheel
That the peacock makes with its tail;
Let her do the same with the mantle,
So that the lining, whether vair or squirrel <note>original: "noyie ou grise"; types of expensive medieval furs</note>
Or whatever has been placed there,
And the whole body is shown openly
To those who make a fine display.
If she is not beautiful of face,
She must more wisely turn toward them
Her beautiful, long, dear tresses,
Blonde and clean and whole,
Making the turn behind her;
It is a very pleasant thing,
The beauty of a head of hair.
A woman must always take care
That she may resemble the wolf
When it wants to steal the sheep;
Which, for fear of failing,
Goes to assail a thousand for one,
<margin>Note the comparison of well-dressed women.</margin>
And does not know which one it will take
Until it holds it captured.
Thus must a woman stretch her nets
Everywhere to catch all men;
For because she cannot know
From which of them she may have grace.

Who never wishes to grant herself

If now she returns from another lover—
For she maintains well more than one,
Though she has placed her heart in none of them,

Let her complain like a wise woman
That her best gown is in pawn

That nothing will be done to please her
Unless he redeems all her pledges <note>Items left as collateral for a loan</note>,
From which she will have very "fat" [heavy] damages.
He who has the source of the money
Will soon put his hand to his purse.

That she receives him with great pleasure,
When she deceives her husband for him,
<margin>Note on the malice of wicked women.</margin>
Or her guards, or her parents;
And that if it were apparent
That she wanted to hide him away,
She would be dead without fail.
She swears she cannot stay,
Even if she were to be flayed alive;
Then she stays at her pleasure
Once she has enchanted him.

<column-break/>

She must remember very well,
When her lover is due to come,
If she fears anyone might perceive him,
To receive him through the window;
For he cannot enter through the door.
She swears she is destroyed or dead,
And that she would be nothing
If it were known he was inside;
Neither soft herbs would protect her,
Nor helmets, hauberks <note>Chainmail shirts</note>, nor maces,
Nor chests, nor closets, nor chambers,
Lest she be torn limb from limb.
Then the lady must sigh
And make a pretense of begging him,
Assailing him and rushing at him,
And saying that such a long delay
He has not made without reason,
And that he was keeping in his house
Another woman with whom he took his pleasure,
Whose solace pleased him better;
And that she is now well betrayed,
Since he has hated her for another;
And she should be called a coward
When she loves without being armed <note>Likely meaning "without being guarded or prepared"</note>.
And when he hears these words,
He will certainly believe
That she loves him loyally,
And that she is more jealous of him
Than ever was the wife of Venus—
Vulcan, when he had found her
With Mars, fully proven,
In his forged chains of brass
Which held them very tightly,
For they were joined and bound
When he had spied upon them.

¶ How Vulcan spied on
His wife and bound her very tightly
With a snare along with Mars, it seems to me,
When he found them lying together.

As soon as this Vulcan knew,

Wherein he was a fool to dare such a thing,
For he has very little wisdom

So that there was never a shame like it.

For Vulcan was so ugly

Each woman common to each man,

Before any marriages were made

For a wise woman has no shame
When she recounts a good authority.

# The Romance of the Rose

She is too foolish and too bold,
And swears by the soul of her father
That he shall pay dearly for his love
By putting himself in such an adventure;
Even though she may be more secure
Than those who go at their own whim
<margin>Note.</margin> Dancing through field and vineyard;
For a delight taken in total safety
Is less pleasing and of less value.
And when they are to go together,
She must take care that he does not join her—
Though she keeps him in her dwelling—
Where he might see sun or daylight;
And let her nail the window shut,
And let the place be well-shadowed,
So that her lover may not know
<margin>☞</margin> If she has any blemish upon her,
And that he sees no filth there;
For otherwise he would soon take to the road
And flee with his tail between his legs,
Which would be a great shame and a grievance.
And when they are set to their work,
Let each of them work so wisely
And so well to the point as is fitting,
That the delight comes together
From the one and the other party
Before the work is finished;
For they must wait for one another
To reach their delight together.
One must not leave the other behind;
They must not cease from rowing <note>A common medieval metaphor for the act of love.</note>
Until they come together to the port;
Then they shall have entire pleasure.

And if she finds no delight in the act,
She must complain if she is too delayed,
And let her feign and make all the signs
That she knows are worthy of the delight,
So that he believes she takes pleasure in it—
Which she actually values not a chestnut.
And if such a man, to reassure them,
Can manage for the lady
That she comes to his own lodging;
Let the lady speak in such a manner
On the day he is to set the hour

So that he has a great desire
Before he holds her at his pleasure.

Is more agreeable and remains so.
Those are less hungry for it
Who have it at their will.
When she has come to the lodging,
She shall be held very dear;

<margin>The good fiction of women.</margin> That she is too much watched by the jealous one <note>The "Jealous Husband," a stock character in medieval literature.</note>,

She can have a pound of herbs
<margin>Note.</margin> More or less, of which without danger

Then he will sleep so soundly
That he will let her do while he sleeps
Everything that she wishes;

Send one here and another there;
Deceive them with a light gift
And receive her lover through them.
<margin>Note.</margin> One can easily give them all a drink
If she wishes to ensure the secret.
If it pleases her, let her say to the jealous one:

They wash the whole body and light it up.
It is necessary that <term>Voysie</term><note>Likely a proper name or personification of Cunning/Shrewdness</note> goes to the steam baths,

Never could Medea hold

<margin>Note.</margin>The woman who has a stain of <term>generosity</term><note>original: "largesse"; in this context, the author argues women are naturally stingy, so a gift is a sign of a trap.</note>.
Let us leave generosity to men,
For we women are not generous;
There are hardly any liberal women

And take good care of what is given to you,
And remember the good woman
From the very tenderest youth,
If everyone could live so long
That they saw old age which never ceases,
So that it approaches every one of us.

# The Romance of the Rose.

So that when you have arrived there
You are not considered a fool/
<margin>Note on giving like a fool.</margin>
But be so well-provided with wealth
That you are not at all enchained/
For he who is old has no hope of acquiring
Even a single grain of mustard seed/
But certainly, I did not do this
Whereby I am poor through my own misdeeds.

The great gifts that those men gave me
Who all abandoned themselves to me
I abandoned to my best beloved/
One gave to me and I gave away
So that I have retained nothing/
Giving has reduced me to "small bread" <note>A French idiom meaning to be reduced to poverty or meager rations.</note>
Without remembering old age
Which has put me in such distress/
Poverty did not hold me back
As time passed as it should
I let it go without taking care
Spending without measure.
If I had been wise, by my soul
I would have been a very rich lady/
For I was acquainted with many great people
When I was dainty and elegant
And indeed I was held in high esteem/
But when I had taken from some
By the faith I owe God and Saint Thibault
I gave everything to a scoundrel <note>original: "ribault" — a rogue, rascal, or low-life lover.</note>
Who caused me too much shame/
But above all others he pleased me
All the others I called friends/
But him alone I loved
And know that he did not value me
<margin>Note.</margin>
A single pea, and he told me so plainly/
He was wicked / I never saw worse
He never ceased despising me
"Common whore" he called me
The scoundrel who did not love me at all
A woman has too poor judgment
<margin>The goods that proceed from foolish love.</margin>
And I am a woman, truly/
I never loved a man who loved me/
But if this scoundrel had cut
My shoulder / or broken my head
Know that once my pain had passed

<column-break/>

It would be gone / and I would thank him for it
So much did I love to follow the path of love/
For he never knew how to beat me so much
That I would not make him lie down upon me.
He knew too well how to make his peace
No matter how much he had crossed me
Nor how much he had mistreated me
Nor how hard he had beaten or dragged me
Nor how bruised or blackened my face was
Before he would cry for mercy
Before he would even move from the spot.
He never said so much shame to me
That he would not urge for peace
And that he would not then refresh me/
And then we had peace and concord
Thus he had me caught on his rope/
For he was too strong a deceiver
The false traitor, thief, and liar/
<margin>Note.</margin>
But without him I could not have lived/
Wherefore I always wanted to follow him.
If he fled, I went to seek him
Even as far as London in England.
His pleasure so enchanted me
That he brought me to shame, and I him/
For he wore the great rings
<margin>Note on ruffians.</margin>
From the gifts he had from me, so beautiful
And he put nothing of it into savings/
But spent it all on dice and in taverns
He never learned any other trade
For he had no need of it then
I delivered enough to him to spend/
For I knew well where to get it.
All the people were my rent-payers <note>Meaning her many suitors provided her income.</note>
And he spent it willingly/
For all went into debauchery
Into lechery and gluttony.
He had such a "tender mouth" <note>A metaphor for being fastidious or having expensive tastes in food and pleasure.</note>
That he wished to strive for no good/
Never did life please him
Except for idleness and fine delight/
But in the end I saw him very poorly
When the gifts failed us.
<margin>Definition of foolish love.</margin>
Then he became a beggar for his bread
And I did not have a penny's worth <note>original: "ferant" — a small coin of little value.</note>
And I had no husband.

# The Romance of the Rose.

<margin>Note on giving foolishly.</margin>
So that when you have arrived there,
You may not be considered a fool,
But be so well-provided with wealth
That you are not mocked;
For he who is old has no hope of acquiring
Even a single grain of mustard <note>A metaphor for something of the smallest possible value.</note>.
But certainly, I did not do this,
Whereby I am poor through my own misdeed.

<margin>☛</margin>
The great gifts that those men gave me,
Who all abandoned themselves to me,
I abandoned to the one I loved best.
Men gave to me, and I gave away,
So that I have retained nothing.
Giving has reduced me to "small bread" <note>A phrase meaning to live in extreme poverty or on meager rations.</note>
Without remembering old age,
Which has put me in such distress.
Poverty did not hold me back;
I let time pass as it should,
Without taking care
To avoid spending without measure.
Had I been wise, by my soul,
I would have been a very rich lady,
For I was acquainted with many great people
When I was dainty and elegant,
And indeed I was held in high esteem.
But when I had taken from some,
By the faith I owe to God and Saint Thibault,
I gave everything to a scoundrel <note>original: "ribault" — a low-life, rogue, or lecherous man.</note>
Who brought me too much shame;
But above all others, he pleased me.
All the others I called "friends,"
But him alone I loved.
<margin>Note.</margin>
And know that he did not value me
A single pea, and told me so plainly.
He was wicked; I never saw worse.
He never ceased to despise me;
"Common whore" he called me—
That scoundrel who did not love me at all.
A woman has too poor a judgment,
<margin>The "benefits" that proceed from foolish love.</margin>
And I am truly a woman.
I never loved a man who loved me;
But if this scoundrel had sliced
My shoulder, or broken my head,
Know that my pain would have passed

<column-break/>

And I would have thanked him for it,
So much did I follow the path of love.
For he could never beat me so much
That I would not make him lie down upon me.
He knew all too well how to make his peace;
No matter how much he had crossed me,
Nor how badly he had treated me,
Beaten me hard or dragged me along,
Nor bruised or blackened my face,
Before he would even move from the spot,
He would cry out for my mercy.
He could never have said so much shame to me
That he would not then urge me to peace,
And then he would comfort me again,
And then we had peace and concord.
Thus he had me caught on his rope,
<margin>Note.</margin>
For he was too strong a deceiver,
The false traitor, thief, and liar.
But without him I could not have lived,
Wherefore I always wanted to follow him.
If he fled, I went to seek him
As far as London in England.
His pleasure so enchanted me
That he brought me to shame, and I him;
For he wore the great rings
<margin>Note on ruffians <note>original: "ruffiēs" — pimps or aggressive scoundrels.</note>.</margin>
From the beautiful gifts he had from me,
And he put nothing into savings,
But spent it all on dice and in taverns.
He never learned any other trade,
For he had no need of it then;
I delivered enough to him to spend,
For I knew well where to get it.
All the people were my rent-payers,
And he spent it willingly,
For it all went into debauchery,
Into lechery and gluttony.
He had such a "tender mouth" <note>Meaning he was fastidious or had expensive tastes in food and drink.</note>
That he wished to strive for no good;
Never did life please him
Except for idleness and fine delight.
But in the end, it went very badly for him
<margin>Definition of foolish love.</margin>
When the gifts failed us.
Then he became a beggar for his bread,
And I did not have the value of a penny <note>original: "ferant" — a small coin of negligible value.</note>,
And I had no husband.

<summary>The Old Woman (La Vieille) confesses how she squandered the wealth she earned from suitors on an abusive, ungrateful rogue, illustrating the ruinous nature of "folle amour" (foolish love). She describes a cycle of domestic violence and reconciliation that eventually left her in the poverty she now endures in her old age.</summary>

# The Romance of the Rose.

I do not believe it, whether it be truth or fable;

Truly, I assure you of this:

### The Old Woman.
Certainly you act as a wise person,

Alone to the castle where they wait for me,
She who does not wish to leave yet,
But rather taught me the way to enter.
