# ¶ The Romance of the Rose.

Never by deeds nor by words
Was he so heavily struck;
His hardness failed him entirely,
Weak and vain, he trembled and staggered;
Shame calls out to him who wishes to listen.

->Shame to Danger.<-

¶ Then said Danger: "A proven coward
You are found to be, so recreant
That Fair Welcome <note>Bel Acueil: the personification of the Lady's receptiveness</note> might escape.
You will soon have us caught,
For he will soon hand over the Rose
Which we keep here enclosed within;
And I tell you truly, without fail,
That if he gives it to the gluttons,
Know that it could soon become
Livid, pale, soft, or withered.
And I can well boast
<note>original: manicule pointing left</note> That such a wind could blow in here,
If it found the entrance open,
That we would have great damage and loss;
Or if one stirred the seed <note>original: "graine" - likely a metaphor for sexual contact or impregnation</note> too much,
Some other seed would rain down there
With which the Rose would be burdened.
God grant that such seed does not fall there!
Too much misfortune could come to us from it,
For before one could escape,
The Rose could quickly, without recovery,
Be entirely deadened.
Or if it escaped being deadened,
And the wind struck such a blow there
That the seeds became intermingled,
So that the flower burst from their weight,
Which, in falling from the petals,
Made a mark, or caused it to split,
And through the split in the petal—
Which thing God forbid—
The green bud appeared above;
Everyone would say everywhere that a glutton
Had it halfway in his possession.
We would have a great ruin from it;
Jealousy, who would know of it,
Would have too great a grief and martyrdom,
So much so that we would be delivered to death.
Devils have truly intoxicated you!"

->The Author.<-

<column-break/>

¶ Danger cries: "Help! Help!"
Immediately Shame ran to him;
She came to Pity, whom she threatens,
For she greatly fears her threat.

->Shame.<-

¶ "You have said too much," she said, "Old Wretch!
I will shatter this shield of yours,
And you shall soon fall to the ground;
In an evil hour you undertook this war."

->The Author.<-

Shame carries a great sword

Out of anxious perception.

<margin>Combat of Shame and Delight.</margin>

So well and so strongly with his shield

She would have split him to the teeth,

<margin>Well-Concealing saves Delight.</margin>

# Leaf XCV.

Never did a hen lie in such a state.
<margin>Note.</margin>
She was surrounded by departing fears
And by hidden returns.
Shame raised the sword and then struck
Such a blow that it almost crushed the brow,
By which she was completely stunned.

### ¶ Discretion <note>original: "Bien celer" - literally "Well-Hiding" or the ability to keep a secret</note> attacks Shame.

Discretion said: "Now Jealousy,
That sorrowful and wretched one,
Shall never know of it as long as she lives.
Of this I would fully assure you,
And pledge it with my own hand,
And make great oaths upon it,
More than any other vows.
Since 'Evil-Mouth' <note>The personification of Slander/Gossip</note> is slain,
You are caught as if in your own bed."

### ¶ How Discretion overcomes
### Lady Shame while fighting;
### Then afterwards Heart and Boldness
### fight most fiercely.

<margin>The combat of Shame and Discretion.</margin>
Shame knows not what to say to this,
And Fear—who used to be such a coward—
Now speaks out quite plainly.
Fear looks at her cousin Shame,
And when she saw her so overtaken,
She set her hand upon her sword,
Which was wickedly sharp.
'Dread of Confusion' <note>original: "Souspecon dembouffissement"</note>
Was its name, for of that it was forged.
When she had drawn it from the scabbard,
It was clearer than any beryl.
A shield of Doubt and Peril,
Bordered with Toil and Pain,
Had Fear, who exerted herself greatly
To hack Discretion all to pieces
In order to avenge her cousin.
She went to strike him upon his shield
With such a blow that he could not recover,
Causing him to stagger, completely stunned.
Then he called for Boldness <note>original: "Hardement"</note>
Who was missing; for had she recovered
And dealt another wicked blow,
Discretion would have been dead without recourse
If she had given him another turn.

<column-break/>

Boldness was brave and hardy,
Apparent in both deeds and words.
<margin>Description of the armor of Boldness.</margin>
He had a good and well-polished sword
Made of the steel of 'Frenzy.'
His shield was very renowned;
'Despite of Death' was it named,
Well-bordered with 'Abandonment'
To all perils, most foolishly.
He comes toward Fear and cries out to her
To strike her with his fury.
She parries the blow and then covers herself,
For she knew much of the work
That belongs to this skirmish;
She was well-shaken by his blow.
Then he strikes her a blow so heavy
That he knocks her down flat;
Her shield did not protect her.
When Fear felt herself cast down,
With joined hands she begs and prays him,
For God's sake, that he not kill her.
But Boldness then says that he shall.
Security <note>original: "Seurete"</note> said, as she rose:
"By God, Fear, you shall die here!
Do the worst that you can.
You used to have the 'white fevers' <note>A contemporary term for the trembling of a coward</note>
A hundred times more cowardly than hares;
Now you have lost your cowardice.
The devils make you so bold
That you take on Boldness,
Who so loves the tournament
And knows so much of it that if he pleased,
He could put us all to death.
Since you first walked upon the earth,
Except in this case, you never fought,
Nor did you make your turns elsewhere—
Elsewhere, I say, in all other battles.
You flee or you surrender,
You, who here defend yourself!
You fled away with Cacus <note>A fire-breathing giant from Roman mythology</note>
When you saw Hercules coming,
Running with his club at his neck.
You were then completely distraught
And you put wings upon his feet
Such as he had never had before,
Because Cacus had stolen..."

That Fair Welcome <note>Bel Acueil: the lady's openness to the lover</note> might escape,
You will soon have us all caught;
For soon he will hand over the Rose
That we keep here enclosed within.
And I tell you truly, without fail,
That if he gives it to those gluttons,
Know that it could soon become
Livid, pale, soft, or withered.
And I can well boast
That such a wind could blow in here,
If it found the entrance open,
That we would have great damage and loss;
For if one stirred the seed too much,
Some other seed would rain down there
With which the Rose would be burdened.
God grant that such seed does not fall there!
Too much misfortune could come to us,
For before one could escape,
The Rose could quickly, without recovery,
Be completely deadened.
And if it escaped being deadened,
And the wind struck such a blow
That the seeds became intermingled,
So that the flower burst from their weight,
Which, in falling from the petals,
Made a mark, or caused it to split—
And through the split in the petal,
Which thing God forbid,
The green bud appeared above—
It would be said everywhere that a glutton
Had it halfway in his grasp.
We would have a great ruin;
Jealousy, who would know of it,
Would have such great grief and martyrdom
That we would be delivered unto death.
Devils have surely made you drunk!"

# How Discretion struck Shame.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Discretion <note>original: "Bien celer" - literally "to hide well," representing the lover's ability to keep secrets</note> said, "Jealousy,

## How Discretion prevails

## Then afterward, Heart and Boldness
## Fight most fiercely.

<margin>The combat of Shame and Discretion.</margin>

She went to strike him upon his shield

Causing him to stagger, completely stunned.
Then Boldness <note>original: "Hardement"</note> rushed in,
Which was necessary; for had she recovered
And worked another wicked blow,
Discretion would have been dead without recourse
If she had given him another turn.

<margin>Description of the armor of Boldness.</margin>

"Despite of Death" it was named,

She was well-shaken by his blow.
Then he struck her a blow so heavy

Her shield did not protect her.
When Fear felt herself cast down,

### ¶ How then Fear and Security

She took Fear by the temples,

Force reinforced the slaughter,
And the trampling was so strong

# Leaf 107

<margin>The assault on the castle.</margin>
Ten intent on fierce warring,
Some assail while others defend;
These against the castle direct
Stones and ladders which they raise
To break the walls, and they toil;
And the gatekeepers shield the walls
With strong, thick-woven hurdles <note>Large wicker frameworks used for fortification</note>
Woven from pliant branches
Which they had, with great mastery,
Gathered in the Hedge of Resistance <note>original: "Dangier" — the personification of a lady's rebuff or pride</note>.
With great barbed arrows
Fletched with promises,
And with services and gifts
To more quickly have their rewards <note>original: "guerdons"</note>,
For no wood ever entered there
That was not entirely made of promise,
Firmly tipped with iron
Of all trust and assurance.
They shoot upon them, and they shield themselves,
And do not delay in defending;
For they have shields strong and fierce,
Neither too heavy nor too light,
Of the same wood as those hurdles
That Resistance gathered in his hedges;
So that shooting there was of no use.
As the matter went thus,
Love <note>The God of Love, Cupid</note> draws toward his mother,
All his state is recounted to her,
Supplicating that she succor him.
"May a foul death seize me," she says,
"Which might soon finish me,
If I ever let remain
<margin>Venus against Chastity</margin>
Chastity living in any woman,
However much Jealousy may strive;
Too often we are in great pain.
Fair son, thus swear by men
That they shall all fail by your paths."
¶ The God of Love.
¶ "Certainly, my lady, willingly;
There shall be no respite for them;
At least, in truth, never
Shall a man be called worthy
If he does not love now, or has not loved."
<margin>Note.</margin>
Great sorrow it is when such people live
Who eschew the delights of love,

<column-break/>

Without wishing to maintain them;
To an evil end may they come.
I hate them so much that if I could
Confound them all, I ought to do it.
Of them I complain and always shall,
And from complaining I shall not feign,
As one who wishes to harm them
In every case that I am able,
Until I am so avenged
That their pride is made foreign to them,
Or that they are all condemned.
Evil were they all born of Adam
When they think to grieve me;
May their hearts burst in their bodies
When they wish to strike down my delights.
Certainly, if one were to beat me well,
Indeed, to confront me with four pikes,
He could not do worse to me.
I am a God, not at all mortal,
But I feel such wrath in my heart
That if I were able to be mortal,
From the grief I have, I would receive death;
For if my game goes failing,
I have lost all that I am worth,
Except for my body and its vestments,
And my hat and my armor.
At the least, son, they have no power;
They ought to have the heaviness
And press their hearts in sorrow
If it behooves them to leave them.
Where can one seek a better life
Than to be in the arms of one's beloved?"

Ten in the host made the oath,
And to hold it firmly,
In place of relics they drew forth
Their cuirasses and their arrows,
Their darts, their bows, and their staffs,
And they said, "We do not ask
For other relics to do this,
Nor any that could please us so well.
If we departed from this,
Never would we be believed in anything."
Upon nothing else do they swear,
And the barons believed them upon this.

As much as on the Trinity
Because they swore the truth.

### ¶ How subtle Nature
### always forges either son or daughter
### So that the human lineage
### by her absence does not fail at all.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a scene in a workshop. A female figure, representing Nature, stands at an anvil with a hammer raised, forging a small human figure. After the oath had been made
And everyone could understand it,
Nature, who was thinking of the things
That are enclosed beneath the heavens,
Had entered into her forge
Where she put all her knowledge
To forging individual pieces <note>Refers to individual human beings as "pieces" of the larger species.</note>
To continue the species;
For she makes the pieces last so long
That Death cannot overtake them,
No matter how fast he runs after them;
For Nature follows so closely
That when Death with his club
Kills the individual pieces—
Those who find themselves indebted to him,
Even though each one is corruptible <note>Subject to physical decay.</note>—
Who do not fear death at all,
And yet go on declining
And die in time and rot,
From which other things are nourished.
When he <note>Death</note> thinks to catch them all,
He cannot grab them all together,
For when he snaps up one over here,
The other escapes him over there;
For when he has killed the father,
There remains a son, daughter, or mother,
Who flee before Death
When they see that one already dead.
Then it befalls these others to die;

<column-break/>

They will never know how to run well enough;
Medicine is of no use, nor help,
Whereby nieces and nephews fail,
Who were born to carry themselves
As long as their feet could bear them;
Where one follows the other in a dance,
Another to the monastery, another to school,
Others to their trading of goods,
And others to their learned arts,
And others to their delights
Of wines, of meats, and of beds.
Others, to flee more quickly
Lest Death make them run away,
Mount upon great warhorses
With all their gilded stirrups.
Another puts his life in a wooden hull <note>A ship.</note>
<margin>The diverse condition of people.</margin>

And guides, by the sight of the stars,
His ships, his oars, and sails.
Another, who humbles himself before God,
Takes up a cloak of hypocrisy,
Wherein, while fleeing, his thought works
Until it appears outwardly through his deeds.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Thus flee all those who live,
Who, like ball-players, dodge Death;
Death, who has tinted his face black,
Runs after them until he reaches them,
So that there is too fierce a hunt.
They flee and Death chases them
Ten years, or twenty, thirty, or forty,
Fifty, sixty, or seventy,
Indeed eighty, ninety, a hundred.
Then he goes about breaking what he holds,
And sons may pass beyond,
<margin>Death takes and kills each one at various ages.</margin>
And he runs after them without tiring
Until he holds them in his bonds,
Despite all the <term>physicians</term> <note>Historical term for doctors or practitioners of medicine.</note>.

Truly no one escapes him—
Be it <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>Ancient Greek physician, the "Father of Medicine."</note> or <term>Galen</term> <note>Prominent Greek physician whose views dominated European medicine for centuries.</note>

Have all left their earthly forms,
And those who cannot run so fast...

# The Romance of the Rose.

<margin>Things counterfeited by art lack any feeling.</margin>
Tame birds and domestic beasts,
Balls, dances, and carols
Of beautiful ladies well-adorned,
Well-portrayed and well-shaped,
Whether in metal, wood, or wax,
Or any other sufficient material;
Whether in paintings or on walls,
Holding handsome knights in their array,
Well-shaped and well-portrayed;
Not for all the shapes or features
Can Art make them go by themselves,
Or live, die, feel, or speak.

<margin>A note on the subtleties of alchemy.</margin>
For those who labor so much at alchemy <note>original: "darquemie"</note>
That they tint all metals in color,
Art would sooner kill itself
Than transmute the species <note>The "species" refers to the essential nature or "soul" of the metal in Aristotelian physics.</note>
Unless it acts so as to return them
To their primary nature.
Work as long as it may live,
Art will never overtake Nature;
And if it wished to strive so hard
That it knew how to bring them back there,
It would need to have the science
To reach that proper temperament
When it would be its choosing,
From which the form ought to issue,
Which divides the substances between them
By specific differences,
As it appears in the definition
For one who knows well how to reach the end.
Nevertheless, it is a notable thing,
Alchemy, and a true art,
For whoever would work wisely at it
Would find great marvels there.
For however it may be with the species,
At least the individual pieces,
Subjected to sensible works,
Are changeable in so many ways
By various digestions <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of exposing a substance to steady heat to mature or transform it.</note>
And change so much among themselves that this change
Puts them under strange species
And takes from them their first species.
Must one not, as from the fern,

<column-break/>

<margin>The subtlety of making glass from fern.</margin>
See the glass placed in the ash?
He who is a good master knows it well,
By a light purification;
Yet the glass is not the fern,
Nor is the fern the glass.
And when lightning comes, or thunder,
Can one not very often see
Stones fall from the great vapors?
<margin>Stones engendered in the air from vapors.</margin>
He can know this who knows the beings
Of the cause that puts such matter
And draws it to this strange species.
Thus are the species changed
And their pieces estranged from them,
Both in substance and in figures,
Some by art, others by nature.
Thus could one do with metals,
Who knew well how to draw out the work,
And take from the foul their foulness,
And put them into a most pure form
By their divine complexions,
Inclined enough toward one another,
For they are all of one matter,
<margin>The manner of refining metals.</margin>
However Nature draws them;
For all, in various manners,
Within their earthly mines,
Are born of sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: "vif argent"; mercury.</note>,
As the books confess.
He who knows well how to refine them
And prepare them for the spirits,
<margin>The birth of metals in the earth by sulfur and quicksilver.</margin>
So that they would not have the strength to enter
And so that they could not fly away
When they entered into the bodies,
But found them well-purified,
And if the sulfur were without filth
For white or for red tincture <note>The "white tincture" was used to create silver, and the "red tincture" (the Philosopher's Stone) to create gold.</note>,
One could do as one wished with metals,
If one knew how to act thus;
For from fine silver they make fine gold be born,
Those who are masters of alchemy,
<margin>Gold is made by refined fine silver.</margin>
And add weight and color to it
By things that cost very little;
And from fine gold, precious stones,
Clear and gracious are they.

# The Romance of the Rose.

Like one foolish and overconfident,
A hundred times more than you believe;
For I acted with too great a presumption
When I set my intention
To achieve so very high a work.
My heart might better have burst,
So noble and exquisite did I find
That beauty which I prize so much.
Though I grasped it in my thoughts,
No matter what labor I put into it,
I did not even dare
To sound a single word, however much I thought of it;
So I am exhausted by the thinking,
And for that reason I have kept silent,
For the more I have thought upon it,
She is so beautiful that I know no more of her.
<margin>Note.</margin> For God, who is beautiful beyond measure,
When He placed beauty into Nature,
There issued from it a fountain,
Always flowing and always full,
From which all beauty derives;
But no one knows its bottom or its shore.
Therefore it is not right that I should give an account
Neither of her body nor of her face,
Which is so becoming and beautiful
That a lily flower in new May,
A rose upon its stem, or a nut upon a branch,
Is not so vermilion nor so white;
But what use is it to compare her,
When nothing can equal her,
Since her beauty and her worth
Cannot be understood by man.

<note>The decorative 'Q' marks a shift in the narrative voice as Nature begins to speak.</note>

For which I consider myself too much a fool.
And when I look upon my folly,

<column-break/>

Alas, foolish; alas, grieving;

Where will faith be found anymore?
Have I employed my pain well?
Am I quite led astray from my senses,
I who always thought to serve
<margin>The complaints of Nature.</margin> My friends, to truly deserve them,
And who have put all my labor

# Leaf C.

If it please you to tell me,
Whatever the cost of the telling may be,
Whether it brings joy or sorrow,
You may well entrust your will to me.
Confess everything at your leisure,
And I, entirely at your pleasure,
Said Genius, shall apply to it
All the counsel I can muster.
And I shall keep your business well-hidden,
If it is a matter that should be kept silent.
And if you have need of absolution,
I must not withhold that from you;
But please, cease your weeping.
¶ **Nature to Genius.**
¶ "Certainly," she said, "if I weep,
Fair Genius, it is no wonder."
¶ **Genius to Lady Nature.**
¶ "Now, nevertheless, I advise you
That you ought to leave this weeping,
If you wish to confess yourself well
And clearly explain the matter,
Leaving nothing behind;
For I believe the outrage must be great,
Because a noble heart
Is not moved by a small thing.
He is a fool who dares to trouble you;
But without fail, it is true that a woman
Easily becomes inflamed with anger.

<margin>The maxim of Virgil regarding the mutability of women.</margin>
Virgil himself bears witness to it—
He who knew much of their affairs—
That no woman is ever so stable
That she is not diverse and changeable,
And she is a most hideous beast. <note>original: "hideuse beste." This reflects the common medieval trope of comparing human vices to animalistic traits.</note>

<margin>Solomon.</margin>
Solomon says that there was never a head
Upon a cruel serpent-beast
That was more wrathful than a woman;
And nothing possesses such great malice,
For in woman lies so much vice
That no one can her perverse ways
Recount by rhyme or by verse.

<margin>Titus Livius</margin>
And so says Titus Livius, <note>Livy, the Roman historian.</note>
Who well knew what the virtues
Of women are, and also their manners:
That toward their character, no prayers
Are worth as much as flatteries.

<column-break/>

They are so deceitful and foolish,
And of a flexible nature.
Furthermore, the Scripture says elsewhere
That of every feminine vice,
The foundation is avarice;
And whoever tells his wife
His secrets, he makes her his master.

<margin>Note on not telling one's secret to his wife.</margin>
No man born of a mother—
Unless he is a total fool or a madman—
Ought to reveal to a woman
The thing that is to be hidden.
It would be better to flee the country
Than, for the sake of pleasure,
To tell a woman a secret that should be kept,
However loyal and gracious she may be.
One must not keep any secret
If he sees a woman entering the place;
For if his body were in peril,
She will surely tell of it, I record,
However long she might wait.
And even if no one asks her,
She will truly tell it

<margin>Women cannot keep silent.</margin>
Without any outside urging;
For nothing would she keep silent.

If he has indeed deserved death—
That she will have him hanged by the neck,

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration depicting a figure, likely the personification of Nature or a scholar, seated at a desk in a study. The figure is writing in an open book. <margin>All things exist in the thought of God eternally before they were made and created from nothing.</margin>
That God in whom all goodness abounds,
When He composed this world,
Of which He carried in His thought
The beautiful, premeditated form
Always in everlastingness
Before it had existed outwardly;
For there He took His model <note>original: "exemplaire" — referring to the Platonic idea or divine blueprint</note>
And that which was necessary to Him.
For if He had wished to seek it elsewhere,
He would have found neither heaven nor earth,
Nor anything with which He could help Himself,
As He held nothing outside of Himself;
For out of nothing He made everything arise,
He to whom nothing can be lacking.
Therefore, nothing moved Him to do this
Except His own gracious will,
Generous, courtly, and without envy,
Which is the fountain of all life.
It was, in the beginning,
One mass only,
Which was all in confusion,
Without order and without division;
Then He divided it into parts,
Which since then have not been separated,
And He summed the whole by number,
And well He knows what the sum is;
For by reasonable measures
He determined all their shapes,
And made them extend in roundness
To move better and encompass more,
According to how mutable they were
And how much they ought to be contained.
The light things flew up high,
And the heavy things descended to the earth,

<column-break/>

<margin>Note the Generation of Nature.</margin>
And the middling things in the middle;
Thus was their place ordained
By right compass and right space.
That same God, by His grace,
When He had now, by His divisions,
Placed His other creatures,
So honored me and held me so dear
That He established me as His chambermaid <note>original: "chambriere" — a high-ranking servant or deputy in charge of a household</note>.
He lets me serve there, and shall let me,
As long as His will shall be.
No other right do I claim there,
But rather thank Him that He loves me so,
That I, a very poor damsel,
Have so great and so beautiful a house.
That great Lord is so esteemed
That He has taken me for His chambermaid;
For a chambermaid, certainly, yes—
For a constable <note>a high officer of the crown</note> or for a vicar <note>a representative or deputy</note>,
Of which I would not be at all worthy
Were it not for His benign grace.

<margin>The description of the four elements.</margin>
I keep so well my honored,
That beautiful golden chain
Which links the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>,
All of them bowing before my face;
And He gave me all the things
Which are enclosed within the chain,
And commanded that I should guard them
And continue their forms,
Wishing that all should obey me
And that they should follow my rules,
So that they should not forget them at all,
But always hold and keep them
Forever and everlastingly.
Thus they do commonly;
All things apply their care to this,
Except for one single creature <note>A reference to Mankind, the only creature who rebels against Nature's laws</note>.

<margin>The elements obey God and Nature and other sensible things.</margin>
Of the heavens I must not complain,
Which always turn without tiring,
And carry in their polished circle
All the stars along with them,
Sparkling and virtuous <note>possessing "virtue" or inherent spiritual/physical power</note>
Above all precious stones.
From here, dedicating the world,
Beginning its course in the East
And toward the West it makes its way...

Through counsel or through manual labor
It would never be more or less;
Neither better nor worse could it be,

It does not follow that they happen

The knot of this question;

The deeds that are to come,

But it is a very great folly to believe

<column-break/>

That God understands so foolishly

And those who follow such judgments
Write wickedly against God,
Wishing by their fine fables

Nor can reason understand <margin>All is possible to God.</margin>
That one could then learn anything,
Nor could anyone certainly
Be perfectly wise
If he were found in such a default
That this case were proved against him.
Therefore this response is worth nothing,
Which hides the prescience of God
And conceals His great providence
Under the shadows of ignorance;
Which <note>God's providence</note> has no power, so certain is it,
To learn anything from worldly work.
And if He could, without doubt,
This would come to Him from a lack of power,
Which is a grief even to recount
And a very great sin to think upon.
Others felt differently
And responded according to their senses,
And they agreed well, without fail,
That regarding things, however they go,
Which proceed by free will
Just as choice <term>election: the faculty of choosing between alternatives</term> delivers them,
God knows what will come of them
And what end each will hold
By a simple condition;
That is to say, in such a manner
As they are to come to pass.
And they wish by this to maintain
That there is no necessity,
Rather they proceed by possibility,
So that He knows what end they will make,
And if they will be or will not be;
All this He knows well of each one:
That of two paths, it will take one; <margin><note>A hand-drawn pointer (manicule) indicates the final lines regarding the choice between two paths.</note></margin>
One will go by negation,
The other by affirmation,
Yet not so determinately
That it might not happen quite otherwise.

### Leaf 106

For it could well happen otherwise
If free will wishes to hold its ground.

But how dared anyone say this?
How dared one despise God so much

The outcome with certainty <note>original: "determinablement"</note>,

<summary>This page argues that God's perfect foreknowledge does not impose "necessity" or "constraint" on human actions. God made this woman for this man to be born,

Thus is this god called—
When he has harnessed them well,
For they have no other charioteer
Who knows how to handle their horses,
He puts such good wings on their feet
That no bird ever had the like.
Then the air takes its indigo mantel
Which it wears very willingly in India,
And wraps itself in it, then prepares
To adorn itself and make a feast,
And to wait in this state for the clouds
Until they have returned,
Who, to solace the world,
Just as if going to hunt,
Are accustomed to take a bow in their fist,
Of two or three, when they wish,
Which are called celestial bows <note>The rainbow.</note>,
Of which no one knows [the nature] unless he is a good master.
To keep a school of observation,
How the sun dapples them,
<margin>Note on the colors of the celestial bow.</margin>
How many colors they have, or which ones,
Nor why so many, nor why such,
Nor the cause of their shape;
It would behoove him to take care
To be a disciple of Aristotle,
<margin>Note.</margin>
Who best has set nature to note.

That no man since the time of Cain,
Not even Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), the Arab mathematician and "father of optics."</note> nor his Lucaim <note>Likely a reference to a commentator or a corruption of a related name in the transmission of optical texts.</note>
Who was neither a fool nor a knave.
He composed the *Book of Aspects* <note>original: "liure des regars"; referring to Alhazen's *De Aspectibus* or *Optics*.</note>
In this, he must have scientific knowledge
Who wishes to know of the rainbow in the sky
For of this he must be the judge,
A natural scholar and observer,
And he must know of geometry,
Of which mastery is necessary
To prove the *Book of Aspects*.
Then he will be able to find the causes
And the powers of mirrors
Which have such marvelous powers
<margin>Note on the mirror</margin>
That all things, even the very smallest,
Slender letters written from very far away,
And minute grains of sand,
Are seen so large and so thick,
And so apparent to those looking in,
That each person can discern them within,
So that one can read and count them
From so far away that anyone who
Would recount it and who had seen it,
He could not be believed
By a man who had not seen it at all
Or who did not know the causes of it.
Yet it would not be a matter of mere belief
Since he would have the science of it.
Mars and Venus, who were caught
Together in the bed where they lay,
If, before they climbed upon the bed,
They had looked at themselves in such a mirror,
Provided that they held the mirror
<margin>Note.</margin>
So that they saw the bed within it,
They would never have been caught nor bound
In the subtle and slender snares
That Vulcan <note>The god of fire and smithing, husband of Venus, who caught her in an invisible net with her lover Mars.</note> had placed there,
Of which neither of them knew anything.
For even if he had made the handiwork
More subtle than a spider's web,
They would indeed have seen the snares,
And Vulcan would have been greatly deceived,
And neither one nor the other would have entered,
For each snare, larger than a great beam,
Would have appeared to them thick and long.

<column-break/>

So that the treacherous Vulcan,
Burning with black jealousy,
Would never have proven their adultery,
Nor would all the gods have known anything of it,
If they had possessed such mirrors.
For they would have fled from that place
When they saw the snares all stretched out there,
And they would have run elsewhere to lie
Where they might better conceal their desire,
Or they would have made some arrangements
To avoid their misfortunes
Without being blamed or aggrieved.
I tell you the truth, by the faith you owe me,
In that which you have heard from me.

### Genius to Lady Nature.

¶ "Certainly," said the priest, "yes,
The mirror is a true thing;
It would then have been very necessary for them,
For they would have assembled elsewhere
When they recognized the great peril there.
Or with a sword that cuts well,
Perhaps Mars, the god of battle,
Would have so avenged himself on the jealous one
That his snares would have suffered much damage.
Then he could have, in honor,
Sported with his wife at his ease
In the bed without seeking another place,
Or near the bed upon the ground.
And if by some adventure,
Which was treacherous and harsh,
Lord Vulcan had come upon them there
At the hour when Mars held her,
Venus, who is a very wise lady—
For there is too much trickery in a woman— <margin>Note.</margin>
If, when she heard him open the door,
She could have well covered her tracks,
Or would have had an excuse
Through some legal quibble <term>cavillation: a deceptive or sophisticated argument used to evade the truth</term>,
And would quickly devise an occasion
As to why Mars came into her house,
And would swear as much as one wished,
Until she took away his proofs,
And then she would make him believe by force
That the thing was never true,
Even if he had clearly seen it."

The Romance of the Rose.

She would have said that her sight
Was obscured and clouded,
So well would she have doubled her tongue
In various entanglements
To find excuses;
For nothing swears nor lies
More boldly than a woman,
So that Mars would have gone away quite cleared.

### ¶ Nature to Genius.

<margin>A woman affirms a lie better than a man.</margin>
Certainly, Sir Priest, you speak well,
As one valiant, courtly, and wise.
Women have too much in their hearts
Of subtleties and malice;
He who knows this not is a fool and simpleton.
Nor do we excuse them for this.
Much more freely than any man,
Certainly, they swear and lie,
Especially when they feel themselves
Guilty of some sin;
They will never be caught
In this case especially.
Wherefore you may loyally say:
He who could perceive a woman’s heart
Should never trust it;
Certainly he would not,
Lest it should otherwise go ill for him.

### ¶ The Author.

Thus accord, it seems to me,
Nature and Genius together.
And yet Solomon says—
Since you see by the truth—
That happy would be the man
Who should find a good woman.

### ¶ Nature.

<margin>Note.</margin>
"Furthermore," she said, "mirrors have
Many other great and beautiful powers;
For great and large things placed
Very near seem to be seated far away.
Even were it the greatest mountain
That exists between France and Sardinia;
For there they can be seen
So small and so minute
That one could hardly discern them,
However much one looked at leisure.

<column-break/>

Other mirrors, in truth,
Show the proper qualities
Of the things one looks at therein,
If there is one who takes good heed.
There are other mirrors that burn
Things when they look upon them,
When one knows how to align them rightly
To gather the rays together
<margin>On the diversity of mirrors.</margin>
Which beam upon the mirrors
When they shine by the sun.
Others make various images
Appear in different positions,
Objects upright and inverted
By diverse compositions;
And from one thing they make several be born,
Those who are masters of mirrors;
And they make four eyes in one head,
If the form is ready for that;
And they make phantoms appear
To those who look within,
And make them appear outside,
Whether it be through water or through air;
And one can well see them play
Between the eye and the mirror
<margin>Note.</margin>
By the diversities of the angles,
Whether the mediums be composite or single,
Of one nature or of diverse,
In which the form is reflected,
Which will be so multiplying
Through the obedient medium
Which comes appearing to the eyes
According to the reflecting rays,
Which it receives so diversely
That it deceives the beholders.

Aristotle also bears witness to us,
Who well knew of this business—
For he held all science dear—
That a man being in poor health,"
She said, "was in a malady
By which his sight was greatly weakened;
Then the air was dark and troubled,
Wherefore he says that for a double reason
<margin>Note on the example of the mirror.</margin>
He says that in the air, from place to place,
His own face went before him."

# Leaf C.vi.

In short, mirrors, if they have no obstacles,
make many miracles appear,
and also through various distances
(even without a mirror) great deceptions
make things that are far apart
seem joined and close together,
and make one thing seem like two,
according to the diversity of the eyes.
From six, three; or eight, from four—
for whoever wishes to amuse themselves with seeing.
One can see more or less of them;
if one knows how to set the eyes well,
many things can be made to seem as one
by whoever orders and joins them correctly.
Even of such a very small man
that everyone calls him a dwarf,
they make him appear to the seeing eyes
as if he were greater than any giant,
and he appears to pass over the woods
without bending or breaking a branch,
so that everyone trembles with great fear;
and yet the giant and the dwarf are the same.
The eyes lead them so far astray
because they see things so diversely.

And when they are thus deceived,
those who have seen such things
through mirrors or through distances
which have shown them such displays,
then they go and boast to the people,
and they do not tell the truth, but lie,
saying they have seen all the great devils—
so much are they deceived in their sight.
And they truly make the eye infirm and troubled,
making a single thing seem double;
and a double moon appears in the sky,
<margin>Note.</margin> and also two candles for one.
There is no one, when looking closely,
who does not often fail in such observation,
whereby many things are judged
to be other than they are proven to be.
But I do not wish now to take care
to explain the figures
of the mirrors, nor will I say
how the ray is reflected,

<column-break/>

nor do I wish to describe their angles;
all that is written elsewhere in books.
Nor why, of the things mirrored,
the images are reflected back
to the eyes of those who look there
when they turn toward the mirrors;
nor the eyes in their appearances,
nor the causes of the deceptions.
I do not wish to declare to you, fair priest,
where these idols <note>original: "ydoles" - here meaning optical phantoms or images</note> have their being,
whether in the mirrors or outside them.
Nor will I recount then
other marvelous visions,
whether they be sweet or sorrowful,
which one sees happening suddenly—
that is to say, whether they are external
or exist only in the fantasy <note>The "fantasy" refers to the faculty of the mind that processes sensory images.</note>.
I shall not declare this at all,
for it is not expedient;
rather, I leave it and pass over it
along with the things said before,
which will not be described by me.
For it would be too long to tell,
and the time would not suffice,
and also it is very difficult to understand
if anyone wished to comprehend it—
especially for laypeople,
if one did not speak in generalities.
So they would not be able to believe
that the thing was truly so,
concerning these mirrors especially,
which work so diversely;
nor the manners of the visions,
which are so marvelous and fierce.
They could not sort out the truth
if one wanted to display it to them,
nor believe the deceptions
which come through divisions <note>Refers to the refraction or splitting of light rays.</note>,
whether waking or sleeping,
at which many are greatly amazed.
Therefore I wish to pass over them here,
and I do not wish to stop
myself from speaking—and you, sweet friends,
it is good to flee prolixity <note>The author is choosing to be brief to avoid being tedious or overly technical.</note>.

# The Romance of the Rose.

Thus women are very troublesome
And contrary in their speech
Wherefore I must pray that it does not displease you
Because I cannot remain entirely silent about it.
For the present, at this time,
I must say this much however:
That many are so deceived by them
That they have moved out of their beds
And warm themselves and dress themselves
<margin>Note.</margin>
And prepare themselves in all their garments
While the common senses <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was believed to be the internal faculty that processed data from the five external senses.</note> are slumbering
And all the particular senses are awake.
<margin>The wonders of the internal senses of man.</margin>
They take up staffs and pouches,
Sickles, axes, or pruning hooks,
And go traveling long ways,
And yet they do not know where;
And also they mount upon horses
And thus pass over mountains and valleys,
Through dry paths and through mires,
Until they come into strange places.
And when these common senses awaken,
They are greatly stunned and marvel
When they then return to their right mind;
And when they are among people,
Then they testify—and not as a fable—
That the devils have carried them thus,
That they took them from their lodgings
And carried them away by themselves.

<margin>Note always the secrets of nature.</margin>
Often this has happened
When someone is seized and held
By some great malice <note>In this context, "malice" refers to a physical ailment or a disordered humor like melancholy.</note>
As it appears by observation,
When one does not have sufficient guards;
Or those in the house say
That they jump up and then travel,
And they do not stop traveling
Until they find some wild places,
Either meadows, or vineyards, or woods,
And there they let themselves fall.
There one can indeed go to see them
If one wishes, though it be too late,
Because they had no guard
Except people of ill will,
Dead of hunger and of discomfort.

<column-break/>

And when one is in one's health,
One sees a great abundance of people
Who many times, without order,
By natural habit,
Are anxious from thinking too much.
If they become too melancholy
Or too fearful beyond measure,
They cause many diverse figures
To appear within themselves,
Otherwise than we said we saw
When we were speaking of mirrors,
Which we passed over so briefly;
And then it seemed to them in everything
That it was truly so on the outside.

Those who, through great devotion
In too great a contemplation,
Cause to appear in their thoughts
The things that they have imagined,
And they believe quite literally
To see them openly on the outside,
Are mocked by this lie,
Just like the man who dreams
That he sees—or so he believes in his presence—
Spiritual substances,
As Scipio did in the past,
Who saw Hell and Paradise,
<margin>Note on the Dream of Scipio.</margin>
And sky and air, and sea and earth,
And everything that one can seek there.
He saw stars appearing,
And the birds flying through the air,
And the fish swimming through the sea,
And the beasts playing in the woods,
And performing very beautiful and noble feats,
And a great diversity of people:
Some taking solace in a chamber,
Others going hunting through the woods,
Through mountains and by rivers,
Through meadows, vineyards, and hemp-fields.
And he dreams of laments and judgments,
And wars and tournaments,
Dances and carols,
Lutes, viols, and citoles, <note>A citole is a medieval stringed instrument, an ancestor of the guitar or cittern.</note>
And they smell joyful spices
And all savory things.

# The Romance of the Rose.

Who can sustain such a fable?
It is true, and I well record it,
That the soul, when disjointed from the body,
Is more open, wise, and clever
Than when it is joined to the body;
For then it follows the <term>complexion</term><note>In medieval medicine, the "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) which governed a person's temperament and health.</note>
Which troubles its intention.
Therefore, the entrance is better known
By the soul then than was the exit;
Whereby it would find it sooner,
No matter how distorted it might be.

On the other hand, that a third of the world
Goes about thus with "Lady Abundance"
As foolish old women prove it
By the visions they find there—
Wherefore it follows, without any fail,
That everyone else must go there too;
For there is no one, be it truth or lie,
Who does not dream many visions—
Not just three in a week,
But fifteen times in a fortnight,
Or more or less, by adventure,
As long as the fantasy lasts.
<margin>Note.</margin>
Yet I do not wish to say of dreams
Whether they are true or whether they are lies,
And whether one should write them all down
Or whether they are entirely to be despised;
And why some are horrible,
And others more beautiful and peaceful,
<margin>Dreams proceed by diverse means.</margin>
According to their appearances
To the diverse complexions,
And according to the diverse spirits,
Of different manners and ages;
Or whether God, through such visions,
Sends revelations,
Or whether the evil spirits,
To put people in peril,
Cause the dreaming—from this I shall withdraw
And set myself to my main purpose.

I said, then, that the clouds,
When they are weary and exhausted
From shooting their arrows through the air—
And more moist ones than dry ones—

<column-break/>

For with rains and dews
They have moistened them all,
Unless some heat dries them
To shoot something dry;
They well unbend their bows together
When they have shot as much as they please.
<margin>Note.</margin>
But the bows from which these archers shoot
Have too strange a bitterness;
For all their colors flee away
When they wipe them while unbending.
Nor ever again from those same bows
Will they shoot, nor are they able;
But if they wish to shoot another time,
They must make new bows again,
Which the sun can polish there,
Which must be shaped in no other way.
<margin>Note.</margin>
Furthermore, the influence of the heavens,
Which have such great power,
Works through sea and land and air;
They make comets appear,
Which are not placed in the heavens,
But are set ablaze amidst the air;
They last but a short time once they are made,
About which many fables are retold.
<margin>Divinations by certain comets.</margin>
Those who never cease from divining
Predict the deaths of princes from them;
But the comets do not cast,
Nor more thickly do they throw,
Their influences nor their rays
Any more upon poor men than upon kings,
Nor upon kings than upon poor men;
Rather, they work, in sum,
Upon the regions of the world
According to the dispositions
Of the climates, of men, and of beasts,
Who are ready for the influences
Of the planets and of the stars,
Which have the greatest power over them.
And for all the significances
<margin>Note.</margin>
Of these celestial influences,
They also move the complexions
Just as they find them obedient.

Yet I do not say, nor do I claim,
That the king should be called rich...

# The Romance of the Rose.

Unless they act so that they are noble

In their hearts, neither great nor small.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Have more and greater advantages

# Leaf 114

<column-break/>

<margin>Philosophers and poets were formerly highly honored.</margin>
The philosophers they honored,
And to the poets they even gave
Cities, gardens, and honorable places,
And many delightful things.
Naples was given to Virgil,
Which is a more honorable city
Than Amiens, truly, or Lavardine.
In Calabria, he had very beautiful gardens
In that time, which were given to him
By the ancients who knew him.
But why should I name more of them,
When it could be proven by many examples
That those who were born of low lineage
Had more noble courage
Than ever did the sons of kings and counts,
Of whom I shall give you no account here;
Yet they were held to be noblemen.
But the times have now come to this:
That the good men who all their lives
Labor in philosophy
And go into foreign lands
To conquer wisdom and honor,
And suffer great poverty
Like beggars and debtors,
And go about all barefoot and naked,
Are neither welcomed nor held dear.
Princes do not prize them at the value of two apples,
And yet they are more valiant men—
So God keep me from having the fevers—
Than those who are used to hunting hares,
And those who are accustomed
<margin>Note.</margin>
To taking birds with hawks.

---

He who, from another's nobility,
Without his own value and prowess,
Wishes to carry away praise and renown—
Is he noble? I say he is not.
Rather, he should be called a churl <note>original: "Vilain," referring to a low-born peasant or someone lacking in character</note>,
And held as vile and loved less
Than if he were the son of a vagabond.
I will hear no one hooting <note>shouting in disagreement</note> at this,
Even if he were the son of Alexander,
Who dared to undertake so much in arms
And continued wars so long
That he was lord of all lands.

<column-break/>

And after those obeyed him
Who had fought against him,
And those had surrendered
Who had not defended themselves at all,
He said—so much was he gripped by pride—
That this world was so narrow
That he could hardly turn around in it,
Nor did he wish to stay in it any longer.
<margin>The said pride prevented him from expanding.</margin>
Instead, he thought to seek another world
To begin a new war,
And was going to break into Hell
To make himself prized everywhere;
So that everyone trembled with great fear,
Even the gods of Hell; for they believed,
When I told them who it was,
That it was he who, with the wooden staff <note>A reference to Christ or a savior figure breaking the gates of Hell</note>,
Was destined to break the gates of Hell
For the souls dead in mortal sin,
And to bind their great pride
To hunt his friends out of Hell.

---

But let us suppose that which cannot be:
That I should make someone be born noble,
And that I should not care about the others,
Calling them "the rabble" <note>original: "Villenaille"</note>.
What good is there in nobility?
Certainly, for him who directs his wit
To truly understand the truth,
<margin>Note.</margin>
He can understand nothing else
Except that it seems the prowess
Of his relatives strongly wounds him
If he does not wish to live in such a way
That he follows all their deeds.
He who wishes to resemble a nobleman,
If he does not wish to steal nobility
And have praise without deserving it,
I make him know for a truth
That nobility gives nothing
That is not good,
<margin>Note.</margin>
Except for deeds alone.
And know quite certainly
That no one should have praise
By the virtue of a stranger;
Likewise, it is not right that I blame
Any person for another's fault.

Each and every one brings forth

# Leaf 156

He who tells the gods that he is their father

# The Romance of the Rose.

And we strive all the more to believe
That the prophecy is true;
For in the *Bucolics* of Virgil <note>original: "buccolicques Virgille"; referring to Virgil's Fourth Eclogue, which was traditionally interpreted by medieval Christians as a prophecy of Christ's birth.</note>
We read the voice of the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses believed by medieval scholars to have foretold the coming of Christ to the pagan world.</note>
Taught by the Holy Spirit,
Saying that a new lineage
Is sent down to us from heaven
To reclaim the straying people,
Whereby the ages of iron shall fail
And those of gold shall return to the world.

<margin>The prophecy of Albumasar.</margin>
Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer whose works were translated into Latin and used to support Christian theology through the stars.</note> also bears witness—
However he knew of this matter—
That within the virginal sign <note>The zodiac sign of Virgo.</note>
A worthy maiden would be born
Who shall be called Virgin and Mother,
And thus shall nurse her Father;
And her husband shall be near her,
Who shall not squint at all <note>original: "ia point ne louchera"; likely meaning he will not look askance or doubt the miraculous nature of the birth.</note>.
This sentence can be known
By whoever wishes to have Albumasar's book;
It is there all ready in the text,
Of which everyone makes a feast—
The Christian people in September
Who remember such a nativity.
But all that I have said above,
Our Lord Jesus well knows.
Have I labored for man?
For that wretched one I have this labor;
It is the end of all my work.
<margin>Man is the consummation of all works.</margin>
He alone works against my rules,
And is in no way appeased,
The disloyal and the renowned <note>original: "renopé"; possibly a variant of "renommé" or implying one who has fallen from grace.</note>.
Nothing exists that can suffice him,
Whatever thing one might say to him;
The great graces I have done for him
Could never be recounted,
And he returns such shame to me
That it is beyond measure or count.
Fair sweet brother <note>Nature is likely addressing Genius, her priest and confidant.</note> whom I so invoke,
Is it then right that I love him
And that I show him reverence,
Since he is of such a disposition?
Tell me, by God the crucified,
I greatly repent that I ever made him!

<column-break/>

But by the death that He suffered,
To whom Judas offered a kiss
And Longinus struck with his lance,
I shall certainly cut short his luck
Before God, who gave him to me
When He carved him in His likeness,
Since he makes himself so contrary to me.
I am a woman who cannot keep silent,
Rather I wish to reveal his deeds;
For a woman knows not how to conceal anything.
Never was he better scolded,
Since he has estranged himself from me;
His vices shall be recited,
And I shall tell the truths of them.

<margin>The Vices of natural man.</margin>
Proud, and murderer, and thief,
Fierce, covetous, miserly, a trickster,
Despairing, gluttonous, a slanderer,
And hateful, despising others,
Unbelieving, envious, a liar,
Perjured, and a very wicked boaster;
Inconstant, foolish, and variable,
A disagreeable idolater;
Traitor, disloyal, hypocrite,
Too lazy, and a sodomite.
In brief, he is too wretched and foolish
When he is a slave to every vice
And harbors them all within himself.
<margin>Man is subject to all Vices.</margin>
See with what irons he shackles himself!
He goes right along pursuing his death
When he devotes himself to such wickedness.
And since all things must
Return to that from which they take
The beginning of their being;
When man shall come before his Master,
Whom always, as much as he could,
He ought to have served, feared, and honored,
And guarded himself from wickedness,
How will he dare to look upon Him?
And He who shall be the Judge,
With what eye will He look upon him,
When he has behaved so badly toward Him
That he has indulged in every fault,
And who has had a heart so slow
That he has no talent for doing good?

Rather, they do the worst, great and small,
So long as they can save their honor,
And they act as if sworn, it seems,
By a common accord all together.
Yet honor is not often
Saved for each by such a covenant;
Instead, they receive many pains from it,
Even death, or great and villainous shames.
But alas! What can he think,
If he wishes to recount his sins,
When he comes before the Judge
Who weighs and judges all things,
And all by right, without doing wrong,
Where neither trickery nor escape holds fast?
What reward can he then expect,
Except the rope to lead him to be hanged
On the sorrowful gallows of Hell?
Where he shall be taken and put in irons,
Riveted in everlasting rings
With the princes of the devils.
<margin>The description of the pains of Hell.</margin> He shall be boiled in a cauldron,
Roasted in front and behind,
Covered in coals or on griddles,
Turned about on great spikes
Like Ixion across the wheels <note>Ixion was a figure in Greek mythology punished by being bound to a perpetually turning fiery wheel.</note>
That devils turn in their mockery.
He shall die of thirst in the marshes,
And of hunger with Tantalus,
Who always bathes in the water;
And though thirst constrains him,
He shall not bring to his mouth
The water that touches his chin;
The more he follows it, the more it recedes,
And then it so presses him
That he cannot be satisfied,
But dies of hunger, all enraged.
And so he cannot take the apple
Which must always hang before his nose,
For as much as he wants to eat it,
The further it wishes to move away.
Or he shall roll the millstone on the ground
From the rock, and then seek it out,
And roll it once again,
And never for a day shall he cease,
As does the weary Sisyphus,

<column-break/>

Who for this task was set up.
A barrel without a bottom he shall strive
To fill, and yet shall never fill it,
As do the beautiful Danaïdes <note>original: "dianes" - a reference to the daughters of Danaus, condemned to fill a leaky jar for eternity.</note>

<margin>Nature demands vengeance for the sins of men.</margin> Many other great pains are down there,

To suffer tribulation

I shall be avenged for the outrage.
Certainly, the Judge mentioned before,

If He were only merciful,
The loan the usurer held
Might be hopeful and delightful;
But He is always righteous,
Wherefore He is much to be feared
By whoever allows himself to fall into sin.
**W**ithout fail, of all the sins
With which the wretched are stained,
I leave them to God; let Him decide
When it pleases Him to punish them.
But of those about which Love complains—
For I have indeed heard the lament—
I myself, as much as I can,
Complain of them, and must complain, since
They withhold from me the tribute <note>term: "treu" (tribute) - referring to the natural debt of procreation owed to Nature.</note>

And always owe and shall owe,
As long as they shall receive my tools. <note>A metaphor for the organs of generation/procreation.</note>

# The Romance of the Rose.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration depicting two figures in an outdoor landscape with a tree and rolling hills. On the left, a man in robes (Genius) holding a long staff stands facing a woman (Nature) on the right, who is dressed in a long gown and gestures with her hands as if speaking.</image-desc>

Genius, the eloquent speaker,
Go now to the army of the God of Love,
Who takes such great pains to serve me;
And he loves me so much, I am certain,
That by his noble and gracious heart
He wishes to draw closer to my works
Than iron is drawn toward a magnet.
Tell him that I send him my greetings,
And also to Lady Venus, my friend,
And then to all the assembly of barons,
Excepting only False Seeming <note>original: "faulx semblant"; the personification of hypocrisy</note>,
So that he might better join company
With the proud felons
And the perilous hypocrites,
Of whom the Scripture repeats
That they are the false prophets.
Also, Constrained Abstinence <note>original: "Abstinence"; personified as a deceptive religious figure</note>
Is much suspected of being proud
And of being similar to False Seeming,
However charitable she may appear.
If False Seeming is found more often
With these proven false traitors,
Let him never be included in my greeting,
Nor his friend Abstinence either.
Such people are too much to be feared;
Love truly ought to kick them
Out of his army, if it pleased him well,
And if he did not know for certain
That they were necessary to him,
And that he could do nothing without them.
But if they are fearful advocates
In the cause of lovers,
By which their suffering might be eased,
I shall forgive them their trickery.
Friend, go to the God of Love
<margin>Note.</margin>
To carry my complaints and my cries

<column-break/>

Quickly, so that he may do me justice;
But let him take comfort and solace
When he hears this news,
Which ought to be very beautiful to him
And grievous to our enemies.
Let it be no pain for him to cast aside
The worry that he must carry;
Tell him that I send you there
To excommunicate all those
Who wish to oppose him,
And to absolve the valiant ones
Who work with a good heart
To follow the rules correctly
Which are written in my book,
And who study this intensely:
That they might multiply their lineage
And think of loving well;
For I must call them all friends,
To place their souls in delights,
Provided they keep themselves from all vices
<margin>Exclusion of the lover.</margin>
Which I have recounted here before,
And that they follow all goodness.
A pardon that is quite sufficient—
Give it to them quickly for ten years?
They would not prize such a thing a penny!
But give them always a full pardon
For all the sins they have committed,
When they have made a good confession.
And when you are in the army of Venus,
You will be held very dear by all;
Publish to them in their hearing
The pardon and this sentence
Which I wish to be written here.
Then he writes here, and she speaks it;
Then she seals it and hands it to him,
And urges him to depart quickly;
But first let her be absolved
Of that which weighs upon her mind.

<margin>Nature is active in all ages.</margin>
As soon as she had been well confessed,
Lady Nature the goddess,
As the law requires, now prepares herself;
Genius, the most valiant priest,
Immediately absolves her and gives her
A fitting and good penance.

Genius then formally absolves Nature of her "sins" (her regret over creating mankind) before departing.</summary>

According to the magnitude of the misdeed

By the authority of Nature,

On behalf of the eternal Emperor
Sitting in the sovereign court
Of the noble worldly city,
Of which He made Nature the minister,
Who administers all good things there
Through the influence of the stars;
For everything is ordained by them
According to the imperial laws
Of which Nature is the official,

<column-break/>

Who caused all things to be born
Since the world first came into being,
And likewise gave them a term
Of size and of growth;
Nor did she ever make anything for nothing
Beneath the sky that goes turning
Around the earth without stopping,
As high below as above,
Never ceasing, neither night nor day,
And always turning without rest;
Let them all be excommunicated,
The disloyal and the renegade,
And condemned without any respite,
Who hold [Nature's] works in despite—
Whether they be of high or low birth—
By whom Nature is sustained.
<margin>Note.</margin>
And he who with all his might
Strives to preserve Nature,
And who takes pains to love well
Without any base or villainous thought,

May he go to flourish in Paradise;

I take the entire burden upon myself,

Nature has given misfortune

Styluses, hammers, tablets, anvils <note>These are metaphors for the male and female reproductive organs</note>,

To serve and honor her,
But wish to destroy Nature
When they wish to flee her anvils,
And her tablets, and her fallow fields,
Which she made precious and dear
To continue her creations
So that Death cannot kill them.

Then it should surely please Him
That every other person did the same,

So that He put such grace in them.

☞ That everything would go to perdition.

<margin>Note.</margin>

Why would He not wish it for the others?
What reason shall turn Him from it?
It seems then that He would not care
If the generation failed.
Let him who wishes to answer, sing of it;
I know no more of it, nor do I torment myself.
Let the diviner come who can divine it,
And who never ceases this divining.

Nor can you begin again
Immediately to advance the work;
Do not be weary in your will.
<margin>Cadmus labored the earth.</margin>
Cadmus, at the word of Lady Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva</note>,
Plowed more than an acre of earth
And sowed the teeth of a serpent,
From which armed knights sprang up
Who fought so much among themselves
That all died upon the spot
Except five who became his companions
<margin>Cadmus, founder of Thebes.</margin>
And wished to give him aid
When he had to masonry the walls
Of Thebes, a city of great estates.
They set the stones for him there
And populated his city for him,
Which is of great antiquity.
Cadmus made a very good sowing
When he thus advanced all his people;
You also, now begin well
And advance your lineages.
Thus you have two advantages,
Very great ones, to save your lineages;
If you do not wish to be the third <note>referring to the third Fate, Death</note>,
You have greatly maddened your senses.
You have only a single hindrance;
Defend yourself easily
When assailed from one side.
Three champions are very failing

<margin>Note.</margin>

There are three aids, as well you know,

Who cuts short all lives.
Know that it comforts me much:
<margin>The three goddesses of human life.</margin>
Clotho, who carries the spindle,

But Atropos breaks and tears
What these two are able to spin.
Atropos wishes to prick you;
She who will dig deep
Will wound all your lineages,
And goes about spying on you yourselves,
And then strikes home with her dart.
You have no greater enemies—

<column-break/>

Lords, mercy! Mercy, lords!
Remember your good fathers

Line yourselves up according to their deeds.
Take care that you do not degenerate;
Pay heed to what they have done,
<margin>Note.</margin>
If there is anyone who keeps their prowess.
They defended themselves so well

Had it not been for their knighthood,
You would not now be alive.
They had great pity for you,
Through love and through friendship.
Think of the others who will come

Do not let yourselves be discomfited;
You have grievances, think to describe them.
<margin>Note.</margin>

Think to multiply yourselves,

## The strong excommunication
Genius places upon all people

Through boroughs, castles, and cities,

My word is very virtuous

Fair lords, Nature in her law
Has a very great need for preachers
To chastise all the sinners
Who stray from her rules,
Which they ought to hold and keep.
And if you preach it thus,
You shall never be hindered,
According to my word and my agreement,
Provided that the deed matches the word,
From entering the park of the beautiful field
Where he leads his sheep,
And leads them leaping through the grass:
The Son of the Virgin Sheep <note>An allegorical reference to Christ as the Lamb born of the Virgin.</note>

Afterwards—not in a great crowd,
But in a chosen company—
Through the narrow, serene path
Which is all flowery and grassy,
So little is it trodden or beaten,
Go the little white sheep,
<margin>Note.</margin> Gentle and noble beasts
Who browse and graze upon the grass
And the little flowers that bloom so much.
But know that they have pasture
Of such virtuous nature
That the delectable little flowers
Which grow there fresh and clean—
Which maidens gather in the spring—
Are fresher and more new
Than the flaming stars.
Through the greening grasses
In the early morning in the dew,
They have all day long dawned
With their own native beauties,
Fine colors, fresh and vivid.

<column-break/>

They do not become withered in the evening,
But rather can be gathered there
The same in the evening as in the morning
By whoever puts a hand to the gathering;
For certainly they are never too dry,
Nor too closed, nor too open,
But rather they blaze through the greenery
At the best point of their sweet age;
For the sun rises shining,
Which is not at all harmful to them;
It does not waste away the dews
With which they are all moistened,
But keeps them in fine beauties,
So much does it sweeten their roots.

I tell you that the little sheep
From the trees or from the little flowers
Can never browse so much
That they cannot browse more.
They cannot browse or graze so much
That more must not always be reborn.
I tell you further—do not take it for a fable—
That they are not at all corruptible,
Even though the sheep graze upon them;
The pastures cost them nothing,
For the skins are not sold
At the final lot, nor spent,
Nor is their fleece used to make woolen cloths
Or blankets for strangers.
Never shall they be estranged from them,
Nor shall the flesh be eaten at the end,
Nor corrupted, nor put to ill use,
Nor overtaken by maladies.
But without fail, whatever I say,
I do not say of the Good Shepherd
Who leads them to graze before him
That he is not clothed in their wool;
Yet he does not pluck them at all,
And takes from them neither hair nor feather;
But it pleases him and seems good to him
That his robe resembles theirs.

<margin>The single day of the Future Life is without night.</margin>
I shall say more, and may it not weary you,
That they never saw night born there,
Except for one single day only.

But there is no onset of evening,
Nor can the morning begin there,
No matter how early the dawn advances;
For the evening joins with the morning,
And the morning resembles the evening.
I tell you the same of every hour:
It always remains in one state,
The day that can never turn to night,
No matter how much the night fights against it.
<margin>Eternal things are not measured by time.</margin> For it has no temporal measure,
That day so beautiful which lasts forever
And laughs with present clarity.
It has neither present nor past <note>original: "present ne preterit"</note>,

All three times are present there;
Which "present" encompasses the day,
But it is not a present that passes away
In part to be deserved,

Never was the past present there;
Also I tell you that God willed

For the resplendent sun,
Which is always appearing to them,
Makes the day in one stable point.
They are in an everlasting springtime;
No one ever saw one so beautiful or pure,

### How Jupiter had it preached
### That everyone should take what they held most dear

Jupiter, a man of pleasure.

Jupiter, who rules the world,

# The Romance of the Rose.

<margin>☞</margin>
Thus the years have come forward,
for all things are conquered
by labor and by harsh poverty,
which causes people great anxiety,
for the evils of their minds are stirred
by the anguishes they find there,
as Ovid <note>original: "ouide"; refers to the Roman poet Ovid, whose *Metamorphoses* describes the Four Ages of Man.</note> said, who had
enough throughout the time he lived
of good, of evil, of boredom, and shame,
as he himself recounts.
Truly Jupiter did not intend,
when he aimed to come to earth,
anything but to change the state of the empire
from good to evil, and from evil to worse.
<margin>The year divided into four parts.</margin>
He was a very poor judge,
and he made the springtime shorten,
and divided the year into four parts,
as they are divided at present:
Summer, Autumn, Spring, Winter;
these are the four diverse seasons
that Spring used to hold all for itself,
but Jupiter wanted no more of that,
he who addressed himself to the reign
and surpassed the ages of gold.
<margin>The worsening of people denoted by the change of metals.</margin>
And now he made the ages of silver,
which then were of bronze; for people
never ceased from worsening since then,
so much did they wish to draw toward evil.
From bronze they were changed into iron,
so much have they estranged their conditions,
whereat the gods of the halls are joyful—
halls always dark and dirty—
who have envy toward men
as long as they see them alive.
These gods have attached in their nets—
from which they are never torn away—
<margin>Note.</margin>
The sorrowful black sheep,
weary, wretched, and sickly,
who do not wish to walk the path
that the beautiful lamb presents to them,
by which they would be entirely free,

when they held to the great wide road,

in such a full company

<column-break/>

that it held the entire roadway.
But now no beast that goes in there
will ever bear a fleece of any value,
nor one from which any cloth can be made,
except perhaps some horrible hair-shirt
which is sharper and more stinging
when it is joined to the side
than would be a garment
made of the skins of a shaggy hedgehog.
But what would it be worth to card the wool
which is very soft, smooth, and full,
provided that one had such plenty of it
to make cloths from such a fleece
which would be taken from the white beasts?
Well would they be dressed for feast days,
emperors and kings, truly even angels,
if they clothed themselves in cloths and linens;
whereby you may well know
that whoever could have such a robe
would be most nobly dressed,
and for that very reason
he ought to hold them more dear,
for of such beasts there are but few.
Nor would the shepherd, who is not foolish,
who guards the flock and the enclosures
in this beautiful place—this is a true thing—
ever let a black beast enter there
for anything one could believe.
He so pleases to sort out the white ones
that they are lodged with him,
for they well know the shepherd,
and they are very well known by him,
whereby they are better received for it.
<margin>Note that all these things are said of Paradise, introduced there by the Lamb who is Jesus Christ without blemish.</margin>
I tell you that the most piteous,
the most beautiful, the most delightful
of all the worthy livestock,
is the beautiful leaping little lamb
who leads the sheep to the fold
through his labor and through his pain;
for he well knows if any go astray,
so that the wolf alone might see her,
who seeks nothing else
but that she should leave the path.

# The Romance of the Rose.

The things contained within
Are frivolous and deceptive;
Nothing there is stable,
Everything he describes is corruptible.
He speaks of dances <note>original: "carolles" - circular dances accompanied by singing, typical of courtly love</note> that failed,
And all those who performed them will fail too.
So shall it be for all the things
That he says are enclosed within those walls.
For the nurse of Cerberus <note>A reference to the underworld; here implying the forces of decay</note>,
Whom no human can escape
Without her bringing them to an end
When she chooses to use her strength—
And she uses it always without ceasing—
<margin>Atropos is death.</margin>
Atropos, who laughs at no one and refuses none,
Spies on everyone from behind,
Except for the gods, if any were there;
For without fail, divine things
Are not subject to death.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'M' showing a human face in profile.</image-desc>

But now let us speak of the beautiful things
Enclosed within this fair park.
I speak to you in general terms,
For I wish to move quickly from this topic,
Since I do not know how to speak properly
Of that which is truly right.
<margin>The joys of paradise are unspeakable.</margin>
No man could conceive,
Nor any mouth recount,
The great beauties and the great worth
Of the things contained within;
Nor the beautiful games, nor the great joys,
Which are everlasting and true,
That the dancers there enjoy
And carry out within the enclosure.
These are the delectable things,
All true and everlasting,
When those who enjoy themselves within—
And it is only right, for they all draw
From one great fountain itself,
Which is most precious and healthy,
And beautiful, and clear, and clean, and pure,
Which waters the entire enclosure.
From its stream the animals drink,
Those who wish to enter and ought to,
Once they are cleansed of the black ones <note>Likely referring to the "black sheep" or the impurities of earthly life</note>;
For once they have been watered there,

<column-break/>

<margin>The joys of paradise make the blessed happy forever.</margin>
They shall never be able to feel thirst,
And they shall live as long as they wish
Without being sick or dead.
In a happy hour they entered the gates,
In a happy hour they saw the Lamb <note>The Lamb of God (Christ)</note>,
Whom they followed through the narrow path
Under the guard of the wise Shepherd,
Who wishes to lodge them with him;
Nor would anyone ever die

This is not that fountain beneath the tree
Which shines in the marble stone;
One ought to make a face at him
Since he praises that fountain.
That is the perilous fountain,
So bitter and so poisonous,
Which killed the fair Narcissus
When he gazed at his reflection in it.
And he himself <note>Referring to the author of the earlier part of the poem, Guillaume de Lorris</note> is not ashamed
To recognize it, but rather testifies,
And does not hide its cruelty,
<margin>Note.</margin>

And says that when he looked at himself,
He sighed many times thereafter,
Finding himself so heavy and burdened.
Such an odor does that water seek out—
God, how dull that fountain is!
Where the healthy man soon becomes sick.
How can it be good to look therein
To see one's reflection in the water?
It rises, he says, in great waves
Through two large and deep pipes;
<margin>All things come from God alone.</margin>
But it does not have, I know it well,
Its pipes or its waters from itself;
There is nothing that it holds
That does not come entirely from another.
Then he repeats that it is without end,
That it is clearer than fine silver—
Hear what nonsense he pleads!
<margin>Sensual pleasure blinds people.</margin>
It is so very murky and so ugly
That everyone who puts his head in
To see himself, cannot see a drop.
All become maddened and distressed
Because they do not recognize themselves at all.
At the bottom, he says, are double crystals...

# Leaf 124

Just as the sun, which is never clouded,
Makes all shine when it casts its rays there,
So clearly that he who watches them
Must always see half of the things
That are enclosed within this Orchard.
And as for the rest, now see:
If he wishes to sit on the other side,
They are neither clear nor luminous,
But are troubled and dark,
So that they make no demonstration
When the sun launches its ray there
Of all things together;
For they cannot, it seems to me,
Because of the obscurity that ennobles <note>The poet uses "ennobles" ironically or to mean "envelops" here, referring to the thick darkness of the worldly mirrors.</note> them,
Which is so troubled and so clouded
That they cannot by themselves suffice
For anyone who looks at themselves within.
When they acquire their clarity from elsewhere,
If the rays of the sun do not strike there
So that they might meet them,
They have no power to show anything;
But that one which I describe to you
Is of a much more beautiful design.

Now raise your ears a little,

That fountain of which I spoke,
Which is so beautiful and so profitable,
And heals—so favored is it—
Every languishing beast,

The sweet, clear, and living waters,
Which are so close to one another
That they all seem as one.
So that when you see them all,
You will find both one and three there;
If you wish to amuse yourself with the count,
You will never find four there;
<margin>The fountain of divine essence.</margin> But always three and always one—
That is their common prosperity.
For it springs out of itself.
These are not like other fountains
Which spring through foreign veins;
For this one conducts itself by itself,

<column-break/>

And holds itself entirely living,
Firmer than natural rock.
It has no need of marble stone,

<margin>God is eternal.</margin> For from a source so high comes
The water, which can never fail,
That no tree can reach so high

This olive tree, while standing,

"Here runs the Fountain of Life

<margin>The inscription of the Fountain of Life.</margin> Which bears the fruit of salvation,
Which is the pine <note>The poet suggests the Olive of Grace surpasses the Pine of Nature/Narcissus.</note> that was worth it."

Foolish people will hardly believe it,
And many will hold it as a fable—
