# The Romance of the Rose.

There shines a carbuncle <note>A "carbuncle" is a legendary deep-red gemstone, often a ruby or garnet, believed in the Middle Ages to emit its own light.</note> more marvelous
Than all other wondrous stones;
It casts all its rays in three directions <note>original: "a trois esquierres" - likely a reference to the Trinity.</note>
And is set within so high
That one sees it clearly
Flashing throughout the entire park;
Neither can its rays be diverted,
Nor by wind, nor rain, nor weakness,
So beautiful it is and of great nobility.
And know that each individual stone—
Such is the power of the gem—
Is worth as much as the other two;
Such are the strengths between them,
That the two are worth no more than the one,
Though each one is beautiful;
No one can divide them,
No matter how well one observes them,
Nor join them so cleverly
That they are not found to be distinct.
But no sun illuminates it,
No matter how fine its clarity,
So beautiful and resplendent;
For the brightening sun,
Which in the other water <note>Referring to the Fountain of Narcissus in the earthly garden.</note> doubles the crystals,
Would seem dark and dim beside this one.
Alas, what more should I tell you?
There is no other sun within
Than this flaming carbuncle;
It is the beautiful sun they have in there,
Which abounds with more radiance
Than any sun that exists in the world;
For it sends the night into exile
And creates the day of which I spoke,
<margin>The divine meaning is eternal.</margin>
Which lasts everlastingly
Without end and without beginning,
And holds itself at a single point
Without passing through any sign or degree <note>A reference to the zodiac; unlike the physical sun, this light does not move through the constellations.</note>;
Without diminishing any part
By which it could be divided.
It has such marvelous power
That those who go there to see it,
As soon as they turn toward that place
And see their faces reflected in that water,
Always, from wherever they may be,
They see all the things in the park

<column-break/>

And know them truly,
And themselves likewise;
And once they have seen themselves within,
Never again will they be deceived
By anything that might exist,
So wise a master does each become.
<margin>All things are seen in God.</margin>

**V**ery marvelous things I shall tell you
That I shall read concerning this sun:
It does not trouble nor hinder
The eyes of him who looks upon it,
Nor does it make them dazzled;
But rather strengthens and rejoices them,
And now reinvigorates their sight
By its beautiful clarity and vision,
Full of temperate warmth,
Which by marvelous value
Fills the entire park of God
Through the great sweetness that issues from it.
And so that I do not keep you too long,
I want you to remember one brief word:
It is that he who could truly describe
The form and matter of this narrow park <note>original: "parc detroit" - likely meaning the enclosed or sacred space.</note>

<margin>Note.</margin>
For God's sake, lords, what then do you think

Give your true judgment on them,
Both of their accidents and their substance <note>Technical terms from Aristotelian philosophy: "substance" is the essential nature, "accidents" are the outward characteristics.</note>.

Which one is of greater beauty?

Which one yields the healthier waters,
More virtuous and more pure?

<margin>The olive tree, always green, signifies Jesus Christ.</margin>

Folio 195.

If you wish to do any wrong there,
To speak falsely and hide the truth,
I will not hide it from you—
I would speak of it elsewhere in my own words.
But to bring you to agreement sooner,
I wish to briefly record for you,
According to what I have recounted,
Their great value and their goodness.
One purifies the living from death,
And this one makes one drunk with death.
<margin>Note.</margin> Lords, know certainly,
If you conduct yourselves wisely
And do what you ought,
You shall drink from this fountain.
And to retain all my teaching
More easily—
For a lesson read in brief words
Is better remembered—
Therefore I wish to briefly recount
All that you must do.

<margin>Instruction from the author to serve and love God well.</margin> Think to honor Nature;
Serve her by honoring her well.
And if you have anything belonging to another,
Return it if you know to whom;
And if you cannot return it,
And have spent the goods,
Have the will to return it.
If goods come to you in plenty,
Let no one approach murder.
Have both hands and mouth clean;
Be loyal, be piteous;
Then you shall go to the delightful field,
Following the Lamb <note>A reference to Christ, the Lamb of God, following the path of salvation.</note> by his tracks,
Living in eternity,
Drinking from the beautiful fountain
Which is so pure, clear, and healthy;
For you shall never receive death
As soon as you have drunk the water;
Rather, you shall go with joy,
Singing in eternity
Motets, rondels, and little songs
Through the green grass beneath the flowers,
Dancing beneath the olive tree.
Why should I keep piping to you?

<column-break/>

It is right that I stop my flute,
For fine singing often becomes tedious.
<margin>Note.</margin> I could keep you here too long,
Wherefore I must finish my sermon.
It will well appear what you will do
When you are up high again
To preach well from the battlement <note>The "breteche" refers to a wooden gallery or pulpit on a fortification; here it refers to the siege of the Castle of Jealousy.</note>.

### ¶ The Author.

¶ Genius preaches to them just so,
And throws the candle into the square,
Which was not made of virgin wax,
Whose smoke-filled flame
Is lit throughout the whole world.
There is no lady who could defend herself from it,
So well did Venus know how to spread it.
She seized the senses so highly
That all living women,
Their bodies, their hearts, and their thoughts,
Are perfumed with that odor.
Love, having thus read the charter,
Has spread the news so far
That there is never a man of valor
Who does not agree with the sentence.
When Genius had read everything,
All the barons had joy from it;
They were joyful together;
Each one behaved happily,
For never, as they said,
Had they heard such a good sermon,
Nor since they were conceived
Had they received such great pardons,
Nor had they received likewise
Such a direct excommunication <note>In this satirical context, Genius excommunicates those who do not practice procreation.</note>.
So that they do not lose the pardon,
All cling to the sentence
And respond quickly and loudly:
Amen, amen; let it be done, let it be done <note>original: "Amen amen/fiat fiat"</note>.
As the matter stands at this point,
There is no delay;
Each one notes the sermon well,
Word for word above all else,
For it seemed to them very saving
Because of the good, charitable pardon;
And they heard it very willingly.
Genius has vanished.

Keep check on your hands and mouth.
Be loyal; be piteous;

Living in eternity,

As soon as you have drunk the water;
Rather, near it, through joyfulness,
Singing in eternity
☛ Motets, rondeaux, and little songs
Upon the green grass beneath the flowers,

For fine singing often becomes wearying.
<margin>Note.</margin>

¶ Genius preaches to them just so,

It caught the winds so high

Their bodies, their hearts, and their thoughts—

Love, having thus read the charter,
Has spread the news so far

They were joyful together;
Each one behaved happily,

Nor had they received likewise

So that they do not lose the pardon,
All cling to the sentence

Amen, amen; let it be done, let it be done <note>original: "fiat fiat"</note>.
As the matter stands at this point,
There is no delay;
Each one notes the sermon well,
Word for word above all else,
For it seemed to them very saving
Because of the good, charitable pardon;
And they very willingly heard it.
Genius vanished away.

There shines a marvelous carbuncle <note>original: "charboucle"; a deep red gemstone, often a garnet or ruby, believed in the Middle Ages to emit its own light</note>

# The Romance of the Rose.

They never knew what became of him,
Of which there were more than twenty in the host.
Now to the assault without further delay!
To anyone who truly understands the meaning,
Our enemies are greatly burdened.
Then they all rose up as one,
Ready to continue the war,
To take everything and raze it to the ground.

Venus now prepares herself in front;
As if to catch the wind,
She lifted her robe before her
And descended toward the castle.
She went faster than a walking pace
To the site, but she did not enter yet.
Venus, who is ready to attack,
First admonishes them
That they should surrender. Do you know what they did?
<margin>Fear and Shame prevent them from doing many evils.</margin>
Fear and Shame answered her:
"Certainly, Venus, this is all for nothing,
For you shall never set foot in here."
"Even if there were only me,"
Said Shame, "I am not dismayed by it."
When the goddess heard Shame:
"Vile, filthy wench, what possesses you,"
She said, "to oppose me?
You shall soon be stormed
If the castle is not surrendered to me.
It shall not be defended against me;
Against me, you shall not hold it.
Certainly, you will surrender it,
Or I will burn you all alive
Like miserable and wretched things.
I wish to set the whole enclosure ablaze
And level the towers and turrets.
I will scorch your buttocks!
I will burn pillars, walls, and beams,
And your moats shall be conquered;
I will have them filled and leveled.
Your fortified outworks <note>original: "barbacanes" — defensive outposts of a castle</note>,
No matter how high they are built,
I will stretch them out upon the ground.
I will let Fair Welcome <note>The personification of the lady's receptiveness</note> take everything—
Buds and roses in abundance,
One hour for sale and the other as a gift."

<column-break/>

"Nor shall you ever be so proud
That the whole world will not trust in it;
All shall go in procession,
Without making any exception,
Through the rosebushes and the roses,
Once I have broken open the barriers.

And to deceive Jealousy,
I will cause everything to be trampled,
Both the meadows and the grasses.
I will so enlarge the passages
That everyone will gather there without delay—
Buds and roses, both cleric and layman,
Monk and secular man alike;
No one could hold themselves back.
All shall do their penance there,
But not without a great difference:
Some will come there secretly,
And others openly.
But those who serve Venus secretly
Will be considered men of integrity;
The others will be defamed
And called ribald brothel-goers,
Even though they are no more guilty
Than those whom no one blames.
Yet it is true that some wicked men—
Whom God and the Holy Father of Rome <note>The Pope</note>
Confound, they and their business—
Will leave the roses to do worse things,
And the devils who incite them
Shall give them a hat of nettles.
<margin>Genius is the god of generation, to be well understood.</margin>
For Genius, on behalf of Nature,
Because of their vice and their filth,
Has placed them all under sentence
Along with our other enemies.
Shame, if I do not outwit you,
I prize my art and skill but little,
And I shall never claim them again.
Certainly, I shall not love you,
Nor your mother, Reason,
Who is so bitter to lovers.
Whoever believed you and your mother
Would never, I believe, have joy."
Venus did not strive to say more,
For that was enough for her.

**V**enus then remembered her purpose,
Looking much like an angered woman.
She strings her bow and notches the firebrand.
When the cord was set in the notch,
She draws the bow back to her ear—
The bow is no longer than a fathom <note>original: "toyse" (toise), a measurement of about 6 feet</note>—
Then, like a skilled archeress,
Through a very small arrow-slit
Which she saw situated in the tower,
Positioned in front and not to the side,
Which Nature had, with great mastery,
Seated between two beautiful pillars.
The beautiful pillars were of ivory,
Very noble, and they supported with silver
A beautiful image in place of a shrine.
<margin><note>A hand-drawn pointer (manicule) indicates the following description.</note></margin>
It was neither too high nor too low,
Neither too thick nor too slender, not at all,
But well-proportioned by the compass,
In arms, shoulders, and hands,
Lacking nothing, neither more nor less.
The other limbs were very noble,
And smelled sweeter than ambergris apples <note>Scented pomanders used for perfume and health.</note>.
Inside was a sanctuary
Covered with a precious shroud,
The most gentle and the most noble
That exists as far as Constantinople.
And if anyone, speaking with reason,
Wished to make a comparison
Of an image to another well-portrayed,
He could compare it to the one
That Pygmalion once made,
As one compares a cat to a lion.

### ¶ Here begins the story
### Of the statue of Pygmalion.

**P**ygmalion was a carver,
The best at portraying in iron,
And similarly in stones,
Wood, and with other tools,
In metals, bone, and wax,
And in all other materials
That can be found for such work.
And to test his skill,

<column-break/>

And also to amuse himself,
He made an image of ivory,
And put such focus into the making
That it was so pleasant and noble
That it seemed to be as alive
As the most beautiful living thing.
Never Helen nor Lavinia <note>Helen of Troy and Lavinia (from the Aeneid), classical standards of beauty.</note>
Were of such fine complexion,
Nor born of such beautiful fashion,
However well-formed they were;
They had not a tenth of her beauty.
All his senses were stunned by it
As he looks at her more and more;
And he, who was not on his guard,
Love entangles him in his nets,
So that he knows not what to do,
And he complains to himself,
But cannot stop his lament.
"Alas, what am I doing?" he says, "Must I?
Many images have I made and forged
Whose value no one could name,
Yet I was never overtaken by love for them.
Now I am poorly treated because of this one;
Because of it, all my senses have failed me.
Alas, from where does this thought come to me?
Where was it taken or conceived?
I love a deaf and mute image
Which neither stirs nor moves,
<margin>Pygmalion in love with his stone image.</margin>
And will never have mercy on me.
How will such a love affect me?
For there is no one who hears of it
Who would not be completely amazed.
Indeed, I am the greatest fool in the world;
What can I do in this situation?
For if it were any queen ever,
At least I might hope for mercy
Because that is a possible thing;
But this love is too horrible,
For it does not come from Nature.
I am behaving too wickedly toward myself;
Nature has a bad son in me.
When she made me, she failed greatly—
Yet I must not blame her.
If I wish to love foolishly,
I must blame no one but myself."

# The Romance of the Rose.

Since my name is Pygmalion.
Since I was first able to walk on my feet
I never heard tell of such a love.
Yet do I love too foolishly?
For if the scripture <note>original: "escripture"; likely referring to Ovid's Metamorphoses or general literary tradition</note> does not lie,
Many have loved more foolishly.
Did not Narcissus love—by the leafy woods
At the clear and pure fountain—
His own reflection?
When he thought to quench his thirst,
He could never recover himself
So that he did not die of it, according to the story
Which is still of great memory.
Therefore, I am at least less foolish;
For when I wish, I go to her,
And I take her, and embrace her, and kiss her,
By which I better endure my unease.
But that man could not have the one
Whom he saw in the little fountain.
On the other hand, in many lands,
Many lovers have loved ladies
<margin>☞</margin> And served them as best they could,
And yet never had a single kiss from them.
Thus they have suffered greatly for it,
Wherefore Love has treated me better.
No, he has not! For despite any doubt,
They have, at all times, hope
Both of kisses and other things,
From which hope is not excluded,
Regarding the delight that those expect
Who seek the pleasures of love.
But when I wish to settle myself
To embrace and to kiss,
I find my beloved as stiff
As a stake, and just as cold;
And when I touch her to kiss her,
My whole mouth grows cold.
<margin>☞</margin> Ha! I have spoken too foolishly!
I ask mercy of my sweet lady,
And pray that you accept my penance;
For as much as you deign
To look at me sweetly and laugh,
That should be quite enough for me;
For sweet looks and piteous smiles
Are very delightful to lovers.

### How Pygmalion asks for pardon while presenting penance to his image for the ugly and foolish words he spoke of her.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'P' depicting a man in 15th-century attire kneeling in prayer or supplication before a statue on a pedestal within an interior setting.</image-desc>

Pygmalion then kneels down
And wets his face with tears;
He offers his pledge and makes amends,
But she cares nothing for the penance;
For she neither hears nor feels
Him, nor any of his gifts,
So that he fears greatly he loses his labor,
He who struggles to love such a thing.
Nor does he know how to recover his heart,
For Love takes away all sense and knowledge,
So that he is entirely comforted by nothing,
Nor does he know if she is alive or dead.
Often he goes to her, and feels her,
And it seems to him as if she were dough,
That it is her flesh that he touches,
But it is only his hand pressing against her.
Thus Pygmalion struggles,
And his strife has neither peace nor truce;
He does not remain in one state:
Now he loves, now he hates, now he laughs, now he weeps,
Now he is joyful, now he is uneasy,
Now he torments himself, now he calms down.
Then he dresses her in many fashions,
In robes made with great designs
Of beautiful cloths of silk and wool,
Of scarlet, of linsey-woolsey <note>term: "tiretaine" - a coarse fabric made of wool mixed with flax or cotton</note>,

He has placed many rich furs upon her:
Ermine, variegated, and gray furs.
Then he takes them off and tries again
To see how a silk robe suits her,
Sendals <note>term: "cendaulx" - a thin, rich silk fabric</note>, fine fabrics, dark cloths,

Satins, cloths of Ypres, and camlets <note>term: "camelotz" - a costly fabric made of camel hair or angora</note>.
She truly looks like a little angel,
So simple is her countenance.
At other times he puts a wimple <note>term: "guimple" - a cloth covering the neck and sides of the face</note> on her,
And over it a kerchief
Which covers the wimple and the head.

But he does not cover her face,
For he does not wish to follow the custom
Of the Saracens <note>original: "sarrafins"; a medieval term for Muslims, here referring to the practice of veiling</note> who with thin fabrics <note>original: "destamines"; a lightweight wool or cotton weave</note>

Where maidens run with hammers

With a well-sharpened needle

Of fine gold, elegantly threaded,

Which he himself blows and plays well,

Motets of treble or of tenor;
Then he sets his care to the chiming bells;
Then he takes pipes and whistles.

# The Romance of the Rose.

Whoever experiences misfortune will never
Truly know how to seek the good;
And he who knows not what shame amounts to
Will never be able to recognize it.
No one ever knew what ease is
If he has not first learned unease.
<margin>☞</margin> Nor is he worthy of having ease
Who does not wish to know hardship;
And he who cannot suffer it well,
No one should offer him comfort.

<margin>Opposite things are better understood when seen together.</margin>

One serves as a commentary <note>original: "gloses" - glosses or explanations</note> on the other.

Must remember the other,
Or else, by no intention,

Will never make a distinction between them,
Without which no definition
That one makes can take place.

<column-break/>

I fully intended to thrust the end into it,
But it springs back and I push again.
Nothing avails; it always refuses,
It will not enter for anything;
For I found a fence in front
Which I feel well, though I do not see it,
With which the aperture was reinforced
From the moment it was first founded,
Which was near the border;
It was stronger and more secure for it.
Often I had to assail it,
Often strike, often fail.
If you could see the jousting there—
Provided you took good notice—
You might remember Hercules
When he wanted to dismember Cacus:
Three times he assailed the door,
Three times he struck, three times he failed.
<margin>Note.</margin> Three times he sat in the valley,
Quite weary from his effort,
So much did he suffer pain and labor.
And I, who labor so much here,
Who sweats all over with anguish
When I do not immediately break this fence,
We are as tired, or more so,
As Hercules, and quite a bit more.
I have struck so much that finally
I perceived a narrow path
Through which I thought to pass beyond;
But the fence had to be broken.

<margin>☞</margin> By the path I have mentioned,
Which was so narrow and small,
Through which I then had the passage,
I broke the fence with my staff
And placed it inside the aperture;
But I did not enter even halfway.
I was sorrowful that I did not enter further,
But I could do nothing else;
Yet for nothing would I leave off
Until I had passed the whole staff
Through the passage without delay;
But the scrip remains outside,
Where the rebellious hammers <note>A metaphor for testicles.</note>
Were hanging outside.

<summary>The Lover reaches the inner sanctuary and uses the metaphor of a pilgrim approaching a shrine to describe his sexual encounter with the Rose. He compares his struggle to enter the "narrow path" to the mythological labor of Hercules fighting Cacus.</summary>
<keywords>pilgrimage, allegory, Hercules and Cacus, courtly love, sexual metaphor, relics, pilgrim's staff</keywords>

--- Page 271 ---
<meta>This page continues the Lover's final approach to the rosebud, marking the climax of the allegorical journey. The language is rich in the double entendres characteristic of Jean de Meun’s conclusion to the Roman de la Rose.</meta>

# Leaf 136

And I was put in such great distress,
I found the passage so narrow
That it was not with much room
That I crossed through the pass.
<margin>Note.</margin> And I know the nature of the pass so well,
No one had ever passed through it before,
For I passed through it as the very first.
The place was not yet accustomed
To receiving travelers.
I know not if it later offered the same advantage
To others as it did to me;
But I tell you truly that I loved it so much
That I could never believe <note>The Lover suggests he was so blinded by love he could not believe any ill of the place.</note>
Even if it were a true thing;
For no one easily believes ill of a thing they love,
<margin>Note.</margin> No matter how much it is defamed.
Nor do I believe it even now;
But I know well at least that then
It was neither worn nor beaten down,
And therefore I cast myself into it,
Because there is no other entry point
To gather the bud <note>original: "bourdon" - literally a pilgrim's staff, but here used as a phallic metaphor for the act of gathering the rose.</note> at the right moment.
Now you shall know how I behaved
When I held the bud to my liking;
You shall hear the deed and the manner,
So that in your need, if it concerns you,
<margin>☞</margin> When the sweet season shall come,
Gallant lords, when it shall be necessary
That you go to gather the roses,
Both the open and the closed ones,
That you go there so wisely
That you do not fail in the gathering.
Do as you shall hear me recount,
Unless you know a better way to succeed;
For if much more easily,
Or better, or more subtly,
You can cross the passage
Without staining or wearying yourself,
Then pass it according to your whim.
When you have learned my custom,
You have at least this much advantage:
That I teach you my practice
Without taking anything of your wealth,
For which you should be grateful to me.
When I was there engaged,

<column-break/>

I had approached the rosebush so closely
<margin>☞</margin> That at my will I could stretch my hand
To the branch to take the bud.
Fair Welcome <note>original: "Bel Acueil" - the personification of the lady's receptivity.</note> begged me earnestly
That no outrage be committed there,
And I gave him my firm promise,
Because he prayed me so often,
That I would never do anything there
Except his will and my own.

->The conclusion of the romance<-
->Is that you see here the Lover<-
->Who takes the rose at his pleasure<-
->In which was all his desire.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration framed by decorative floral corners. It depicts the Lover in a tunic and hat standing in a landscape with rolling hills and a sun. He is reaching with his right hand toward a stylized rosebush with a single prominent bloom.</image-desc>

By the branches I seized the rosebush,
<margin>☞</margin> Which was more supple than any willow;
And when I could join both my hands there,
Very softly and without pricking myself,
I began to shake the bud;
For I could hardly have it without shaking.
I made all the branches
Tremble and move to shake them out,
Without ever breaking any of the large ones,
For I did not wish to wound anything there;
And yet I was forced by necessity
To cut a little of the bark,
For I knew no other way to have
That for which I had such great desire.
->In the end, I tell you this much:<-
That I scattered a little seed there
When I had shaken the bud;
That was when I had touched the inside
To turn back the little leaves,
For I wished to search everything
Down to the bottom of the little bud.

<summary>The Lover reaches the rosebush and, after promising Fair Welcome to be gentle, successfully gathers the rosebud. The passage uses the metaphor of gardening and pilgrimage to describe the physical consummation of the Lover's quest.</summary>
<keywords>Roman de la Rose, Jean de Meun, The Lover, Fair Welcome, allegory, courtly love, erotic metaphor, rosebud, consummation</keywords>

--- Page 272 ---
<meta>This page concludes the narrative of the Romance of the Rose, following the Lover's successful entry into the sanctuary to pluck the rosebud. It maintains the allegorical tone of the previous sections.</meta>

# The Romance of the Rose.

As it seemed to me that it was good,
I then caused the seeds to be so mingled
That they could hardly be disentangled,
So that I caused the whole tender bud
To enlarge and extend;
I took everything that I could force out/
But I was so successful in what I did
That he never felt any ill-will toward me,
The sweet one <note>Referring to Fair Welcome (Bel Accueil), the personification of the lady's receptivity</note> who thought no evil there,
But rather allowed and suffered me to do
Whatever he knew would please me;
Yet he reminds me of the covenant
That I had behaved unsuitably toward him,
And was too outrageous, so he says/
But he puts up no further opposition
To my taking, giving, and gathering
Rosebushes and branches, flowers and leaves.

<margin>Conclusion of the Romance</margin>
When I saw myself in such a high degree,
Having so nobly enjoyed myself
That my deed was no longer in doubt,
So that I might be firm and agreeable
Toward all my benefactors,
As good debtors ought to do/
For I was greatly beholden to them,
Because through them I had become
So rich that, to tell the truth,
Wealth <note>The personification Richesse</note> was not so rich as I.

To the God of Love and to Venus,
Who helped me more than anyone;
To Fair Welcome and to my friends,
Who have been such good friends to me;

<column-break/>

Then to all the barons of the host <note>The army of Love that besieged the castle</note>
Whom I pray God does not remove
From the aid of true lovers;
Amidst the savory kisses
I rendered thanks ten or twenty times/
But of Reason I had no memory,
Who wasted her efforts so much on me;
Despite the villainous Riches,
Who never showed any pity
When she refused me entry
To the path she was guarding;
She did not guard herself against this step
By which I have come in here,
Secretly, with small leaps,
Despite my mortal enemies
Who were so far set back;
<margin><note>A small decorative floral or pointing-hand symbol</note></margin>
Especially Jealousy,
With her crown of marigolds <note>original: "soufie" (souci), a flower symbolizing anxiety or jealousy</note>,
Who guards the rose from lovers;
She keeps a very good watch over it now!
Before I stirred from that place,
Where I would have gladly remained,
With great joy I gathered
The flower of the beautiful leafy rosebush;
Thus I had the vermilion rose.
At that moment it was day, and I awoke.

---

¶ End of the Romance of the Rose,
seen and corrected/ and newly
printed at Paris the 9th day of
June, the year 1531.

<summary>The Lover successfully plucks the rose, thanks his allegorical allies while mocking his enemies like Jealousy and Reason, and finally awakens from his dream. This page contains the 1531 Paris colophon marking the end of the printed edition.</summary>
<keywords>Romance of the Rose, Venus, Fair Welcome, Jealousy, allegory, courtly love, dream vision, Paris printing 1531, colophon</keywords>

->J. LE CONTE, <term>GILDER</term><note>original: "DOR." — an abbreviation for *doreur*, the artisan specialist who applies gold leaf to leather bindings. J. Le Conte was a highly regarded practitioner of this craft in 19th-century France.</note><-

This exquisite <term>binding</term><note>original: "reliure"</note> is crafted from deep red <term>morocco leather</term><note>A high-quality goatskin leather known for its visible grain and durability, favored for luxury books.</note>. The cover is adorned with a <term>semé</term><note>A French term meaning "sown," referring to a decorative pattern where small motifs—in this case, rose sprigs—are repeated at regular intervals across the surface like seeds in a field.</note> pattern of gold-tooled roses. Each individual sprig consists of a central blooming rose, two smaller buds, and several leaves on a stem, arranged in a precise grid across the central field.

The composition is enclosed within a multi-line gold border featuring several thin <term>fillets</term><note>Plain decorative lines stamped into the leather.</note> and a decorative outer edge in the <term>dentelle</term><note>A lace-like decorative border style.</note> style. At the very bottom center, just inside the border, the artisan's signature is stamped in gold.
